#3280. Microsoft is winding down its deal to rent AI computing from Oracle

The rented servers ran older Nvidia chips, and Microsoft is rethinking billions in outside cloud deals.

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Microsoft is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle after declining to renew it, Bloomberg reports. The servers ran older Nvidia chips. Microsoft is reassessing more than $80B in contracts with outside cloud providers.

Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI computing power from Oracle, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Microsoft has been switching off the rented capacity in recent months after deciding not to renew the contract.

The servers ran older Nvidia chips and no longer matched what Microsoft needed, the people said. Ageing hardware is a growing worry: Gartner has warned that much AI infrastructure spending could face large write-downs as newer chips arrive.

The deal, announced in 2023, gave Microsoft Oracle servers to run its AI-powered Bing search, and Bloomberg could not determine its full size. Separate talks for Microsoft to lease more Oracle capacity collapsed in June, Business Insider reported.

Microsoft declined to comment. Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for older chips, and its shares fell about 3%.

Microsoft has committed more than $80B to rent capacity from other cloud firms such as CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius. Its leaders have grown frustrated with their costs and delays, Bloomberg said. This week, it reportedly turned down an option to expand a Nscale deal in Texas, weeks after pulling out of a Nscale site in the UK.

The news adds to Oracle’s troubles. Heavy spending on AI data centres has pushed its free cash flow negative and its credit rating to one notch above junk. Its shares have more than halved since a June peak.

#3279. Dauch Corporation (DCH) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Synergies beat the year-end target early, but inflation pressures reshaped the full-year outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Dauch Corporation (DCH +2.26%) reported third quarter results that included a full three-month contribution from the Dowlais acquisition closed in Feb. 2026. Management reported that the company achieved a $100 million run rate for synergies ahead of its year-end target and adjusted its full-year guidance to reflect inflationary pressures and production volatility at select customers. The company stated that it secured new business for high-margin components on European luxury SUV and military vehicle programs while prioritizing debt reduction to achieve a long-term leverage target below 2.0x.

Operator: Good morning, everyone. My name is Jamie, and I will be your conference facilitator today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to the Dauch Corporation Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. I would now like to turn the floor over to Mr. David Lim, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead, Mr. Lim.

David Lim: Thank you, and good morning. I'd like to welcome everyone who is joining us on Dauch Corporation's third quarter earnings call. Earlier this morning, we released our third quarter of 2026 earnings announcement. You can access this announcement on the Investor Relations page of our website, www.dauch.com, and through the PR Newswire services. You can also find supplemental slides for this conference call on the Investor page of our website as well. A replay of this call will be available through November 13. Replay details are in today's press release. In addition, I want to remind the investment community that we will be hosting a Capital Markets Day on November 17 in New York City.

At the event, the leadership team will discuss what differentiates Dauch Corporation and share our vision. The formal presentation will begin at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time, and it will be webcasted. Please mark your calendars. Now before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that the matters discussed in this call may contain comments and forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties, which cannot be predicted or quantified and which may cause future activities and results of operations to differ materially from those discussed. For additional information, please reference Slide 2 of our investor presentation or the press release that was issued today. Also, during this call, we may refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures.

Information regarding these non-GAAP measures, as well as a reconciliation of the non-GAAP measures to GAAP financial information is available in the presentation. With that, let me turn things over to our Chairman and CEO, David Dauch.

David Dauch: Thank you, David, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today to discuss Dauch's financial reports for the third quarter of 2026. Joining me on the call today is Chris May, our Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer; and Senior Vice President, Nathan Iles, who will assume the role of CFO on December 1. So let's begin. Despite production volatility and rising input costs, we generated strong cash flow in the quarter while supporting new program launches. At the same time, we are making excellent progress on our synergy realization. 9 months into the combination, it is increasingly clear that we have created a stronger company.

We have greater scale, broader customer relationships, a more diversified geographic footprint and a significantly expanded product portfolio. These advantages are helping us navigate market volatility while positioning us to create substantial long-term value for stakeholders. As for today's agenda, I'll review the highlights of our third quarter financial performance. Next, I'll touch on our synergy progress, some business updates and commentary about the industry and provide guidance, which we announced last week. I will then turn the call over to Chris to cover the details of our financial results, after which we will take any questions that you all may have. Now for the details.

The company's third quarter 2026 sales were approximately $2.9 billion and adjusted earnings per share was $0.22 per share, and adjusted free cash flow was approximately $127 million. In the third quarter, global production declined approximately 2% and North America production declined approximately 5% year-over-year. However, Europe increased approximately 1%. Against that backdrop, we did benefit from good performance on key GM crossover and Land Rover utility vehicle programs. That stated, we experienced lower Ram Heavy Duty volumes, which declined approximately 15% year-over-year in the third quarter, as well as the impact of major launch activity underway at GM for its large pickup truck program with planned downtime realized both in September and in early October.

From a profitability perspective, our adjusted EBITDA in the third quarter was $358 million or 12.3% of sales, driven by performance and Dowlais contribution. Chris will provide more details about our overall financial performance during the prepared remarks. Next, on Slide 5, I'd like to share an update on our synergy and value capture progress. We have now been operating for nearly 3 full quarters as a combined company, and we have already realized $100 million of run rate synergies and savings to date. As such, we will clearly deliver on our goal or more than $100 million of run rate synergies by year-end.

We have made excellent progress in optimizing our SG&A, and we've reduced duplicative corporate costs, and we continue to capture global engineering efficiencies. We continue to gain positive momentum on our operational synergies while we are navigating purchasing opportunities in today's challenged macro environment. As communicated earlier, these 2 categories, by nature, will take more time to realize their full potential from a synergy standpoint. Turning to business development. Among the businesses that we won in the quarter, I want to particularly highlight 2 important wins that reflect the strength of our product technologies, but also more -- our more diverse customer base.

We secured the next-generation business for propshafts, sideshafts and electronic limited slip differentials on a premier European luxury SUV program that is expected to run deep into the 2030 period of time. Within next-generation business remains a core strategy, reflecting the strength of our customer relationships, the competitive value proposition and our proven execution. Beyond our incumbent positions, we will continue to aggressively pursue new and incremental conquest opportunities to drive profitable growth. In addition, we also secured sideshaft content for an infantry squad vehicle program, demonstrating our technology portfolio extends well beyond traditional passenger vehicles.

The sideshaft product on this platform is a very unique product because it's engineered to provide power to the wheels under extreme drive angles and conditions. We are very proud to be on this program to deliver high-quality, highly engineered products that can support traditional automotive markets as well as adjacent markets. Now let's talk about the industry. In the third quarter, we began to experience additional inflationary pressures across the supply chain, driven in part by significantly higher fuel prices versus last year. As you all know, energy is an important driver for our industry, both as an input cost, but also consumer demand.

Production volatility has increased across select customers and supply chain challenges are beginning to become more apparent, especially with some of the Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers. That stated, we can't control these factors and do not know when they will abate, but we can control how we respond. We've managed through challenging environments before, and we'll continue to do so by flexing our variable cost structure, driving productivity and optimizing our operations. In addition, we'll work to mitigate these inflationary costs. Shifting to our full year guidance, which we provided on October 30. Here's the update.

Sales now in the range of $10.8 billion to $10.875 billion, adjusted EBITDA in the range of $1.35 billion to $1.375 billion and adjusted free cash flow of approximately $270 million to $310 million. In summary, we had a solid quarter and delivered strong operating cash flow. The Dowlais integration is on track and making good progress. We are ahead of schedule in achieving our year 1 synergy target of greater than $100 million. While near-term industry headwinds exist, we are confident in our ability to navigate these challenges and even more confident in the long-term strength and cash-generating power of our business.

So now let me turn the call over to our Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Chris May, for the financial details. Chris?

Chris May: Thank you, David, and good morning, everyone. I will cover the financial details of our third quarter 2026 results and our updated guidance with you today. I will also refer to the earnings slide deck as part of my prepared comments. In the third quarter of 2026, our sales were $2.91 billion as compared to $1.51 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Slide 8 shows a walk of third quarter 2025 sales to third quarter 2026 sales. For legacy Dauch, sales were up slightly year-over-year to $1.52 billion from $1.51 billion last year. Volume, mix and other was lower by approximately $15 million.

However, this was more than offset by metal market pass-throughs and FX, which increased sales by approximately $33 million, driven primarily by increasing metal market pass-throughs. Dowlais contributed $1.41 billion in gross sales for the third quarter. Versus last year, volume, mix and other decreased sales by approximately $26 million. The sale of certain businesses decreased sales by approximately $35 million and metal markets and FX decreased sales by approximately $8 million. Overall, we experienced lower production on the Ram Heavy Duty program on both a year-over-year and sequential basis and also on certain other Stellantis crossover programs versus last year. These were partially offset by GM's full-size light-duty truck volumes and Land Rover programs that we support.

Now let's move on to adjusted EBITDA. For the third quarter of 2026, adjusted EBITDA was $358.5 million and adjusted EBITDA margin was 12.3% versus $195.7 million and 13.0% last year. You can see a year-over-year walk down of adjusted EBITDA on Slide 9. In the quarter, adjusted EBITDA for legacy Dauch was $193 million versus $196 million last year. Volume mix and other decreased EBITDA by approximately $10 million. This was partially offset by approximately $8 million in net favorable performance. While we incurred increasing headwinds due to some challenged suppliers and the impacts of inflation, we did have year-over-year improvement in our Metal Forming segment as well as lower SG&A costs.

Legacy Dowlais contributed approximately $140 million of adjusted EBITDA during the quarter. Versus the third quarter of last year, volume, mix and other increased EBITDA by approximately $3 million and performance and other increased EBITDA by approximately $4 million. This was more than offset by approximately $30 million from onetime commercial settlements that Dowlais recognized in 2025 and $5 million from the sale of certain businesses that I discussed earlier in my sales commentary and the impact of approximately $6 million from metals and FX. In the third quarter, we grew our realized synergy benefit momentum with a positive $25 million in savings as we continue to eliminate duplicative corporate and SG&A costs, realized engineering and indirect purchasing efficiencies.

As David highlighted, we have already realized $100 million of run rate savings to date, and we will, therefore, achieve our goal of more than $100 million run rate savings by the end of the year. We have a great market basket of potential savings that we continue to drive to completion. So let's move on to interest and taxes. Net interest expense was $80.9 million in the third quarter of 2026 compared to $35.7 million in the third quarter of 2025. The year-over-year increase in interest expense primarily reflects the issuance of new and assumed debt in connection with the acquisition of Dowlais.

The weighted average interest rate of our outstanding long-term debt was approximately 7.1% at the end of the quarter. As for taxes in the third quarter of 2026, we recorded an income tax expense of $13.9 million compared to a tax benefit of $10.9 million in the third quarter of 2025. As we described previously, due to the acquisition-related activity this year, our tax rate and resulting impact remains quite involved in 2026. We expect our adjusted effective tax rate to be approximately 25% to 30% this year. As you may recall, this is a somewhat elevated rate primarily due to the valuation allowances and partial interest deduction limitations in the U.S.

As for cash taxes, we expect approximately $165 million to $175 million this year. Taking all these sales and cost drivers into account, our GAAP net loss was $45.3 million or $0.19 per share in the third quarter of 2026 compared to net income of $9.2 million or $0.07 per share in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted earnings per share, which excludes the impact of items noted in our press release, was $0.22 per share in the third quarter of '26 compared to adjusted earnings per share of $0.30 for the third quarter of 2025. Let's now move on to cash flow and the balance sheet.

Net cash provided by operating activities for the third quarter of 2026 was $150.1 million compared to net cash provided by operating activities of $143.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. Capital expenditures, net of proceeds from the sale of property, plant and equipment for the third quarter of 2026 were $94.7 million. Reflecting the impact of these activities, our adjusted free cash flow was $126.7 million in the third quarter of 2026 as compared to $98.1 million in the third quarter of 2025. In the third quarter, we redeemed the remaining $125 million of our 2028 notes and prepaid a portion of our upcoming term loan amortization. We now have no significant debt maturities until 2029.

From a debt leverage perspective, we ended the quarter with net debt of approximately $4.1 billion and net leverage ratio of 2.6x at September 30, 2026. We ended the quarter with total available liquidity of approximately $2.4 billion, consisting of available cash and borrowing capacity on our global credit facilities. So now let's talk about our updated financial guidance on Slide 7. Our updated targets are as follows: for sales, we raised and tightened the range of our sales outlook to $10.8 billion to $10.875 billion versus $10.6 billion to $10.8 billion previously, reflecting the results through the first 9 months of 2026 and our expectations for the remainder of the year, including metal market pass-throughs and currencies.

This sales target is based upon current global production assumptions and certain assumptions for our key programs, and we anticipate GM's full-size pickup truck and SUV production in the range of approximately 1.4 million units this year. From an EBITDA perspective, we anticipate a range of $1.35 billion to $1.375 billion versus $1.36 billion to $1.425 billion previously. The new range reflects several factors, including increasing inflationary pressures, particularly stemming from higher fuel and energy costs, which take time to mitigate or recover. With the challenged macro environment, we're experiencing a somewhat elevated Tier 2 and Tier 3 supplier stress level and lastly, pockets of some production volatility stemming from customer schedule adjustments.

As a reminder, our adjusted EBITDA guidance also reflects our proportionate share of income from SDS, our joint venture in China with HASCO. We continue to expect our JV share to be in the range of $70 million to $80 million this year, unchanged from our previous guidance. We anticipate adjusted free cash flow to be in the range of $270 million to $310 million from $260 million to $325 million previously as we manage all elements of our cash flow pieces. And lastly, from a share count perspective, please continue to use approximately 245 million shares for the fourth quarter for modeling purposes.

As for 2027, we would expect to provide our official outlook when we announce our fourth quarter earnings call next February. But let me provide some initial commentary on some puts and takes for the year. First, we expect to continue the positive synergy momentum and capture the next wave of benefits. Second, we are very excited about the next generation of truck products our customers are launching and will be in the market next year. And lastly, we do expect to continue to navigate through an inflationary environment, at least in the early part of 2027. It does take time to work through these cost headwinds, either in the form of productivity or commercial settlements.

And in conclusion, the company delivered a solid operating cash flow in the third quarter, and we continue to benefit from supplying products across a broad and diversified customer base. As we are into the fourth quarter at this point in time, our priorities remain very clear: manage factors that we can control, execute our integration plan, deliver on our outlined synergy targets and prepare for 2027. Thank you for your time and participation on the call today. I'm going to stop here and turn the call back over to David so we can start the Q&A. David?

David Lim: Thank you, Chris and David. We have reserved some time to take questions. I would ask that you please limit your questions to no more than 2. So at this time, please feel free to proceed with any questions you may have.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question today comes from Tom Narayan from RBC.

Gautam Narayan: So if I look at the Q4 implied downshift from Q3, I understand the 3 factors you called out, the higher fuel, energy, the HD truck issue, GM changeover. But it is a sizable downshift, I think like $50 million, and it does incorporate higher sequential synergy capture. I guess how should we think about these incremental headwinds bleeding into 2027? And how confident are you could pass through these headwinds to the OEMs?

Chris May: Yes, Tom, this is Chris. I think you absolutely identified the key items between Q3 and Q4. Clearly, maybe we'll level set there. From a production standpoint, as you know, in Q4, we have generally 4 or 5 less production days than we do in Q3. So a volume and mix is a key piece of the Q3 to Q4 transition. I would expect some continued uplift in our synergy performance, but also some of these impacts, I think, that you're referring to in terms of inflationary pressures driven by energy costs, et cetera, I would expect probably an impact in the range versus Q3 of around $10 million.

In the current macro environment, some of these pressures would probably continue into the early part of next year. And at that point in time and currently now, we are putting in places or putting in actions to mitigate some of these ourselves from, I'll call it, self-help program to mitigate this inflation, but also we'll be in discussion with our customers in terms of forms of compensation. But as you know, we've gone through this before in the past. These things take time to play out.

Gautam Narayan: Got it. For my follow-up, it's probably for Chris too. On the '26 guidance change versus the prior guide, so adjusted free cash flow is essentially unchanged. I think CapEx is cut by $50 million. I understand the $30 million cut on adjusted EBITDA guidance, and you've explained that already. But what accounts for that -- those remaining pieces that offsets the full $50 million CapEx cut? I assume it's like working cap, interest, taxes. Anything important there to highlight? It seems like maybe those are some sizable changes as well.

Chris May: Yes, I wouldn't put them as sizable. Our cash taxes are up slightly as we completed some final audit settlements, not significant, but a little piece of that. And then you have working capital timing with the shift in the top line sales, obviously, that moves around your receivables from a collection standpoint. It's working capital timing would be the remaining difference. But you hit the main ones. We've been very focused on optimizing our spend with CapEx with a larger enterprise, also leveraging a broader asset base. You point out the change in EBITDA at the midpoint, obviously, would impact cash flow.

And then we've been working on our, I'll call it, our nonoperational cash flow elements, some timing associated with that, but also the final billings that came in with our acquisition.

Gautam Narayan: Good to see the CapEx cut and looking forward to the Investor Day.

Operator: Our next question comes from Joseph Spak from UBS.

Joseph Spak: I just want to offer my congratulations. I really enjoyed all our talks over the years. And Nathan, welcome. Look forward to working with you. Maybe just to follow up on that. I just wanted to -- like within EBITDA, the $50 million lower, but then that's sort of more at, I guess, like an operational level. It was mitigated, I guess, somewhat by that mark-to-market. Can you just remind us what that is? And is that also one of the discrepancies in cash flow? Because that's not -- right, like that's not cash, right? That's just sort of an accounting measure. Is that the other factor for the free cash flow change?

Chris May: Yes, that does not impact our adjusted EBITDA. It is noncash in nature. You would not see that impact our cash flow statement or cash from operations at all for that adjustment. Those were the nondesignated dollar derivatives that we had to put on our balance sheet during the acquisition. These will burn out relatively quickly.

Joseph Spak: So that's not something that continues -- like that's not something that continues into future years. That's just something you inherited and you don't expect to continue to use or do?

Chris May: Correct. They'll start to go away as they lapse, correct.

Joseph Spak: Okay. And Chris, I know you mentioned no significant debt maturities until '29. And maybe I don't know if this is for Nathan or David or Chris, but like I can't say I followed Standard Motors closely, but it does look like there was a concerted effort there to delever post an acquisition they made. And so it seems like there's some similarities there between what they went through and what you're going through now in the wake of the Dowlais deal even if it wasn't sort of, I guess, higher leverage overall.

But I guess, should we read into what you did there, Nathan, in terms of a template of what Dauch would like to do over the coming years?

David Dauch: Yes. Joe, this is David. Let me speak first. We have been very consistent as a company over the years in regards to what our objectives are in regards to our targets for net debt to EBITDA or the leverage target. I mean, clearly, we want to work our way under 2x. I'm proud that we've been able to get it to the 2.6x. At the same time, we're very focused on paying down the debt, which we've consistently been doing quarter-to-quarter. So we'll continue to do that. Obviously, the strength of our business is going to be generating free cash flow to service that debt on a go-forward basis.

At the same time, as always, we'll be opportunistic to refinance select debt at the appropriate time. But what I've always been proud of Chris and the team and even Mike Simonte before then is they've always kept a financial runway in front of us. So we never had an overhang from a maturity standpoint there. And I think dealing with Nathan here, obviously, he's just getting on board, up to speed. There are some similarities in regards to what was done at Standard Motor Products. But at the same time, he's going to have to adjust slightly to just the way we've approached things here within the Dauch Corporation. But I think we're all aligned on our task.

We understand the mission, and we're committed all the way up to the Board of Directors to address this leverage situation. And that was part of the reason we wanted to do this larger strategic combination or acquisition with Dowlais to accelerate that cash generation opportunity through the synergies that we're realizing and then ultimately service this debt a lot quicker. So hopefully, that addresses your question.

Operator: Our next question comes from James Mulholland from Deutsche Bank.

James Mulholland: Synergies continue to be recognized faster than what the original outlay had been. Is there anything specific that's enabling you to reach them at that speed? Or should, I guess, we simply view it as a faster realization? Are you finding maybe extra areas that weren't necessarily in your original guidance, and so you're just being able to take them out now? And could that then pretend to maybe raising what you can do over the longer term?

David Dauch: This is David Dauch again. What I would say is this is, I mean, we committed to $300 million at the time that we announced the strategic combination of the 2 businesses. We also expressed at that time the mix of what that $300 million would be with SG&A and engineering being approximately 30% of that, purchasing being 50% and the operations being 20%. At the time, we also identified that we were limited in regards to the ability to visit their plants. So we're not able to see the full potential of some of the operational items. What I would say is we have been very aggressive in regards to going after SG&A cost as well as engineering efficiencies.

So -- and obviously, that's the low-hanging fruit that we can get after the quickest. So we're clearly ahead of schedule with respect to that. Purchasing, it's a difficult market to navigate in right now. So we're trying to manage our way through that, but still making meaningful progress in that area. And then we're making some substantial progress also on the operations side. So we're really excited the fact that we've already met our year 1 target after 3 quarters together as a combined entity. We think there's more opportunity here and hold tight for future discussions.

James Mulholland: Great. That's helpful. And I guess as my follow-up, as we think about your European footprint that came over from Dowlais, we know that some significant OEMs have been clear that capacity cuts are on the horizon and in some cases, fairly significant capacity cuts. So Dowlais just went through its own large restructuring there. I guess, do you have any early thoughts on what more might be needed in terms of that midterm environment? Or is it at this point that you're fairly comfortable with where the footprint is and whether or not it can be flexed up and down based on whatever production environment it's in?

David Dauch: Yes. This is David again. What I would say is this is legacy AAM did not have as much of a footprint in Europe as obviously legacy Dowlais or GKN did. Legacy Dowlais had done a lot of restructuring, as you acknowledged and was on the downside of that restructuring effort there. There are still efforts that were in their base plan as well as other efforts that are included in our synergistic plan. So that was all identified as part of the process of going through diligence and the combination of the 2 businesses.

The one thing that we're watching very closely is the penetration of the Chinese and their aggressive approach to Europe and the incremental restructuring or the challenges it's creating, especially for the legacy OEMs in Europe. And obviously, we'll have to respond accordingly based on where we're at. The good news is that -- we do supply several of those Chinese OEMs that are gaining market share. So at the same time, we'll just have to balance that out in regards to what we think our capacity utilization and our facility footprint needs to be on a go-forward basis. So to answer your question, I think directionally, we're where we need to be right now.

However, there is some restructuring that is planned as part of this combination, but we'll continue to monitor the market. And if other changes are required, then we'll make those adjustments no different than we would in any other market around the world to optimize the business appropriately and adjust it to the market demand.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dan Levy from Barclays.

Dan Levy: Chris and Nathan, congratulations to both of you. I wanted to start with the question on the inflationary pressures. And maybe you could just refresh us back to the inflation that we saw in the 2022 time frame. How you dealt with that back then in terms of -- I'm pretty sure you ended up sort of getting fully recovered on all those. But what was the split between OEM recoveries or customer recoveries versus your own productivity measures? And now that we're arguably later in the cycle, what do you sense is the receptivity of your customers to help support?

And maybe you could just unpack some of the productivity measures that you have on your end that if you don't get the customer recoveries that you can do it on your end to be EBITDA neutral after all this?

Chris May: Yes, Dan, this is Chris. I'll certainly take the first part of that question. If you go back to the inflationary environment that you're referring to in the past, would have been in the 2022 calendar time period based on really the invasion of Ukraine triggered a lot of inflation in that period of time, and it manifested its way through several elements of our cost structure. Through the course of the year, meaning the full year of 2022, we put in various things to mitigate, optimize some of our spend through where we saw those different pockets of inflation.

But we also, as you know, did have dialogue with our customers that took ultimately the better part of the year to reach conclusion with, which was fairly standard inside the industry at that point in time. So if you think back to some of my prepared remarks I mentioned today, our expectation is a very similar path. We are doing things to help mitigate some of the inflationary impact where you've seen, obviously, a lot of inflation sort of stem from petroleum-based products such as coolants, diesel fuel surcharges on logistics, entering into various metals such as tooling, et cetera.

So things that we can do to either optimize freight routes to minimize fuel costs associated with that, look at different ways or different alternatives for coolants that we can use in our factories. These are the type of productivity initiatives that we would like to do on our own. But as you know, this is a very macro event and would be in some discussions with customers, but would take time to play out. Very similar pattern probably from what we saw back in '22.

Dan Levy: Okay. Great. Second is just a follow-up to, I think, one of the prior questions around your Europe exposure. And I'll just maybe broaden it to China and Europe. So it looks like your China equity income, that's still intact and you generally feel like your Europe footprint is where it needs to be. We've seen from some of the other suppliers that there's been some underperformance within Europe. I realize this is all very customer-specific. But maybe you could just give us an early read on these newer regions where you're operating now where you maybe haven't had as much of a footprint for in terms of China and Europe that those are still holding intact?

And what levers you have in the event that the customer mix moves against you to keep those earnings streams intact?

David Dauch: This is David. I guess I'll start, and then, Chris, I'll ask if you want to add anything in. I'll start in the China side of things. Clearly, legacy AAM had a very strong presence there with our wholly owned foreign enterprise. Our business was both with the global OEMs as well as the local China OEMs. That business with the local China OEMs has grown over the years. So that's been a positive for us. So we're doing very well supporting those programs in China today. With the acquisition of Dowlais, we picked up the joint venture, which is a 35-plus-year-old joint venture that's been very successful over there and profitable.

Like legacy AAM, they were supporting both global OEMs and the local Chinese OEMs. Their share has grown over the years with the China OEMs. So there is pressure in the local China market right now as far as it being down. The demand internally within China is around 24 million units, but they're exporting close to 10 million units on top of that. So -- or as part of that, I should say. So that's an important thing to note. So our volumes have been able to stay fairly steady and strong there. I mean, obviously, we're going to continue to demonstrate the size and the scale of our company, the portfolio.

When it's all said and done, you got to be cost competitive. And so we'll bring the technology and the cost competitive base, and we're where we need to be in China and quite honestly, across Southeast Asia. In Europe, as I said earlier in the earlier question, I think we're positioned right now. There's still some remaining things that are being done as part of the original, base Dowlais plans that we inherited. But as we said, some of those costs would be coming down.

But that's no different than like I said, we would do in any other market in the business. Our business, especially a capital-intensive program or business is all about facility utilization, capacity utilization and manpower utilization. And so we'll just -- as we've always had, we've got downside playbooks -- we'll adjust the businesses to those downside playbooks and flex our cost structure appropriately.

But we feel very confident about where we are in regards to protecting the value streams and the profit pools of China. Obviously, we're watching closely what's going on in Europe, but we're delivering in Europe at this point in time. And we'll make adjustments around the world as required on a go-forward basis. Chris May: No. I think, Dan, I'll tell you, David summed it up pretty well. Yash Beswala: Helpful. But you're also now seeing reinvestment in ICE and a lot of new investment into hybrid applications. The good news for us is our product portfolio spans that ICE and hybrid. There's a little bit of modification on some of the hybrid. And you also know that we've continued to develop on a selective basis, the proper electrification capabilities to support growth in the various markets around the world.

Alexander Perry: I just wanted to ask, is there sort of any line of sight from pressure from some of the heavy-duty platforms easing? How much of that is sort of expected to continue here into the fourth quarter and into next year? And what are some of the offsets?

#3278. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

The communications blackout offers a chance to learn things about handling errors autonomously and recording and storing data autonomously that should useful for other deep space missions. I wonder what the engineers are most worried about for that phase of the mission!

#3275. Google takes over the Wyoming data centre site Crusoe had planned

The AI data centre developer is handing over the site a day after Google pledged $17B there.

Google has bought Crusoe’s data centre site in southeast Wyoming and will build the project itself, after pledging $17B there. Bloomberg had reported Crusoe was pushed aside after failing to sign customers. Terms were not disclosed.

Google has bought Crusoe’s data centre site in southeast Wyoming and will build the project itself, Crusoe said on Friday. Neither company disclosed the terms.

The deal comes a day after Google said it would spend $17B on its first Wyoming data centre, in Laramie County. It ends Crusoe’s early work on the site, which included choosing the location, winning government approvals and planning its power supply.

Crusoe announced the project with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass Energy in July 2025, saying it could eventually grow to 10 GW. In June, Crusoe was being pushed aside after failing to sign customers, with Google raising concerns about costs and timing, Bloomberg reported.

Crusoe said it still has more than 6 GW of capacity under contract and over 40 GW in its pipeline. It is also building a data centre campus for Google near Amarillo, Texas, and raised $3.9B at a $30.9B valuation in September. Elsewhere it has landed customers, including deals with Meta in June and a reported $13B contract with Jane Street.

Developers face a tougher climate. Several new governors elected this week have promised to rein in data centres, Bloomberg said, and voters rejected data centres in 40 of 41 local ballot measures.

I detailed the iPhone Duo app experience in my full review last month. At the time, I emphasized the big difference between using an app updated for iPhone Duo and one that isn’t. I’m thrilled to see how quickly the apps I use every day are being updated for iPhone Duo.

#3271. I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro – and it’s the fastest Android I’ve ever seen

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If it's possible to release a flagship phone while at the same time making it appear more like a midrange phone, Red Magic has found a way.

RedMagic just announced the international launch of the RedMagic 12 Pro — its latest flagship phone. Typically, the company releases devices in China first and then slowly rolls them out to the rest of the world. This time around, the company knew it had a phone that could compete with other flagship devices.

Also: I’ve been a Google Pixel fan for years, but this $500 Android phone is giving me pause

RedMagic’s phones are high-performance devices known to do one thing especially well: mobile gaming. The RedMagic 12 Pro is no exception. It houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 CPU with up to 5.01 GHz, which is paired with the RedMagic R5 Gaming Chipset, and I can honestly say it’s the fastest Android phone I’ve ever tested.

After the initial setup, I installed Geekbench 7 to benchmark the phone and compare it to my Pixel 9 Pro. As for the latest iPhone, according to Geekbench, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes out ahead in single-core performance, but it just barely falls behind in multi-core performance.

The RedMagic 7 Pro nearly doubled the Pixel 11 Pro’s multi-core score. And Google’s device couldn’t beat the single-core score either. As I said, I’ve never seen a Geekbench score this high.

Real-world usage confirms these numbers, because the phone reacts faster and behaves more smoothly than any Android device I’ve owned or tested. It’s so smooth and fast, it feels like magic. But it’s not just the speed that makes this phone special.

First off, I’ve always liked RedMagic’s Android “skin.” As you use it, it seems to be some amalgamation of Android and iOS. RedMagic is essentially doing what Google’s been trying for years: making the smoothest possible animations on Android.

Also: I switched to an Android with liquid cooling for a week – now I wish every phone had it

The interface is as elegant as any I’ve seen on a mobile device. Pull down the notification shade, and it glides down like it was made of silk. Tap on an app launcher, and it opens immediately. Switch between apps, and there’s zero lag or jitter. On top of that, there’s hardly any bezel to speak of — the display goes nearly to the edge of the device.

There’s also no indication of where the front-facing camera is. There’s no pinhole (as you’ll find with many Android devices), and there’s no island (like on iPhones). It’s just a solid display with no interruptions.

The Pro 12 also feels really good in the hand. Both the back and the front are glass. Yes, it invites fingerprints, but it feels so smooth. The back of the phone also has that typical RedMagic look and feel with integrated RGB lighting zones. You can customize the lighting zones for things like fan on/off, game key atmosphere, media atmosphere, incoming calls, charging, and the alarm clock.

Also: This 15-inch portable monitor solved my big issue with cheaper models – and rivals my Mac display

Everything, and I mean everything, about this phone is fast.

The RedMagic 12 Pro is 100% a gaming phone. I installed “Diablo: Immortal” and found it to perform better than the last RedMagic gaming-specific tablet I tested. Not only was it fast, but the graphics were gorgeous. Crisp, smooth, and responsive.

Since the RedMagic 12 Pro is advertised as a serious gaming phone, why does it include preinstalled games that are decidedly non-serious?

On this powerful gaming phone, you’ll find apps like Puzzle Spark, Mahjong Blast, Bolt Twist, GoGo! Blast, and Little Kitty, Big City preinstalled. These are not serious games. In fact, these game titles sound more like they belong on a list of malicious apps (they aren’t).

Also: This 9-inch tablet singlehandedly changed my mind about gaming on Android

I would rather see the Red Magic 12 Pro have zero preinstalled games than the collection it ships with. Yes, you can easily delete those apps, but their being on the phone kind of cheapens it. Given how amazing this phone is, I think RedMagic could get away with shipping a bit less cheese, and a lot more wine.

Either way, the RedMagic 12 Pro is a phone that belongs at the top of the heap among flagships, even above every Pixel phone ever released. If there is a phone that can impress me more than the RedMagic 12 Pro, I’ve yet to see it.

#3270. iOS 27.2 adds Apple Photos invisible watermark feature, here’s how it works

iOS 27.2 arrived last week, and among its changes for Apple Photos, the update adds an invisible watermarking feature when you use certain editing tools. Here’s how it works.

In the age of AI, what looks like a genuine photo might actually be a fake—or partly fake. That’s why tools like SynthID have been used to apply invisible watermarks to AI-generated content.

Starting with iOS 27.2, Apple now uses SynthID watermarks when you make AI-generated edits to photos in Apple Photos, or create all-new images with Image Playground.

Starting with iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, and visionOS 27.2, some Apple Intelligence tools will add an invisible SynthID watermark to images that you create or edit:

Image Playground generates entirely new images, so it’s more what the average person would consider an “AI image.”

However, as Apple notes, the SynthID invisible watermark is also applied to genuine photos in your Apple Photos library if you use the AI-powered Clean Up, Extend, or Spatial Reframing tools to edit them.

It’s worth emphasizing the word “invisible” here. You won’t see evidence of a watermark anywhere on your photos, nor will others unless they explicitly check the image with a SynthID detector.

If you do want to check for the watermark, Apple recommends going to synthid.com, where you can upload an image and see its result.

How do you feel about Apple Photos adding SynthID watermarks in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

A sweeping AI ban is being proposed in the US, with penalties of up to 20 years in prison

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI is advancing at a pace that's making some lawmakers uncomfortable. Now, Senator Bernie Sanders wants to put the brakes on the most powerful AI systems before they become too difficult for humans to control.

Sanders, an independent from Vermont, and Democratic Representative Greg Casar of Texas have introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, a sweeping proposal that would permanently prohibit the development of artificial superintelligence in the United States.

But the legislation goes further than banning a hypothetical future technology. It would also temporarily halt development of certain advanced AI models, establish an entirely new federal department to oversee AI and impose serious penalties on those who break the rules.

Those penalties could include up to 20 years in prison for certain individuals responsible for violations.

The bill was introduced in September and remains in committee. It hasn't become law, but it offers a look at how some lawmakers want to change the direction of AI development.

Sanders argues that AI development has reached a point where government oversight is no longer optional.

"When you are racing towards a cliff, you don't just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes," Sanders said in his September 23 announcement.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The concern is that companies developing advanced AI could eventually create systems with capabilities they don't fully understand or control. Supporters point to warnings from AI researchers and industry leaders about the potential dangers of increasingly autonomous systems.

The bill also calls for international agreements designed to prevent artificial superintelligence from being developed outside the United States.

That could be one of its biggest challenges. The Trump administration has emphasized AI development and American competitiveness in the AI arms race.

The biggest part of the proposal is a permanent ban on artificial superintelligence, or ASI.

Unlike today's AI chatbots, artificial superintelligence generally refers to a theoretical system capable of outperforming humans across most intellectual tasks.

Under the proposed legislation, that definition also includes systems powerful enough to plan and carry out actions that could destroy humanity or take away human control.

The legislation would prohibit developing, deploying, acquiring or distributing these systems. It would also restrict certain AI systems that demonstrate dangerous capabilities associated with superintelligence.

One of the more unusual aspects of the legislation is its proposal to create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence. This department would have the authority to monitor advanced AI development, establish safety requirements and inspect powerful models before they're released.

Companies would need government authorization to develop or distribute qualifying advanced AI models, and those models would require approval before deployment.

The department could also order potentially dangerous AI systems to be disconnected from the internet, modified or rendered inoperative.

The bill's enforcement provisions are particularly strict. For example, certain company decisionmakers and unaffiliated individuals who recklessly violate the law could face fines and prison sentences of up to 20 years.

Companies could also lose authorization to operate, while intellectual property and assets associated with violations could be subject to forfeiture.

For anyone using ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini today, there's no immediate reason to worry about losing access.

The legislation has not passed Congress, and there are no new restrictions on consumer AI services resulting from the proposal.

Even if it eventually became law, the bill wouldn't automatically prohibit every existing chatbot. Its restrictions focus on artificial superintelligence, dangerous AI capabilities and advanced systems that meet certain technical requirements.

However, it could affect the next generation of AI models. Companies such as OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are working to make AI more capable of reasoning, completing complicated tasks and operating with greater autonomy. Under the proposed legislation, qualifying future models would face federal reviews and restrictions before they could be released.

For consumers, that could mean slower releases of more powerful AI tools, although the actual impact would depend on how the law was implemented.

The larger issue is whether the government should restrict the development of AI technology before the potential risks become reality.

For now, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act remains a proposal rather than a law. But it puts a significant question before Congress: How powerful should AI be allowed to become?

#3268. Here's How Many Shares of Procter & Gamble You'd Need for $1,000 in Yearly Dividends

Even if generating $1,000 in dividend payouts from Procter & Gamble isn't in an investor's budget, it's still a stock worthy of investment consideration.

From paper towels to razor blades, people can look around their homes and likely spot a few products from Procter & Gamble (PG -1.02%). And selling those consumer-goods essentials helped P&G haul in $15.9 billion in net earnings for fiscal 2025 and pass some of that on to shareholders as dividends.

With a consistent payout yielding 2.6% as of this writing, investors may be wondering whether P&G could help them generate extra income amid higher fuel and grocery costs. We'll look at what it would take to generate an extra $250 every three months, or $1,000 a year, from the company.

For Procter & Gamble to pay a shareholder $1,000 in yearly dividends, it's going to take quite a few shares. With a quarterly dividend payout of $1.09, it would take roughly 230 shares to earn $1,000 in yearly dividends.

At an opening stock price of $164.65 on Nov. 4, that would require purchasing approximately $37,869 worth of stock, so it will take a fairly large investment to generate $1,000 in yearly dividends.

That said, there's still a reason Procter & Gamble may be worth considering as an investment even with a smaller budget: stability.

As investors worry about the same level of uncertainty swirling around the markets in 2027 as in 2026, companies that allow their shareholders to sleep well at night are receiving more attention. Some of those types of stocks include Dividend Kings.

To earn the title of Dividend King, a company has to have increased its dividend payouts for 50 or more consecutive years. Procter & Gamble has easily cleared that hurdle, increasing its payout for 70 consecutive years.

That shows a strong business model with products that people will always buy no matter what's happening in the economy. Its brands include Tide laundry detergent, Bounty paper towels, Charmin toilet paper, Gillette razors, and more. And while not known for its stock price appreciation, shares are up 16.5% thus far in 2026, outperforming the S&P 500's (^GSPC +0.31%) 8.2% return.

Ultimately, while it may not work out for some shareholders to receive $1,000 in annual dividends from Procter & Gamble, it can still serve as a valuable portfolio addition thanks to its dependability.

#3266. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.
