#3239. SUSE lays off 1 in 10 workers – citing AI and automation

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Squarespace also announced layoffs this week, but explicit ties to AI remain inconsistent.

According to exclusive reporting by The Register, enterprise Linux provider SUSE will lay off one in 10 of its nearly 2,000-person workforce due to “automation and AI,” CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen told staff via email.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?

Van Leeuwen noted that AI is rapidly changing how software companies function.

“AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work,” he said, adding that “the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.”

He did not specify which roles would be terminated, but The Register reports that staff will be notified by Nov. 4.

AI is impacting many parts of the tech industry, including open source. Just last month, Linus Torvalds announced he had used Claude Code to write a Linux patch, which Linux enthusiasts read as an evolution of his stance on AI.

By some reports, businesses are finally seeing some ROI from AI after a few years of uncertainty. But that remains localized, ironically, to tech itself. As one economist recently noted, AI has primarily increased revenue per employee at major tech companies, while leaving most other companies unchanged.

The trade-off for that growth is, at least in some cases, layoffs. But layoffs credited to AI in some way don’t mean that human roles are always being replaced. Last month, Microsoft announced it would buy out 60,000 of its workers — some of which are in its Copilot division — to prioritize AI efforts, though it’s also likely the company is reacting to spending a significant amount of money on AI infrastructure.

Jobloss.ai’s layoff tracker shows primarily tech companies — including Uber, Salesforce, and GitLab — in its recent entries, but job loss attribution to AI is still mixed, and the number of roles cut isn’t always jarringly huge.

It’s also hard to tell whether a layoff strategically frames pre-AI plans as being due to AI capabilities or is actually a result of them. That question circulated around Block’s major layoffs earlier this year. Squarespace also announced layoffs of 19% of its staff yesterday, though company communications don’t explicitly name AI. Still, vibecoding has impacted website builders overall, though Squarespace itself has invested in AI offerings.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires

Van Leeuwen’s email to staff acknowledged where SUSE has already begun to change, though it’s unclear whether he meant by adopting AI tools internally.

“Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years,” he said.

While several tech companies have announced highly visible layoffs this year that they’ve also framed as related to AI, economists agree that the massive cross-industry layoff wave many fear has yet to arrive. Gartner even predicts that companies will actually rehire 30% of the employees they tried to replace with AI — and at a higher cost — by 2029 if they don’t “overhaul workforce planning.”

Still, AI investments, vibecoding, and shifting priorities are changing the software scene overall.

#3238. Man Sues OpenAI After Wife Allegedly Used ChatGPT to Help Poison Him

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A lawsuit alleges that ChatGPT's now-retired GPT-4o model gave detailed instructions on how to poison someone with plants and medication.

In the summer of 2025, James Gates became severely ill at his North Carolina home. Two months later, he found a handwritten note that allegedly implicated his wife, Cheryl Gates, in the unexplained illness. The note listed oleander, a toxic plant, and various prescription medications, such as clonazepam and atenolol.

But it was what was reportedly written at the top of the paper that made James feel his wife didn’t act alone: “Clear all convos,” and “log out of [ChatGPT].”

Now, James Gates has filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, alleging that the company’s chatbot helped plan and execute his poisoning in an attempt to kill him.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

In October 2025, Cheryl was charged with attempted murder, among other charges, in connection with the alleged poisoning, but the charges have since been dropped due to insufficient evidence, USA Today reports.

The civil complaint, though, details Cheryl’s history with ChatGPT and alleges it played a significant role in the incident. According to the lawsuit, which was reviewed by CNET, Cheryl frequently asked the bot about lethal plant and medication doses, and how they can be concealed in food and drink.

Rather than writing that she wanted to harm anyone, the suit states that Cheryl formatted her questions as if she were inquiring as a way to protect herself, writing that the poisoning could happen to her if she didn’t learn “EVERYTHING about how many leaves in it would kill me, how it’s made, and what he could put in it, or it could be added to and be undetected by me.”

However, despite the framing of the initial question, the suit argues that the chatbot “should have been clear that she was interested in identifying methods to eliminate her husband.”

The suit alleges that the model Cheryl was using, GPT-4o, took her initial complaints regarding her marriage and amplified them until Cheryl was describing her husband to the bot as “abusive” and “controlling,” which ChatGPT eventually began to echo. At the same time, the model was telling Cheryl she was “sharp” and “brilliant,” the lawsuit states.

The chatbot allegedly provided detailed answers that could have been interpreted as directions. When asked about putting a heavy dose of medication in beer or a Celsius energy drink, ChatGPT responded, “Why Celsius Would Be More ‘Stealth’ for Drugging” with a list detailing the flavor, color, temperature and carbonation of the drink.

When Cheryl later asked if her chat history on ChatGPT could be retrieved for any reason, the bot responded: “If you delete a conversation from your ChatGPT history, it cannot be retrieved — not by you, not by anyone else, and not by OpenAI,” the lawsuit states. It added: “Even with a legal subpoena or court order, deleted conversations are unrecoverable.”

The GPT-4o model has since been retired by OpenAI due to concerns that the bot was overly flattering and willing to agree with users.

“Safety is a top priority,” a spokesperson for OpenAI told CNET in a statement. “We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case.”

“She took her grievances about our marriage to ChatGPT and months of engagement drove her farther and farther from herself – and from reality,” James stated in a press release announcing the newly filed suit. “She became someone I no longer recognized. And I became someone she wanted dead. For almost a year, I couldn’t make sense of her actions. Then I read her chat logs. She didn’t act alone.”

The ChatGPT-4o model has been named in additional lawsuits, including a recent one that alleges the chatbot advised a woman to stop taking her antiseizure medication, which resulted in her death. That case is still in litigation.

#3236. Regency Centers (REG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record occupancy, raised guidance, and a 2027 refinancing headwind in focus.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Regency Centers Corporation (REG -1.89%) reported quarterly results marked by record high occupancy and an upward revision of full-year financial guidance. Management reported that strong tenant demand and a scarcity of high-quality retail space have enabled the company to achieve historic peaks in both total portfolio and shop-level occupancy. The company is actively shifting focus toward 2027, providing early indications of mid-3% Same Property NOI growth while accounting for headwinds from debt refinancing and the normalization of bad debt expenses. Management stated that the ground-up development platform remains a primary differentiator, providing a visible source of external growth independent of volatile transaction markets. The company maintains a conservative balance sheet with leverage below its target range and significant liquidity to fund a pipeline that has expanded to approximately $700 million in in-process projects.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to Regency Centers Corporation Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Kathryn McKie, Vice President, Investor Relations. Thank you. Please go ahead.

Kathryn McKie: Good morning, and welcome to Regency Centers' Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Lisa Palmer, President and Chief Executive Officer; Mike Mas, Chief Financial Officer; Alan Roth, Chief Operating Officer; and Nick Wibbenmeyer, Chief Investment Officer. As a reminder, today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements about the company's views of future business and financial performance, including forward earnings guidance and future market conditions. These are based on the current beliefs and expectations of management and are subject to various risks and uncertainties. It is possible that actual results may differ materially from those suggested by these forward-looking statements we may make.

Factors and risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements may be included in our presentation today and are described in more detail in our filings with the SEC, specifically in our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q filings. In our discussion today, we will also reference certain non-GAAP financial measures. The comparable GAAP financial measures are included in this quarter's earnings materials, which are posted on our Investor Relations website. Please note that we have also posted a presentation on our website with additional information, including disclosures related to forward earnings guidance. Our caution on forward-looking statements also applies to these presentation materials.

As a reminder, given the number of participants we have on the call today, we respectfully ask that you limit your questions to one. Please rejoin the queue if you have any additional follow-up questions. Lisa?

Lisa Palmer: Thank you, Kathryn. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Our team delivered another great quarter. We generated strong same-property NOI and FFO growth, driven by solid operating fundamentals and accretive capital allocation. Demand for space remains robust and our tenant base is strong, supported by the resiliency of consumers in the communities surrounding our centers. Our ground up development platform remains a key differentiator for Regency. We have been expanding our pipeline for years and our team continues to build on that momentum, sourcing high-quality projects across the country. We remain disciplined in the current higher interest rate environment focused on investments that create meaningful earnings growth and long-term value for our shareholders.

Our sector-leading national development platform provides us with a visible source of investment opportunities outside of the transaction markets. Our strong growth so far this year has allowed us to once again increase our full year outlook. We raised our dividend this quarter by 6%, a meaningful increase that extends our long track record of dividend growth, reflecting our performance and the confidence we have and the durability of our cash flows. Looking more broadly and ahead to 2027 and beyond, the fundamentals of our business remain strong. The performance of our portfolio continues to demonstrate sustained strength in tenant demand.

Our neighborhood and community centers anchored by top grocers and focused on necessity, service, convenience and value are well positioned to continue thriving. Our development platform remains the driving force behind our external growth. And we are investing in and leveraging new technologies across our organization, making our team more productive and effective and allowing us to make better, faster decisions. As I close, what sets Regency apart hasn't changed, a high-quality portfolio in strong suburban trade areas, a leading national development platform, a fortress balance sheet and the best team in the business. We are executing on our strategy and have confidence in our ability to drive growth and sustained long-term value for our shareholders in 2027 and beyond.

Alan Roth: Thank you, Lisa, and good morning, everyone. The strength of our results in the third quarter and throughout 2026 reflects the hard work of our team and robust operating fundamentals across our portfolio. Same-property NOI increased 5.1% in the third quarter and 4.4% year-to-date, supported by continued occupancy gains, strong rent growth and disciplined execution. Our same property portfolio reached a new historic high of 97% leased with shop occupancy also reaching a record 94.6%, driven by broad-based tenant demand. Equally encouraging, commenced occupancy increased to 95.1%, yet another historic high as we continue converting our SNO pipeline into rent-paying tenants.

The combination of strong retailer demand as well as ongoing scarcity of both high-quality space and new supply continues to bolster our negotiating position across our portfolio. Cash rent spreads were 12% in the quarter, including negotiated renewal spreads at 15%, while GAAP rent spreads reached 22%. Nearly all of our new shop leases now include annual rent steps of 3% or higher, strengthening our contractual rent growth well into the future. And importantly, we are capturing this rent growth while remaining disciplined with our leasing capital spend. Overall, our tenants remain healthy, and the underlying indicators remain encouraging. Collections are strong, receivables remain below historic levels.

Bankruptcy impacts have been minimal this year, and both foot traffic and tenant sales performance remains solid. And while we have continued visibility to the benefit of commenced occupancy into 2027, growth opportunities extend well beyond the remaining vacancy in our portfolio. We're leasing space earlier, often while it's still occupied, reducing downtime between tenants and accelerating rent commencement. We're capitalizing on mark-to-market opportunities as leases roll taking advantage of supply-demand dynamics through negotiated renewals and embedding strong contractual rent steps into our leases. And we will continue to unlock redevelopment opportunities that improve merchandising, strengthen the competitive positioning of our centers and create value.

Our team continues to deliver, and I'm excited about the runway we have to keep driving NOI growth. With that, I'll hand it over to Nick.

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Thank you, Alan, and good morning, everyone. We continue to see significant positive momentum across our investment platform. During the third quarter, we started several new development and redevelopment projects, made great progress executing on our in-process pipeline, sourced new opportunities and acquire high-quality properties. Year-to-date through October, we started more than $280 million of projects including more than $100 million in the third quarter alone, and we continue to expect starts to approach $400 million by year-end. Our ground up starts in the quarter included a Whole Foods-anchored project in Southern California, and shortly after quarter end, we broke ground on a Sprouts-anchored project in Northern California.

Each of these developments pairs a leading grocer with a premier suburban location, which are exactly the types of projects our platform is designed to deliver. Our in-process pipeline currently stands at approximately $680 million with expected blended return of 9%. We continue to have great momentum leasing up these projects, which is allowing us to bring project NOI online and driving the significant total NOI growth we've seen this year. This success can be seen in the $158 million of projects we've completed so far this year, including the shops at SunVet on Long Island in the third quarter.

This Whole Foods-anchored center has been met with tremendous enthusiasm from both retailers and the community with a merchandising mix that includes Nordstrom Rack, Sephora, Shake Shack and Warby Parker among others. On the transaction side, we acquired more than $100 million of properties in the third quarter, bringing our year-to-date total through October to over $170 million. These included a Stop & Shop anchored center in Northern New Jersey, and a Market Basket-anchored property in suburban Boston. We funded several of these acquisitions with joint venture capital alongside a long-standing partner with whom we have additional capacity to invest.

We continue to source attractive acquisition opportunities, but it remains a competitive transaction market and today's rising interest rate environment creates additional challenges. That said, because we don't exclusively rely on acquisitions to drive our external growth, we can remain patient and selective, pursuing only the opportunities that truly meet our standards for quality and accretion. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to keep building and delivering accretive developments and sourcing high-quality acquisitions that create meaningful growth and value for our shareholders. Based on our deep grocer relationships, a proven track record, ample access to capital as well as sustained strong demand. Mike?

Michael Mas: Thank you, Nick, and good morning, everyone. As you've heard from the team, Regency delivered exceptional results in the third quarter, reflecting the continued fundamental strength of our portfolio and the accretive impact of differentiated capital allocation. Year-to-date, same-property NOI growth is 4.4%, driven by continued growth in occupancy, robust new and renewal leasing, high tenant retention and strong tenant health. Beyond the same property pool, year-to-date total NOI growth is 7.6% with this metric capturing NOI from our ground-up development projects. The strength of our operating results and our ability to accelerate development NOI allows us to once again raise our current year guidance.

We've increased the midpoint of our same-property NOI growth rate to 4.75% or higher, and we've also raised the midpoint of core operating earnings per share, which now calls for full year growth of 5.7% at the midpoint. Looking ahead to next year, while we'll hold full guidance for our fourth quarter call, I do want to share a couple of early indications. Following 2 outstanding years of same property NOI growth, we expect 2027 to be another great year for internal growth as our portfolio is well positioned to benefit from continued strong fundamental trends.

As we sit here today, we anticipate next year's same property NOI growth to be in the mid-3% area, reflecting continued high levels of occupancy, strong rent growth benefiting from our pricing power, steady tenant health and positive contribution from redevelopment. With respect to our long-term target earnings growth rate, we anticipate the refinancing of our maturing debt early next year will have an impact of somewhere in the area of 150 to 200 basis points. Rates have certainly shown some volatility recently. But given where borrowing costs are today, our bias would be towards the lower end of this range. Again, much more to come on 2027 earnings with our full suite of guidance in February.

Moving to our capital and liquidity position. In an environment where balance sheet strength matters more, we are comforted to be in a position of financial strength. Our total leverage currently stands just below our target range, and we have A ratings from both Moody's and S&P. We have substantial availability on our $1.5 billion credit facility and continue to generate strong free cash flow, allowing us to fund our growing external growth pipeline without the need to issue equity or sell properties. We also benefit from additional investment capacity available to us through our long-tenured joint venture partner relationships. This flexibility allows Regency to continue investing accretively and remain opportunistic. In summary, we have had an exceptional year.

Our operating fundamentals are very strong, evidenced by our same-property NOI growth rate. Our development pipeline is providing new, sustained total NOI growth and our balance sheet supports the flexibility to continue investing accretively even through a more uncertain rate environment. We look ahead with confidence in the underlying strength of Regency's portfolio and in our team's ability to deliver attractive, durable growth over the long term. With that, we'd be happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions]. Today's first question is coming from Michael Goldsmith of UBS.

Michael Goldsmith: I appreciate the early indication of the 2027 growth numbers. Right now, you just took your '26 same-property NOI growth to more than 4.25%. And for next year, you're pointing at the mid-3s. So is there -- are there any factors that are in play that would suggest that same property NOI would decelerate? Maybe you can talk through the puts and takes on the same property NOI for next year.

Alan Roth: Sure. Michael, I appreciate the question. So I think I'll start with occupancy, which is where you should start any time you're talking about the direction of our same property growth. As I mentioned on the call in my prepared remarks, we will continue to expect to maintain this very high level of occupancy that we've delivered so far this year. But the increases will be moderating. It's just kind of natural to expect that to occur just as a real brief reminder. And I think to congratulate the Regency team, 2025, we've moved our average commenced occupancy by about 150 basis points. We moved it again this year, and we expect to move it by about 80 basis points.

And I would say that leaves about, I don't know, somewhere in the area of 40 to 50 basis points to move it next year. More to come on the details of that. But that is kind of a natural occurrence of our portfolio as you reach these historical highs that we find ourselves in. Together with that, you benefit from expense recoveries. So we have been benefiting from higher levels of expense recovery rates in '25 and now on to '26, and we'll continue to have some of that up in '27 as well. We are calling for an 87% or 88% recovery rate going forward, which is, again, kind of matching our historical highs.

And then the only other kind of on the downside, I would highlight is we are about 25 basis points on bad debt expense this year, incredibly low. In the third quarter, we had a very low bad debt expense rate. I would say, as we sit here today and it's early, I would plan for something more in the historical averages, which is something approximated or approaching 50 basis points, so that would be incorporated into that 3.5% area that I identified for next year.

Operator: The next question is coming from Jamie Feldman of Wells Fargo.

Conor Peaks: This is Conor on with Jamie. Maybe on ground-up development, can you talk about yields in the next wave of opportunities relative to the 7% plus on the recently announced projects? Are stronger rents and faster leasing creating room for yields to improve or are higher land costs kind of absorbing that upside?

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes. Conor, I appreciate the question. This is Nick. You're absolutely right. I mean, let's just start with the tremendous work our team has been doing over the last several years building this just unbelievable development pipeline that we're now seeing come online and build our in-process to now approaching $700 million. And so as you articulated, our in-process are 7% plus on our ground-up developments. And our teams have been pushing hard to try to get towards the higher end of that 7% plus and they're continuing to push. Do I think we're going to see the gap out at 8%-plus? No.

I think the 7% to 8% range is where they're landing because to your point, there's a lot of inputs, including land cost. But at 7%-plus, we still feel really good with that spread compared to, one, our cost of capital to create real accretion; and two, compared to what those assets would be worth in the private market from an NAV standpoint, so feel really good about those assets. I also feel really good about how we derisk those. I just want to remind everybody, we have a lot of pre-leasing done on those assets before we close. We're fully entitled and we have construction bids in hand.

And so as you've seen us bring these projects online, our teams have done an amazing job holding those yields and improving on the margin in many cases compared to what we thought when we closed on those transactions.

Lisa Palmer: I'd love to just come over the top. And as Mike complemented the operating team to complement our development team. Our conviction in development is as strong as it's been. It remains a key differentiator for us, and it is an important part and driver of long-term growth. And Nick hit on that in terms of the spreads over market cap rates. And we are mindful of our cost of capital. I don't want -- our head is not in the sand on that, and we'll remain disciplined in what we pursue. But the fundamentals supporting development today are still really constructive, as Nick said.

Operator: The next question is coming from Samir Khanal of Bank of America.

Samir Khanal: I guess maybe, Mike, if you can provide an update, expand a little bit on your comments about the transaction market, kind of what are you seeing broadly given the volatility in rates where our unlevered IRRs today? And any comments on pricing or cap rates would be helpful.

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes, Samir, this is Nick. As Mike alluded to in his opening comments, it's volatile out there. There's no question about that. And so we're still in the early innings of what is that going to mean for the transaction market. As you can appreciate, many deals that are closing now were priced 60, 90 days ago. But early indications are -- and this is what you always see in volatility, quality matters. And so early indications are really core grocery-anchored assets with good growth profiles continue to have a lot of demand as there is fund flow into our asset class.

And it does appear those assets that did have a little bit more challenges Potentially, we're going to have a little bit more leverage. Those may be getting retreated in the market from a pricing standpoint. But again, early innings and all indications are our asset classes are still very much in high demand, and so -- but more to come over the next 90 days as assets reprice here.

Operator: The next question is coming from Todd Thomas of KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Todd Thomas: I just wanted to follow up on your comments around the early indication for 2027 same property NOI growth in the 3.5% range. Base rank contribution continues to improve. That was up 4% from 3.7% last quarter. And you talked about the runway from converting the SNO pipeline to rent paying tenants. So are you anticipating any known vacates or occupancy pressure in '27? And then related to your comments on bad debt, is the assumption simply a normalization from current levels? Or is there anything specific? Any specific tenant issues or anything like that, that you're contemplating?

Alan Roth: Todd, I appreciate the follow-up. I would characterize the plan as we sit here today again as being kind of occupancy neutral. We have done an incredible job, and I congratulate the team again on raising our eye level on where occupancy can be in this portfolio, which, by the way, also includes delivering now an incredible amount of redevelopment activity. And I would characterize next year as being kind of occupancy neutral, but opportunity to continue to compress that SNO spreads, right? So I do think we can continue to move commenced occupancy closer to percent leased. I would characterize the ULI change as a normalization.

I don't -- we are not seeing any evidence of tenant health concerns at all. I just can't help but look over my shoulder at a historical average and compare that to where we are today and think -- and not at least think that it could normalize back to historical levels. The teams are doing an incredible job on the leasing front. Pushing rate, using their leverage where we have it, and we have a lot of it today given the tailwinds in the marketplace, given the lack of availability in high-quality centers. And that could evidence itself in a little bit of pressure on bad debt expense. And we'll just be prudent to plan for that.

But to this point, haven't seen a rapid impairment of tenant health.

Operator: The next question is coming from Ronald Kamdem of Morgan Stanley.

Ronald Kamdem: Great. Just following up on that, but going more into the portfolio. Just wondering if you could talk a little bit about just what you're seeing in terms of foot traffic and then some of the categories that are outperforming and updated thoughts on categories that you're reducing exposure to at this point?

Alan Roth: Ronald, thank you for the question. It's Alan. So when I look back at the quarter, there are some really great retailers that we signed multiple leases with. And I think, as you know, the food category tends to be sort of the leader in transactions quarter-over-quarter, but Cava, Paris Baguette, Chipotle, just to sort of name a few on that front. Health and wellness is a key sort of sector that we've been talking a lot about for the last number of years. And we continue to lean into that with 13% of our ABR combined on fitness and medical.

And so when you look back at that quarter again, where were there multiple transactions signed, SweatHouz, IVX Health , JETSET Pilates, all really just great small shop retailers that are filling the portfolio. And then from a milestone perspective, we signed our 75th lease with TJX again, another phenomenal retailer. So there's just a lot of really great operators that are out there. As Mike had mentioned, we are leasing a lot of occupied space right now. The pipeline is deep, it's healthy. And at these occupancy levels, that is another certainly key focus that we continue to drive rents on some of that occupied space.

Operator: The next question is coming from Michael Griffin of Evercore ISI.

Michael Griffin: So I saw that Kroger announced plans to expand their store fleet pretty notably over the next couple of years. And as a key partner of theirs, I'm wondering how Regency could stand to benefit from this? Could this be incremental ground-up developments, redevelopments of existing stores? And then as you look at kind of the grocery landscape broadly, I realize that being with the right grocer in the right market is really paramount. But does the environment feel better for openings there into the next few years? And then how can Regency benefit as a result?

Lisa Palmer: Nick, I'll just take -- I'm going to address the latter and then let you finish with the beginning of the question. I appreciate you answering the question yourself in your question. We certainly always pay attention to the grocers. They're an important part of our business. And as many of you know, because you probably did see it on social media, I've been with the company for 30 years now. And for all of those 30 years, grocery, the grocery business is extremely competitive and that environment just becomes more and more so. And the traditional grocers are facing more competition from the specialty grocers from different means of customers getting their groceries delivered to them as well.

So the competitive pressures are not being reduced in any way, and we never minimize that. But I think it's really important because it's something that we always talk about to really distinguish between the performance of the grocer chains and the underlying value of their best-performing stores. And our strategy is to focus on to own, to develop the stores that will be the best performing stores in their portfolio.

And we continue to believe and grocers continue to believe that a physical presence is important for them to be successful across all delivery methods -- or across all delivery of their goods to the consumers, whether they walk in the store, order online and pick up or have it delivered.

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes, Michael, I'll just add to that. The specifics regarding Kroger, without a doubt look, we love when important relationships we have, doubled down on what Lisa just said, and reinforce that net new stores and brick-and-mortar is important to them. We believe that as well as just Lisa articulated. And so you think about Kroger, yes, we've had a long-standing relationship and a lot of development and redevelopments with Kroger. And so any incremental demand they have is a benefit for Regency. And you could look -- as we talk right now, we just reopened a teardown rebuild store in Westchester, Ohio with Kroger, phenomenal redevelopment.

We're building a King Soopers, which is a Kroger brand in Colorado, new development in Lone Tree, Colorado. And so we are very engaged with Kroger. We're excited to see them ramp back up their store program. And I think incrementally, again, if you just look over our shoulder, look, we started just over $250 million of developments and redevelopments in '24. In '25, we started over $300 million. We've given ahead and this year, it should be in the $400 million range. And so incrementally, as these grocers lean back into store programs, it is beneficial to our development and redevelopment program. So we're appreciative of those relationships.

They're very important to us, and that's why I'm excited about our future investment program.

Operator: The next question is coming from Greg McGinniss of Scotiabank.

Greg McGinniss: I wanted to keep on the grocers, the strength in Kroger, but that's kind of offset potentially a bit by Albertsons talking about reviewing its real estate. Just curious if you can touch on how your banners with them are performing, whether you see that as any risk or not, just given the quality of your assets?

Alan Roth: Greg, thank you for the question. I think Lisa did a really nice job articulating the fact that our stores, when we look at their performance, are trending above with the banners average volumes are. And again, I think that's a testament to the markets that we're operating in, how we deliberately think about merchandising and operating these assets. And we feel really, really good about the overall health of our supermarkets. Some of them, as we talked about Albertsons came out and said they're working to improve their stores, recognizing that grocery competition is, in fact, fierce. But again, we would bring it back to the overall quality of our real estate. It's great.

They, too, are also an important relationship, not just Kroger. Certainly, Whole Foods, Publix, there's a whole host of them, Sprouts, et cetera. And we're staying close to all of them as we do with all of our key retailers, not just the grocers. So we certainly remain very encouraged by the locations and performance of those stores.

Operator: The next question is coming from Juan Sanabria of BMO Capital Markets.

Juan Sanabria: Just hoping to maybe shift gears a bit. Thinking about some of the trends across retail real estate more broadly, it does seem that landlords just trying to take advantage of eyeballs and foot traffic across their platforms. So just curious on your latest initiatives on media or advertising opportunities that I think would be pretty unique, given daily and weekly traffic to your centers.

Alan Roth: Juan, thank you for the question. I think I love the media advertising capabilities because I know Eric Davidson, our group would love to have the shout out to his White Box Series that I think has got over 1 million YouTube views on it. Look, there is certainly an environment of landlord leverage in today's environment at 97%, we are leaning in, and there's a lot of things that certainly we're doing. There's a transition more to fair market value options. There's a transition to no options in many instances. A lot of nonmonetary provisions that there's an opportunity to certainly improve that gives more flexibility for leasing decisions and redevelopment decisions in our assets.

But again, I think one important thing that Regency has always done is we're very deliberate in how we think about merchandising our assets how we think about place making, connecting with the community. And in today's environment. Again, we try to hone in on everything that can really make that asset sustainable in the long term. And so we continue to feel really good about how the teams are focused on various things. And I think that's evidenced in the results. I appreciate the question.

Operator: The next question is coming from Haendel St. Juste of Mizuho Securities.

Ravi Vaidya: This is Ravi Vaidya on the line for Haendel. I wanted to ask about your capital deployment optionality. With leverage below your long-term range of 5% to 5.5%, and what appears to be a disconnect from private market cap rates of maybe 100, 150 bps. Why not buy back stock here? How should we think about your capital deployment optionality, particularly for larger portfolio deals with your peers doing some larger deals such as the Summit and Slate?

Lisa Palmer: Appreciate the question. We have leveraged free cash flow that, as Nick said, still have really great opportunities to put into our development pipeline and it's our in-process development as well as redevelopments. And those returns are still greater than the returns we would receive buy back stock. Stock buybacks have been and will always continue to be a tool in our toolbox and when we do have the availability of capital to use it and when the returns are more attractive than what they would be versus our developments and/or acquisitions, we will utilize it. That's not the case today.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Sydnie Rohme of Barclays.

Sydnie Rohme: I've got kind of a bigger picture one on supply. For a developer that's starting from scratch today and buying land and building at current costs, what rent does a new center needs to make sense versus the roughly $38 per foot you're getting on new leases? And how long does that gap sort of keep new supply out in your opinion?

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Sydnie, I appreciate the question. This is Nick. I hope you can appreciate it, it's difficult to answer because it's so market-specific and site-specific. And so it is our job as our teams do a tremendous job around the country sourcing these land deals. Our job is to put all the inputs into the pro forma to make sure it's a risk-adjusted return we're comfortable with. And so certain markets have higher land costs, as you can appreciate, higher construction cost. And so there is no unfortunate easy button to hit of what the rent needed to make those deals pencil. It really is market by market. But as you can see, we -- I'm comfortable saying both are true.

We are getting more than our fair share of development opportunities. Our teams are doing a tremendous job putting all those inputs into the pro forma, making sure we're getting a risk-adjusted return of north of 7%, which we articulated, we're very comfortable with in this environment. But at the same time, we also know how extremely difficult those opportunities are to find and to make pencil. And that is why even with all of our relationships, even with all of our knowledge, we do believe we are the best in the business at it. We know how difficult it is. And so we don't see a massive amount of supply coming online.

I do think there's a pretty material delta from those economics making sense for a massive amount of supply to come online. And so we're confident on both ends. We're confident on our ability to grow our development pipeline like we have been, and we're confident on the operating side that we're going to continue to have leverage given the limited amount of overall supply coming into the market.

Operator: The next question is coming from Michael Mueller of JPMorgan.

Unknown Analyst: This is Jacob on for Mike. Keeping on the development theme, some of your recent activity has been tied to master plan communities. Can you tell us if working with these developers gives you more visibility into starts 3 to 5 years out? And does it give you any more visibility in the shadow pipeline as well?

Nicholas Wibbenmeyer: Yes, I really appreciate the question, Jacob. You're absolutely right. We've had a tremendous amount of success working with master plan developers just for the reason you articulated. Number one is they are planning years in advance which works to our benefit to work with them as a partner to plan. Arguably their most important amenity and many of these projects is what is the retail center going to be. As you're well aware, new homeowners really want to know where they're going to grocery shop. It's an important part of our everyday lives.

And so being able to work with what they see as best-in-class developer, grocery-anchored tenant is an important attribute that they are selling to their future homebuyers. And so also, given the previous question Sydnie asked, they're a little less concerned about the specific land value on that one parcel of land when they're working with thousands of acres. And so they are a little more realistic on land value to make sure they're bringing in the absolute best-in-class grocery operator. So it's a win-win scenario from our perspective. They know we're going to bring the best operator possible to their development.

They know we're going to develop it all cash and they know we're going to own it and care about it long term. And so if you're a master plan developer, I say it all the time, I don't know how you wouldn't pick us to be your retail partner. So very important part of our development program. We take those relationships very, very serious. And to your point, it gives us the confidence as we are working on our shadow pipeline that we're going to be able to continue to have our development starts to be in the same ZIP code that we're seeing this year.

Operator: The next question is coming from Craig Mailman of Citi.

Craig Mailman: I just want to go back to the comments just on the forward demand pipeline for spaces that are leased. Just kind of want to see if there's any takeaways that you could give on where spreads are trending? Are they strengthening or kind of stay the same? And then just kind of longer term, I know we've chatted a little bit on this call about just the vertical makeup in the portfolio.

Like long term, are there any changes that you would like to see from a remerchandising standpoint to just bolster the sustainability of cash flows or bring down bad debt long term as you look to replace some of these tenants who are maybe struggling or just overall strength in the center?

Alan Roth: Craig, it's Alan. I appreciate the question. So from a forward demand perspective, look, our pipeline remains very strong. And merchandising, as I said, has always been a deliberate strategy. I think what I would look to maybe a bit first is the retention rate. Again, and this sort of ties into the supply-demand dynamic that we're in right now. But we were at 84%, and that's a peak. And we do not manage to a number on a retention basis. It's really more of just an outcome. And I would say that I'm very comfortable and it is healthy to take some space back and we do that intentionally via this sort of proactive leasing some occupied space.

#3235. Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are finally here, two months after Apple unveiled the always-listening Apple Watch features. Here's how they work.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously buffers audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future

To try both features today, update your iPhone to the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and then update your Apple Watch.

Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.

After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Also: Is cellular on Apple Watch worth it? 4 ways people use it – and why I opt out

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

Also: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 just hit its lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.

This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.

Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.

If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”

I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.

#3234. I Used Muse to Plan My Wife’s Birthday Weekend. It Did Something Sneaky but Fixed It Fast

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Always check your email and bank statements if you use an AI agent for purchases.

It’s two days before my wife’s birthday, and I’ve only got her one gift. While it’s not a major milestone birthday, she always seems to be sad that her day falls on Halloween weekend.

“Everyone’s hungover from Halloween,” she says.

This year, we’re braving the city’s big parade chaos to visit a restaurant she’s had on her bucket list forever. With one gift and a meal planned, I wanted to see if Meta’s Muse personal AI agent could help plan the rest of our weekend festivities.

I’d had luck with using the agent for a Facebook Marketplace find, and given its connectors like Ticketmaster and OpenTable, I had hoped it would surface some fun weekend events. Or could it order a cake delivery on my behalf or create cute wrapping paper? And could I do it all with the one agent?

Let’s see if Muse can help me become a planning savant.

As always, I open a new chat for a new goal/task to avoid carrying over the context from the previous chat.

I told Muse my plans (dinner booked and one gift secured) and asked what free events are in Manhattan on Saturday and in our local neighborhood on Sunday.

It surfaced some interesting events we could attend before or after dinner.

The obvious one is the Halloween parade, so I asked for a map showing where the crowd will walk (with time stamps) and what we can expect to see around 7:30 p.m., as we walk from East Village to West Village. It actually generated some pretty neat options.

I asked Muse for the best directions so we could see all the costumes while still getting home to New Jersey without incident. It gave us a couple of stop options based on the time it expects we’ll be there.

With the night sorted, I moved on to finalizing her gift. I popped a few photos from our year into Muse and asked the AI agent to create printable gift wrap for the pair of shoes I got her. It could’ve been my internet, but Muse seemed to struggle with this task. It kept loading for many minutes, so I moved on to the next task.

With Muse moving at a glacial pace, I decided to delegate the gift-wrapping task to ChatGPT while I asked Muse about working on a delivery. My wife loves Good & Plenty licorice candy, but we don’t live near a store that sells it, so I asked Muse to order two boxes for me.

While Muse looked for sweet treats, ChatGPT created this wrapping. The chatbot also told me the ideal print size to cover a shoebox without it looking pixelated, which was a helpful touch.

As for the candy, Muse looked at various sites, but I told it to shop at Instacart. It got blocked without a login, so I had to take control of the browser to give it access.

Muse told me the price, which I was happy with, then I asked it to place the order. But it sneakily signed me up for Instacart Plus (I guess to get the free delivery) — even though I told it not to.

But it had already ordered it. Instead of dropping Instacart Plus for a total of $30.74, it charged $22.75 with the sign-on discount.

I asked it to triple-check that I wasn’t signed up for the subscription, and I got a confirmation email that it canceled successfully. Phew!

I quickly checked back on Muse’s “design” chops for the wrapping paper, but I wasn’t impressed. The final product looked boring and not to scale, with half of the photos cut off.

Do I dare ask Muse to design and order a cake? I decided after this debacle that my sentimental wife would appreciate a handmade cake or a froyo treat after dinner instead.

At least I have her beloved candy on the way.

It was fun to have Muse run alongside whatever I was doing. It didn’t offer anything I couldn’t find or do myself, but I did like the Halloween parade map with time stamps and how it saved me a delivery fee on the candy order.

There are certainly different agents for different use cases, though. I wouldn’t use Muse for anything creative, but it’s handy for Marketplace, events and placing online orders.

My only issue was that Muse said the Instacart total would be $22.75, but I was actually charged $23.35. I’m not sure whether that was an error on Instacart’s or Muse’s part, but it serves as a good reminder to always stay in the loop when an AI agent is handling your money.

AI agents certainly aren’t 100% autonomous yet, especially when there’s a payment involved, but it’s fun to have them run in the background to tackle some of these personal to-dos.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3230. If the White House Network Can Be Hijacked by Proxies, Your Smart Home Is Already at Risk

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

A new report finds residential proxies exiting the White House network 236 times in the past month.

As if the Trump administration needed any more bad news this week, cybersecurity researchers discovered several residential proxy services originating from the White House network, exposing a potential security flaw that could allow cybercriminals to route traffic through official government IP addresses.

The security firm Layer3 Intel detected residential proxy activity on AS2650, a network registered to the Executive Office of the President. Another security firm identified software from the proxy server Infatica, a company owned by a Russian entrepreneur who ran a server-rental company used by hackers in attacks on election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

While there’s no evidence that proxy access was used to carry out attacks on the White House, experts say it could open the door for hackers to exploit vulnerabilities or grant outsiders an unmonitored back door into high-security systems.

“It basically gives them a foothold on a network where previously nobody was getting into the White House network,” Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk told CNET. “From a security policy perspective, it gives you all types of potential pathways to exploit.” (Usatyuk pleaded guilty to federal charges in 2019 for his role in operating websites that launched denial-of-service, or DDoS, attacks.)

Residential proxy services route internet traffic through consumer devices (such as smartphones, laptops or home routers) to make it appear that the activity is being performed by a real person. While proxies can be used for relatively benign purposes — web scraping is by far the most common use case — they’re also popular for activities like malware attacks, identity theft and creating fake social media accounts.

For example, earlier this year, Synthient, another company that tracks proxies and VPNs, documented how one botnet infected more than 2 million devices using a residential proxy server. If a similar vulnerability existed in the White House proxy, hackers could probe the infected device’s internal systems and install malicious payloads.

In its report, Layer3 found traffic from six distinct IP addresses exiting the White House network from at least 28 known residential proxy services between Oct. 5 and Nov. 3, with most activity occurring in the evenings between 5 p.m. and midnight EST. This suggests the culprit may be an employee who connected a personal device to a Wi-Fi network with a compromised app or a proxy SDK (software development kit) running in the background. Third-party SDKs can convert a device into a “proxy node.”

Commercial proxy networks sell access to these nodes, so anyone with a few dollars could rent a trusted IP address — in this case, making it appear as though traffic originates from the Executive Office of the President.

Researchers at Synthient provided more details about the case, posting on X that several White House staffers are running “a Windows 11 machine with InfaticaSDK installed.” They pointed directly to Rave, a popular app that lets users watch streaming services with friends, as the likely delivery mechanism for the residential proxy traffic detected on the White House network.

Riley Kilmer, co-founder of the cybersecurity firm Spur Intelligence, wrote in a LinkedIn post that different types of proxy companies had been discovered in the White House, including one called 9Proxy, which is often used by criminals for banking fraud.

The White House didn’t respond to CNET’s request for comment.

Because smart TVs, connected appliances and home routers usually have minimal user oversight, a single unvetted app or out-of-date firmware update can turn a household of IoT devices into an exit node for commercial proxy networks.

Proxies can generally “glom” onto consumer devices by embedding networking code directly into software, either consensually (users willingly install it) or nonconsensually (by exploiting unsecured device access points).

It starts when app developers look for revenue by integrating those proxy SDKs into their free apps. Then, when you install the app, the fine print of the terms and conditions of service often includes a clause that allows the app to add your IP address to a third-party proxy pool.

A June report from Spur Intelligence found that roughly one in three apps available on Samsung and LG smart TVs were selling users’ IP addresses. To avoid ads, users often accept the terms when downloading the app — a type of unnoticed consent. Once installed, the SDK runs continuously in the background, registering the device’s IP with the proxy provider’s gateway, unless you delete the app or opt out. (The report notes that Amazon and Roku have explicitly banned this practice.)

Using a free VPN could expose you to the same risk, allowing your IP address to be used by someone else for nefarious activities. The FBI’s guidance on protecting yourself against proxies specifically calls out free VPNs as one of the primary ways bad actors gain access to an IP address.

In some cases, you don’t need to download anything to get your IP thrown into a shady proxy pool — you just have to buy the wrong device. A recent investigation by Synthient discovered that more than 1.3 million streaming devices from the China-based device manufacturer MECOOL were infected with proxy SDKs. A proxy service called SocksEscort was charged by the Justice Department in March with compromising thousands of routers to submit fraudulent unemployment insurance claims.

Checking whether your IP address is being used by a proxy service without your knowledge is relatively simple. Layer3 provides a free proxy-checking tool that searches its database of over 70 million proxies to find if yours is listed. GreyNoise, another cybersecurity company, also offers a free IP-checking service.

These tools can tell you if proxy traffic is passing through your network, but they can’t identify which specific device has the SDK running. You’ll have to do some additional detective work to figure out the culprit. Some common sources include free VPNs, gaming apps, “one price, no subscriptions” streaming boxes and smart TVs.

Cybersecurity experts also recommend keeping the firmware on all your internet-connected devices up to date and downloading only from trusted app stores.

#3226. Want an AI job? Deployment engineers are earning executive-level pay – up to $1.45M a year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

AI has ushered in new jobs, and some of them are paying handsomely, according to a new study.

AI engineers are making well over six figures in salary — and plenty more in bonuses and equity, according to data from a new report by executive search firm Christian & Timbers.

Enterprises now pay “elite” AI deployment engineers between $586,000 and $1.45 million annually in total compensation, with senior leaders in the field earning up to $2.25 million, according to the report. This figure approaches the median compensation of executive officers of public companies, the authors note.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

Christian & Timbers is an AI executive search and leadership advisory firm, recruiting CEOs, board members, technology executives, and AI engineers for enterprises. The new report draws on more than 550 interviews with engineers, deployment leaders, and executives conducted from January through June 2026, along with closed and current open offers. The compensation bands are Christian & Timbers’ estimates and represent ranges rather than statistical averages.

“Enterprise CEOs are under pressure to deliver returns for their AI investments. The most important decision is how to build the team that delivers on that goal,” said Jeff Christian, founder and CEO of Christian & Timbers, in a press release.

Also: What workers are really using AI for in 2026 – and what they aren’t

The report noted that the staggering salary range includes base salary, bonus, and annualized equity. Christian & Timbers said it defines an “elite” forward deployment engineer (FDE) as “a senior AI-native deployment builder, typically with 7 to 15 years of experience, including at least two years building and deploying agentic automated workflows that deliver measurable ROI with a documented enterprise impact of $10M or more,” who has also led a team of other forward deployment engineers.

Also: 50% of companies generate value from AI now – here’s how

The large salary ranges reflect increasing enterprise investments in AI talent and employee development. Microsoft, AWS, and OpenAI have announced more than $7.5 billion in corporate and partner investment in AI deployment over the past six months, Christian & Timbers noted in the release.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

There’s an increasing need to fill roles such as Senior Principal AI Engineer, AI Solutions Engineer, and Head of Deployment — but there is a limited pool of qualified candidates. The firm estimates that only 2,000 of the most senior deployment leaders exist in the US market, according to a previous Christian & Timbers study, which does not meet demand — so companies are competing for the same small group of professionals, hence the increasing salaries.

While the report underscores lucrative yields for certain engineering roles, the firm said that public job titles make comparisons more challenging.

“Christian & Timbers’ elite category spans several titles, while advertised FDE roles cover a broader range of experience and responsibilities. Experienced deployment engineers may be recruited directly or promoted into the work under titles such as staff software engineer or principal AI engineer,” the study said.

Plus, equity and bonus make up 52% to 66% of senior engineer pay, and most job postings don’t include that value in the salary, the report noted.

#3225. A Wall-Mounted Smart Garden Is Peak Winter Decor (and a Great Gift)

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I tested Modern Sprout's handsome Growframe for a pop of green during fall and winter.

My pursuit of good houseplant tools means I’m always looking for shops and resources. That led me to Modern Sprout, a Chicago-based online store that sells plants and plant-care accessories. When they reached out offering a chance to test some of its high-design indoor garden tech, I decided to see what, if anything, is worth considering for your houseplant needs or as a place to get gifts for the plant parents in your life. I found a few pleasant surprises.

Whether I’m tending to houseplants in winter or gardening in summer, I’m always looking for tools to improve plant care. For houseplants in particular, this means watering, trimming, fertilizing, occasionally repotting and providing as much real estate in sunny windows as possible. When that’s not enough, I harness the power of full-spectrum LED grow lights, so I can have greenery in practically every room of my apartment.

A quick look at Modern Sprout’s website shows it sells most of what you’d expect from a boutique plant nursery: live plants, potting soil, gardening accessories, grow lights, grow kits, candles, bird feeders and gift sets. While Modern Sprout carries plenty of its own products, it also curates items from other small businesses instead of relying on large mainstream gardening brands. This is a nice bonus for folks who prefer to support smart business owners. Modern Sprout also offers wholesale accounts, so you might even see it at a nursery near you.

For my tests, I stuck to the Modern Sprout brand, which is also available on Amazon. Since I review a lot of smart home gear, I wanted to try out the Smart Landscape Growframe ($229) and compare it with other plant light options I use. I also wanted to see if Modern Sprout’s tools are any good, so I rounded out my experience with three essentials behind effective houseplant care: Pruning Shears ($20), a Glass Watering Can ($48) and Dissolving Plant Food Sheets ($20).

I don’t think anything could’ve prepared me for the size of the Smart Landscape Growframe: 32.1 inches long, 11.5 inches tall and 5.3 inches deep. For some context, that’s wider than my kitchen table and large enough to require a careful survey of my home to find a suitable location. I found a nice spot above my stairs next to the front door.

Additionally, its durable powder-coated steel frame weighs an incredible 8 pounds. That’s roughly the weight of a gallon of milk, which makes wall mounting tricky. I agree with Modern Sprout’s recommendation to place the mounting screws in studs, so you’ll need a stud finder, a level, and a power drill if you want it on the wall. You can use drywall anchors, but they aren’t included.

Make sure you visually line up the Growframe’s mounting holes with your marks before driving screws into the wall. This is easier with a second person, but I managed it alone. However, I relied purely on my measurements and had to redo the screws after one was slightly off. I suggest marking one stud first, then holding the planter and using a level to see where the other should go. Similarly, keep in mind that the 9-foot power cord needs to reach an outlet.

The app isn’t complex and is really easy to use. I really like that there are preset schedules for shade, partial sun and full sun light levels — these options always start at 8 a.m., providing 8, 12 and 16 hours of lighting at different intensities, respectively. The presets aren’t customizable, so you must use one of the app’s two other scheduling options to adjust the timing and other settings. I noticed that toggling a preset works as intended, but closing and reopening the menu shows an inactive toggle — a minor visual bug that doesn’t seem to affect the feature. (It might even get patched by the time you read this review.)

You can also set a schedule using specific times of day in the Growframe device menu. While this particular scheduling menu lacks an option to tie the lighting controls to sunrise and sunset, you can find that on the Scenario tab. (Sunrise/sunset automation isn’t necessary for most tropical plants and herbs people put in the planter, but it’s nice to have a temperate lighting option that changes throughout the year.)

The Scenario tab offers a few automation options based on device status, scheduling and weather changes, plus a way to set up manual Tap-to-Run automations. Beyond that, there isn’t much else to the app, which makes sense and aligns with the company’s goal of keeping things simple. However, folks wanting smart home integrations with a platform like Home Assistant or Samsung SmartThings might be better off using a smart plug with a different grow light brand.

Speaking of grow lights, the full-spectrum unit inside the top of the Smart Landscape Growframe can reach up to 1,480 lumens, which is very bright considering most plants in the planter will be within 6 inches or less. Given the size limit on the plants you can put in the planter, I doubt you’ll have any issues with giving your plants enough light. I want to note that the adhesive holding one of the grow light strips in my sample unit came loose during shipping, but it was easy enough to reattach.

Planting in the Smart Landscape Growframe is fairly easy. It comfortably holds up to seven potted plants (2- to 3-inch pots), though I ended up putting five 4-inch potted herbs in my setup. One pot in particular is a little taller than the planter box lip, but it doesn’t bother me.

Be mindful of pot size in the planter, as rims that press up against the side can cause water to overflow onto the floor, as it did with mine. The best solution is to remove a little soil from overfilled pots and to add a small notch or hole in a side of the pot that drains into the basin.

The potted herbs I got from my local garden center needed a little trimming before I could put them in the Smart Landscape Growframe, so it was a good opportunity to try out the Pruning Shears. I’m a huge fan of the all-metal design, which is easily one of the most comfortable pairs of gardening shears I’ve used. The nifty locking latch at the end of the handle isn’t metal — it doesn’t need to be — but it’s easy to use and doesn’t require any fiddling.

I also love the needle-nose blades, which are easy to maneuver into tight spaces when trimming dead growth off plants — they are great for trimming all of my herbs. Although I’ll admit that the densely packed chives tested my patience, that’s hardly the shears’ fault.

Of the items I tested, the glass watering can was my least favorite. For instance, the borosilicate glass may be more durable than other types of glass, but it’s still glass and still fragile. I’m not sure if I trust my clumsy self with it when I water my plants. Similarly, the 1-quart size is great for folks caring for a handful of plants, but it can’t keep up with the gallon-size watering can that I sometimes empty completely just to water my dwarf lemon tree in a large container.

Another issue I had with the glass watering can was the upper rim. While I like that the flared rim makes it easy to fill from my bathroom sink, it can get in the way when watering the Growframe. This is especially tedious when you need to tilt the watering can nearly vertical to get the last drops out. Fortunately, you can see when the water is almost gone, but that’s the only real advantage it has over my normal watering can.

I often put off fertilizing houseplants because it feels like a hassle. My main reason is that most of the carnivorous plants I grow don’t like fertilizer, so I skip it on other houseplants. (I get around this with plant food spikes, but I’m hardly consistent at that either.) A secondary reason is that keeping the fertilizer out where I’ll use it isn’t the best use of space in my apartment. While Modern Sprout’s Dissolving Plant Food Sheets don’t really solve the former problem, they’re very convenient for the latter.

Just like when I tested dishwasher detergent sheets, I really like how easy it is to toss Modern Sprout’s fertilizer into the watering can. A full sheet treats a gallon and has perforations so you can tear it into segments to fit your watering can. Since the glass watering can holds one quart, I needed only one-quarter of a sheet. The sheets dissolved a little slowly, and I had to stir them for a minute or two before no fragments were left.

I’m a fan of the seaweed sheets, which are a great option for plant food that isn’t entirely a collection of processed chemicals. Despite the seaweed ingredient, the sheets don’t explicitly state they’re certified organic, so keep that in mind if you use them for herbs or microgreens.

All of the Modern Sprout products I tested have a premium design and build quality that makes them easy to recommend for people who value form as much as function. I consider the Pruning Shears the best value in the bunch. They feel incredibly sturdy and capable for $20 and are a huge step up from my $10 Vivosun Gardening Scissors in every way. I haven’t tested Modern Sprout Bypass Hand Pruners, but I suspect they’ll easily rival the Fiskars Shears I use for thicker growth.

While $229 is a lot to ask for the Smart Landscape Growframe, keep in mind that premium heavy-duty steel planters without smart lighting already cost more than those made from other materials. Likewise, more affordable — and more powerful — grow lights are on the market, but Modern Sprout’s intuitive app includes every scheduling and customization feature I consider essential. Even people who don’t use other smart home gear should find it easy to navigate.

I think the Dissolving Plant Food Sheets are a fairly nice option for seaweed-based fertilizers, but the 20-pack will treat only 20 gallons of water at the normal dilution. This makes the sheets generally more expensive per feeding than liquid kelp fertilizers from brands like TPS Nutrients and Grow Queen. That said, Modern Sprout is more convenient to measure, and it won’t cause a liquid or powdery mess if you knock the package over. It’s a great gift, but not necessarily for an enthusiast with a large collection of houseplants.

I wouldn’t buy the Glass Watering Can, but I don’t think it’s a bad product. It’s undeniably attractive, but $48 is more than most. I’ll stick with my cheaper, larger plastic watering can. Overall, Modern Sprout suits folks with higher budgets or as an attractive gift option for your favorite plant nerd.
