#3194. Delek US Holdings (DK) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management outlines a balance sheet shift and a raised logistics outlook heading into year-end.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Delek US Holdings, Inc. (DK +2.34%) reported record third quarter net income driven by operational reliability and the successful monetization of regulatory exemptions. Management emphasized a financial transformation underpinned by the Enterprise Optimization Plan and a disciplined capital allocation strategy that includes significant share repurchases and an 18% dividend increase. The company transitioned its stand-alone balance sheet to a net cash position while advancing a sum of the parts strategy aimed at the eventual deconsolidation of Delek Logistics.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Delek US Holdings Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Robert Wright, EVP and CFO. Robert, please go ahead.

Robert Wright: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us today. Participants joining me on today's call will include Avigal Soreq, President and CEO; Mohit Bhardwaj, EVP, Strategy and Investor Relations; as well as other members of our management team. Today's earnings release and management call presentation material can be found on the Investor Relations section of the Delek U.S. website. Before we get started, I want to remind everyone that our comments today may include forward-looking statements, reflecting management's current expectations and assumptions. These statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from those discussed today.

For additional information regarding the factors that could cause actual results to differ, please refer to our filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Except as required by applicable law, we do not undertake any obligation to update these forward-looking statements. I will now turn the call over to Avigal for opening remarks. Avigal?

Avigal Soreq: Thank you, Robert. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today. Third quarter was a landmark quarter for us. Given our performance, we finished the quarter in a strong financial position. We are taking incremental steps in Q4 to advance our financial transformation. Our transformation has been made possible by our strong operation and our surgical execution to capture the market opportunities. Our operations play an essential role in the communities we serve by providing reliable fuel supply that support everyday needs and economic activities. We take great pride in being committed community partner.

Highlights in the third quarter includes: one, we continue to successfully navigate the volatility in the crude and product markets caused by the events in Middle East and Eastern Europe. Second, we made further progress in increasing our free cash flow profile and have increased our EOP improvement guidance to at least $250 million. And third, we have also maintained our disciplined and balanced approach to capital allocation through balance sheet improvement, dividend increase and strong buybacks. As I've mentioned in the past, maintaining discipline is critically important during periods of strong margins. We maintain prudent approach reflected in our disciplined capital deployment, focused on creating sustainable long-term shareholder value.

As I mentioned during our last earnings call, the events in the Middle East and Eastern Europe have created many ripple effects in the markets. We continue to see elevated freight rates that impact crack spread and crude differentials. In the current environment, we believe that we have a key advantage through access to pipeline delivered inland crude, limited exposure to elevated freight cost, high distillate yield and most importantly, the ability to respond quickly to changes in the market conditions. This advantage are critical to maintaining operational flexibility and delivering strong performance. Now I will cover some of our third quarter highlights and strategic initiatives in detail. Starting with refining.

Our refining system operated reliably with all 4 refineries running well. Big Spring has shown strong operating performance since its turnaround. It's exceeding its value creation target of improved reliability, higher crude flexibility, improvement in overall product yield and higher octane and blending capabilities. I'm very pleased with this improvement, and I'm confident that the Big Spring team will further improve this important asset. With no planned turnaround for the remainder of the year, our refining system is well positioned to capture the continued strength in crack spread. Moving to EOP, enterprise optimization plan continue to drive significant value. We are again increasing our EOP target to at least $250 million on an annual run rate basis.

During the third quarter of 2026, we estimate approximately $60 million of EOP contribution to our P&L. We have come a long way from our initial target of $100 million of annual free cash flow improvement. And I'm proud of the continuous improvement culture that we have created. Our sum of the parts initiative also continued to progress with raising strength of our midstream business. DKL today raised its 2026 EBITDA guidance to $530 million to $560 million. DKL is also on target to add an additional $60 million in EBITDA in 2027 from its organic growth projects on a run rate basis. This is in addition to the $15 million that we have realized in 2026.

DKL has completed the construction of the first sour compressor station and AGI well and is in the process of commissioning the facility. The sour gas solution will provide DKL the ability to fully capitalize on its growth opportunity in the Delaware Basin and maintain its best-in-class EBITDA growth and yield. On a pro forma basis, we continue to expect DKL third-party annual adjusted EBITDA to exceed 80%. This level of economic separation is a cornerstone of our sum of the parts strategy and continues to bring us closer to our deconsolidation goal. DKL is on the right path, and we continue to work hard to write the next chapter in its growth story.

As I mentioned last quarter, we are pursuing a proactive strategy to manage our obligation under the RFS. The SRE provision of the RFS serves the important purpose of mitigating the impact felt on small refineries from the RFS burden. We have felt this burden in the past and are pleased to have received all 4 small refinery exemptions for 2025 period. This will allow us to reduce our 2025 RVO burden and expect to receive approximately $425 million in proceeds in the fourth quarter. We expect the EPA to continue to provide a relief to small refineries for the year 2026 and beyond.

We believe the current administration, Senate, Congress and EPA realize the importance of SREs, not only for the refineries which qualify under the program, but also to the local communities they serve. The final piece of our strategy is being shareholder-friendly and having a strong balance sheet. During the quarter, we paid approximately $16 million in dividend and $50 million in buyback. Our strong balance sheet, improved reliability, EOP and confident in our outlook continue to support disciplined approach to capital allocation to continuing dividend and buyback. We remain committed to balanced and disciplined capital allocation strategy and are dedicated to rewarding our shareholders. In this regard, we have increased our quarterly dividend by approximately 18% to $0.30 per share.

And after buying back $50 million worth of our shares in Q3, we expect to do approximately $100 million in shares buyback between now and the end of the year. In closing, thank you to our team for the hard work and dedication. I'm immensely proud of the progress Delek has made, and I look forward to building on this momentum for the remainder of the year and beyond. Now I will turn the call over to Robert, who will provide additional color on the quarter.

Robert Wright: Thank you, Avigal. For the third quarter, Delek reported net income of approximately $1.13 billion or $18.22 per share with EBITDA of approximately $1.64 billion. On an adjusted basis, net income came in at approximately $843 million or $13.55 per share, with adjusted EBITDA of approximately $1.28 billion. Turning to our investor presentation. On Slide 4, we show the breakdown of adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EPS for the quarter. Excluding the 50% RVO adjustment and the impact of small refinery exemptions or SREs, granted during the quarter, adjusted EBITDA was approximately $1.04 billion and adjusted EPS was approximately $10.53 per share.

On Slide 5, we walk through the bridge in adjusted EBITDA from the second quarter to the third quarter on the same basis, excluding the 50% RVO adjustment and the impacts of SREs. Quarter-over-quarter performance was led by stronger refining margins and higher capture rates. Supply and Marketing margin was approximately $37 million in the quarter, with wholesale marketing contributing $36.7 million, driven by continued success of our EOP efforts and strong market environment. Asphalt was a loss of $4.6 million, fully offset by a $4.6 million profit from our supply business.

Our Logistics segment continues to deliver strong results, posting approximately $143 million in adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter as momentum continued across our crude, gas and water offerings. Let's move to Slide 6 for a review of cash flow. Cash flow from operations was $567 million for the quarter. This reflects net income adjusted for noncash items, offset by a net working capital outflow of approximately $809 million. Excluding working capital, operating cash flow for the quarter was approximately $1.38 billion. As to the working capital outflow, the majority of this was related to SRE receivables of approximately $425 million, and we expect these proceeds to come in the fourth quarter.

The remainder of the impact is split between timing-related items of roughly $200 million, which we expect to normalize in the coming quarters and roughly $160 million, which is tied to other financing-related items. Investing activities were a use of $117 million for the quarter. This includes capital expenditures of approximately $111 million with $55 million associated with DKL. Of that $55 million, $48 million of that went to growth projects at DKL and the remainder supported scheduled maintenance and regulatory spending across our system, ensuring our ability to run safely and reliably in the current macro environment. Financing activities provided approximately $256 million of net cash during the quarter.

Inflows were approximately $415 million of net proceeds from our 0 coupon convertible notes offering and approximately $220 million of net proceeds from the DKL equity offering. These were partially offset by $247 million of DKL revolver payments, $50 million of share repurchases, $16 million in dividend payments and approximately $22 million in DKL distribution payments to public unitholders. In addition, as Avigal mentioned, we are pleased to announce we're increasing our dividend to $0.30 per share and are expecting to spend approximately $100 million on buybacks in the fourth quarter. Slide 18 breaks out our net debt position between Delek and Delek Logistics.

On a stand-alone basis, excluding Delek Logistics, Delek's net debt has improved $224 million versus the second quarter and has moved to a net cash position of approximately $22 million. Now turning to Slide 19 and our outlook for the fourth quarter. Our total throughput guidance is as follows: Tyler, 75,000 to 80,000 barrels per day; El Dorado, 67,000 to 72,000 barrels per day; Big Spring, 68,000 to 73,000 barrels per day; and Krotz Springs, 78,000 to 83,000 barrels per day. Taken together, this implies a total system throughput target of 288,000 to 308,000 barrels per day for the fourth quarter.

In addition to the throughput guidance for the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect operating expenses to be between $225 million and $235 million; G&A between $50 million and $55 million and D&A to be between $115 million and $125 million. As committed last quarter, we are also breaking out our interest expense between Delek and Delek Logistics. We expect total net interest expense between $52 million and $67 million, with DK contributing between $12 million and $17 million and DKL contributing between $40 million and $50 million. As shown on Slide 8, on a run rate basis post the term loan payout, we expect interest expense on a DK stand-alone basis to be around $10 million.

With that, we will now open the call for questions.

So we need to remember, SREs are disproportionate economic hub. That's the essence of the law, right? And we need to make it clear that it's not a Delek issue. John Abbott: Appreciate it. And then for our follow-up question here, it's really on use of cash. So if we look at your free cash flow for 4Q, it looks like it could be significant, and it's not even included in your deleveraging guidance. and 2027 could be significant as well. So the question is, what do you do with the cash? Is DKL restructuring even a consideration given the value gap you perceive?

#3193. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3192. Do You Speak Geek? 5 Tech Terms That Endure, and 5 That Got Defragged

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Level up your vocab with these tech phrases that'll give you major rizz.

Real talk: I’m not that up to speed on today’s tech vocabulary. That realization clocked me over the head this week when the Scotland-based Collins dictionary came out with its list of new and notable words for 2026. The words include p(doom), which refers to the probability of AI-caused doom; mogging, meaning to outshine or upstage someone; friendslop, a type of low-budget video game played among friends; and ghost jobs, jobs advertised with no real position or intent to hire someone.

Vibe-coding, which was Collins’ Word of the Year for 2025, refers to a conversational way to teach an AI model without typing in all that pesky code. Enshittification, which the American Dialect Society chose as its 2023 Word of the Year, means the gradual, profit-driven decline in the quality of, well, I guess, everything.

Maybe you know and use these terms regularly; maybe you don’t. But, in an effort to stop myself from becoming that Steve Buscemi faking-it-in-high-school meme, I wanted to lay out some tech terms that have a permanent home in the popular lexicon and the words, phrases and abbreviations that haven’t quite stood the test of time. (Note to self: Stop saying “emoticon.”)

Selfie: You know what a selfie is; my mother, on the other hand, may not. The word for taking a photo of yourself with any camera-enabled device was first coined in 2002 on an Australian internet chat forum, of all places, but didn’t become mainstream until 2013.

Content creator: “Influencer” also works here, to refer to a person who shares information on a tech platform and builds an audience of online followers. A related word, “parasocial,” refers to the one-sided relationship listeners or viewers may have with the creator or influencer, who, in contrast, doesn’t know they exist.

Podcast: The Oxford Dictionary named podcast the Word of the Year back in 2005. Since then, the term, which is a mashup of iPod and broadcast and refers to a digital program made available on-demand for streaming or download, has remained relevant. The iPod, however? Not so much. It was discontinued in 2022.

WFH (work from home): The trend of working from your own home via computer saw a substantial uptick during and after the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. According to a 2022 survey by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 23% of Americans work remotely.

Unfriend: The New Oxford American Dictionary‘s 2009 Word of the Year became popularized thanks to Facebook, but the term that means ending a friendship has actually been around for quite some time. NPR called it “the Sleeping Beauty of words,” as the term dates back to the 17th century, when it basically meant the same thing.

Metaverse: Remember when Mark Zuckerberg poured like $80 billion into a virtual reality project that was being touted as the internet platform of the future? The metaverse and its flagship app, Horizon Worlds, were announced in 2021. Five years later, it all fell apart. Now, Zuck is investing a ton in AI, which he’s touting as the internet technology of the future. Second verse, same as the first?

NFT: Just a couple of years ago, you couldn’t go online without reading about NFTs. Nonfungible tokens are digital identifiers to certify ownership of, well, a digital thing of value. Heck, remember when President Donald Trump released an NFT? After the boom in popularity, and the subsequent crash in value of most of them, the term NFT has all but left the public consciousness.

World Wide Web: It’s the internet, folks. Or, the information superhighway if you’re nasty.

Defrag: Back in my day, when we needed better performance from our Windows-based computers, we’d defragment the hard drive. There were plenty of tools you could use to do so. Apparently, this is no longer a thing people do, which is fun, since I still like to use the term in everyday situations. While we’re at it, I’ll be right back. I need to go defrag the car.

Emoticon: Technically, emoticons are made from standard keyboard characters read sideways, such as 🙂 to generate a smiley face. Emoji are graphical images that you can select in various communication programs. (Sometimes, if you try to type an old-school emoticon, the program you’re working in will just grab it and turn it into an emoji.) These days, we just say emoji, even if the word sounds more like a dessert.

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.

#3190. Good Riddance: Tesla to End Cybertruck Production in 2027

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tesla says it will wind down its most notorious model at Gigafactory Texas to make room for its self-driving Cybercab.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced the end of the brand’s most ostentatious model, the Cybertruck, in a post on X late Thursday night. Tesla will begin winding down production of the wedge-shaped pickup at its Texas Gigafactory “around the middle of next year,” Musk said, to boost manufacturing capacity for its Cybercab robotaxi.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

The Cybertruck will not be missed by many. Sales have been so low that Tesla doesn’t even separate them out in its financials — lumping it into an “Other models” column — with experts estimating numbers significantly lower than Tesla’s built-out manufacturing capacity and far below Musk’s sales goals. Meanwhile, Tesla and Musk have increasingly shifted their focus to AI, robotics and autonomy as the brand’s future.

Tesla unveiled the edgy, all-electric pickup truck at an event in 2019, and the cracks were already beginning to show in many of Musk’s most outlandish claims surrounding the truck. (In the case of the “bulletproof” glass, the cracks literally showed.)

After multiple delays, deliveries finally began in 2023. Musk had spent the intervening four years baffling people by making (and subsequently retracting) many truly bizarre statements about the EV’s capabilities, but the first nail in the Cybertruck’s coffin was the starting price, which had ballooned to $60,990, up from the initial $40,000 target touted at debut.

Over its lifetime, the Cybertruck struggled to meet even the most basic expectations, contending with reliability issues, multiple recalls and a penchant for eating its owners’ fingers. It didn’t help that the sci-fi-styled EV arrived around the same time Musk became deeply involved in US politics and policy, and has become known as something of a rolling dog whistle for those who agree with the billionaire’s increasingly unpopular ideologies.

Customers were presented with a niche EV that was more expensive than expected, unsafe, unreliable, unpopular and unattractive. It’s no surprise that sales have suffered, with some experts predicting that since its arrival on US roads, Tesla has sold only about 10% of Musk’s Cybertruck goals. That’s despite Tesla building out an estimated 125,000-unit annual manufacturing capacity at the Texas Gigafactory where the truck is built, leaving the automaker with a huge stock of unsold, unwanted inventory sitting on its lots. One of Musk’s other companies, SpaceX, bought $131 million worth of Cybertrucks last year.

The Cybertruck’s 2027 wind-down will make way for increased capacity for the fully autonomous Cybercab, which debuted in 2024 and is slated to ramp up production in Texas next year. Pitched as a robotaxi that you could own for “under $30,000,” Tesla began offering rides in its steering-wheel-free Cybercab in limited parts of Austin in early September — a stunt that immediately prompted a federal investigation into whether the self-driving vehicle meets federal safety standards.

The Cybertruck joins the Model S and X on Tesla’s 2026 chopping block. The electric sedan and SUV were discontinued in January to make room for production of the Optimus humanoid robot at Tesla’s factory in Fremont, California. That will leave just the Model 3 and Model Y in Tesla’s consumer car lineup until the brand’s next rolling publicity stunt, the high-flying Tesla Roadster, allegedly arrives in 2028.

#3189. TOKEN2049: Fundamentals Are Shaping Crypto Investing

Discover why now is the perfect time for Foolish investors to seize opportunities in the digital asset space.

Two days at the biggest crypto conference in the world are exciting. It's also exhausting listening to and meeting with so many of the major builders and thought leaders from both the crypto and the traditional finance world. I took it in for you, and this article is to share some of my major takeaways -- many of which you're less likely to read anywhere else -- but that I think are very encouraging for Foolish crypto investors.

Let me present to you the story of why right now is exactly the right time for Foolish investors to enter the digital asset space. It comes in five chapters, plus a bonus for the truly Foolish investors.

Alliance's Will Robinson shared a few charts based on hundreds, if not thousands, of conversations with crypto founders. They depict what founders have in mind for building applications over time.

Nonfungible tokens (NFTs), for example, had the highest share in November 2021, with 37% of all founders. This dropped quickly and kept dropping to basically zero right now. The decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) had a peak later in December 2021 at 24%, dropping to less than 4% a year later and are at almost zero now. Other themes, such as play-to-earn, show virtually the same curves. One theme that may have just peaked and is already dropping sharply is prediction markets.

This is not surprising. New things cause hypes that then quickly subside. This may never change because it's human nature. We have to consider such cycles in our fundamental investing approach, being careful about when and how we buy into hype.

But something has changed in crypto that makes it easier for fundamental investors to succeed. Real Vision's Jamie Coutts pointed this out very well in his presentation.

The above-mentioned hypes led to massive investments into building and scaling infrastructure. In 2021, for example, $36.5 billion was raised, according to Coutts. This paid off in a sense because we now have massive blockspace available across diverse ecosystems, and it costs very little to use. Even the notoriously slow and expensive Ethereum (ETH +0.28%) blockchain went from a median fee of more than $10 in 2021 to just around $0.04 now.

Most other blockchains are even cheaper. This enables use cases that simply were not possible before. More on that below.

The challenge in the past was that a lot of the investments went into incentives. Read: token issuance. According to Coutts, typical token supply growth was 14% a year about five years ago, leading to an increase in token supply of 78% since January 2021.

What has this meant? Total crypto market capitalization, excluding Bitcoin (BTC +0.25%) and stablecoins, has grown from around $330 billion at the end of January 2021 to nearly $820 billion today. This is a decent 150% growth.

However, if you consider that 78% of this growth has come from new token issuance and not from price increases, you realize that, despite 150% growth in market capitalization, portfolios of passive investors who haven't participated in this new token issuance have increased only 40% over the past five years. Actually, it's even less because this analysis hasn't yet factored in the added market capitalization of completely new projects launched after 2021. This has been devastating for investors.

But this is also where the next good news enters. New token issuance is down by 87%, according to Coutts, so that typical token supply growth is down to 3% per year. These are inflation figures investors are familiar with. Beating a 3% inflation rate is a very different story from beating the previous 14% inflation rate!

If you've followed the digital asset space, you've noticed that suddenly people are talking about protocols that use the revenues they generate to do token buybacks. Hyperliquid (HYPE +1.83%) is the most well-known example of using 97% of its massive revenue to buy back its own token, but there are others.

These projects have started to outperform that market. Hyperliquid, Pump.fun (PUMP +0.69%), and Aerodrome Finance (AERO +3.33%) are currently the top three protocols measured by how much revenue has been used for buybacks over the past 30 days, according to DefiLlama. These tokens' year-to-date returns are 236%, 191%, and 105%, respectively, compared to a total crypto market capitalization that has declined by 6% over the same period.

I believe this shows that the market is starting to pay more attention to cryptos that actually do have solid, proven fundamentals. This hasn't necessarily been the case in the past.

Coutts has found the same. According to his calculations, a basket of cryptos that have passed a basic fundamental filter has returned a negative 35% per year between 2022 and 2025. If you held a basket of the market capitalization-weighted Top 200 cryptos, on the other hand, they would have returned a positive 3% per year over the same time period. In 2026, the same basket of fundamentally filtered cryptos has outperformed the market capitalization-weighted basket by 4 percentage points!

Everybody is talking about AI, and I believe fewer and fewer people doubt that AI agents will play a major role in the future. Most everyone is probably going to have several agents basically performing their work and other tasks.

I think the general public and general investors underestimate one thing that has been a topic of several presentations and discussions. What will be the financial layer all these agents use? Will they all get bank accounts? Or will they get connected to our bank accounts, which we give them permission to use?

I don't think this makes any sense. What makes much more sense is that these agents will have their own wallets with which they transact. Permissionless blockchain is the one technology that makes this possible. Coupled with the tons of now-existing low-cost blockspace available, it's not difficult to see a future where agents are the major users of blockspace in massive quantities.

But there's one more thing that excites me even more than all of the above.

One of the quotes that hit me only later during the conference was Akshay BD saying, "AI for discovery, tokenization for access." He made a great point that tokenization enables access to asset classes for people excluded from investing in them before. This is obvious if you think about it.

What I haven't realized before is what this does in combination with AI.

Not only does tokenization enable a world where you and I and everybody else can invest in hundreds of thousands or maybe millions of different stocks and other assets all over the world. But AI makes it possible for us to actually discover the few specific investing opportunities we may be looking for that otherwise we may not be able to find.

When it really hit me was during a conversation with an African start-up currently looking for investors. Africa is a very diverse continent where market participants are dealing with challenges you and I have long forgotten. According to materials provided by this start-up, inefficient cross-border settlements lock up billions of dollars in capital. There are hundreds of billions of outstanding receivables, with tens of billions of unmet demand and trillions of dollars of loan books that simply cannot trade today. According to the same presentation, Africa makes up 2.7% of world gross domestic product (GDP), but only 0.2% of world equity trading happens there.

These are massive numbers, and, in my opinion, they're a big reason why prosperity is struggling to find its way in Africa.

However, this may change. All the things discussed above, in combination with regulations being put in place in Africa that clearly define the frameworks about how crypto and blockchain technology may be used, for the first time ever make a solution for these challenges absolutely feasible.

The combination of all of this, in my opinion, is a perfect reason for virtually anybody to seriously consider investing in the crypto space -- and maybe for the first time ever.

But what I came away with from TOKEN2049 is even more exciting for truly Foolish investors.

Good fundamentals are a necessary ingredient for a successful investment. But if we want to be comfortable with a Foolish investing approach of buying and, ideally, holding for years, decent revenue and growth today are not enough. There are other special ingredients that differentiate a fundamentally good business from one that lasts. One of these special ingredients I personally value is a good company culture. I heard some encouraging words during presentations and conversations at the conference pertaining to this.

For example, Illia Polosukhin, founder of NEAR Protocol (NEAR +0.24%), made the point that "we need to build products that meet user experience expectations," and "Crypto hasn't achieved that in the past." Such focus on the customer was even more ingrained in Hyperliquid Co-Founder Jeff Yan, who said, "We're not really optimizing for revenue. That's a byproduct of providing value."

Such statements are music to my ears and tell me there are people working in the space who aren't in it just to get rich. At their core is building something that adds value to customers.

This differentiates great companies from good ones. They focus on providing value first, and business success is a natural result from that.

Of course, there are other things that have to come together for a great long-term investment. But these are the types of companies I'm looking for as a Foolish investor.

As I reflect on the discussions and data from TOKEN2049, it's clear: For Foolish investors, there has never been a better time to dive into the digital asset space. The infrastructure is robust now, capital is more efficiently managed than ever before, AI integration is rising, and fundamentals are just starting to matter. In my view, the tide is uniquely in our favor, and this year will be a pivotal turning point in crypto investing.

#3188. Re-releases of Wing Commander, Ultima titles hit Steam and GOG

It’s mostly bad news from EA lately, but preservation efforts are nice to see.

Many people are not big fans of game publisher EA right now for good reason, but for those who remember a better time in the 1990s, there’s a little good news. Twenty-five classic games from that EA era have been lightly remastered and updated, then placed for sale on Steam and GOG, including several Wing Commander games and nearly the entire Ultima series.

Below is the full list of remastered or re-released games:

In a lengthy blog post published this week, Jim Vessella, a senior producer at EA, described the efforts that went into remastering Wing Commander I-IV and Prophecy, Privateer 2, and Road Rash.

It’s a long, detailed story that’s worth reading yourself, but here’s a top-level summary. After working on the mostly widely acclaimed Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection in 2019, Vessella writes that he learned about and visited a room at EA’s Redwood Shores campus that contained a large archive of poorly labeled or sorted physical media from ages past.

In his free time, and with the help of others, he began cataloging this archive and discovered, among other things, that it contained virtually the entirety of the original masters of Wing Commander III and Wing Commander IV‘s full-motion-video cutscenes.

The story that ensues involves building a small team of contractors, poring through the footage 17 hours a day on swing shifts to label and digitize it, and then coordinating with several key community members—particularly Matt Wells, who has made community enhancement patches for some of the Wing Commander games—to put together remasters of those games.

The flagship offering of those remasters is much, much higher-quality full-motion video sequences than have ever been available before, but other enhancements include 60 frames-per-second gameplay, a plethora of newly available .INI tweaks, and full controller support (though looking at the Steam forums for the games, some folks are having trouble with said controller support).

For Privateer 2—the little-remembered sequel to Wing Commander: Privateer—the crew couldn’t find the original, high-quality remasters of the FMV scenes, and ended up getting in touch with the game’s original cinematics director, Steve Hilliker, who had the tapes in his attic. Hilliker had always wanted to take a new color-grading pass, and he did just that, while also remastering and upscaling all of the cutscenes.

Similar updates were given to Wing Commander Prophecy. The blog post also details GOG’s involvement in restoring and remastering Prophecy and Road Rash. For the latter, EA re-licensed the entire original soundtrack for re-release.

The e collection is on sale on GOG and Steam right now; previous owners of the old versions of the games on GOG and the EA storefront get these remasters for free. None of the games cost more than $5 each.

One good story doesn’t undo a lot of bad news and questionable decisions from EA, but this shows that a few passionate people can do something remarkable for game preservation, even if some of the work was done on a volunteer basis outside normal working hours. (EA committed some resources to the restorations as the project progressed, though.)

While the remasters aren’t perfect, the gaming industry could use news like this. It’s worth reading the full story in the blog post for a journey down memory lane and a look at how involved a restoration process like this can be.

#3187. Broadcom's AI Revenue Is Exploding. Here's What Investors Should Watch Next.

Investors shouldn't ignore the macro and regulatory headwinds.

Broadcom (AVGO +0.74%) is one of the fastest-growing AI chipmakers in the world, but it usually doesn't attract as much attention as Nvidia (NVDA +2.77%). Unlike Nvidia, which produces general-purpose GPUs for data centers, Broadcom produces customized AI accelerators (XPUs) for hyperscalers. When deployed at scale, Broadcom's XPUs can process AI inference tasks faster and more efficiently than Nvidia's stand-alone GPUs.

In fiscal 2025 (which ended last November), Broadcom's AI chip sales soared 65% to $20 billion, or 31% of its top line. In fiscal 2026, it expects its AI chip revenue to surge 186% year over year to $58 billion, or 55% of its projected revenue.

But that could just be the beginning. Broadcom expects its AI chip revenue to nearly double to $115 billion in 2027 and double again to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Assuming it hits those targets, analysts expect its revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 62% and 78%, respectively, from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2028. Those are incredible growth rates for a stock that trades at just 18 times forward earnings -- but investors should keep a close eye on its upcoming challenges.

Broadcom's AI business is firing on all cylinders, and it's bundling its other products -- including chips for Ethernet switches, optical interconnect components, and infrastructure software -- with its XPUs. That stickiness gives it tremendous pricing power and widens its defensive moat.

However, Broadcom could face intense macro and regulatory headwinds over the next few years. On the macro front, high interest rates could force AI companies to rein in their spending. On the regulatory front, the Democratic takeover of the House and Senate -- as well as five flipped governorships -- could force data center operators to stop expanding.

Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa already plans to suspend construction of new data centers in the Lone Star State -- and other states could soon follow suit. That pressure, which already crushed many AI stocks, could force Broadcom to reduce its long-term estimates.

To reduce its dependence on the AI market, Broadcom converted VMware's business model (which it acquired in late 2023) from perpetual licenses to recurring cloud-based subscriptions. However, the expansion of its infrastructure software business (which accounted for 30% of its revenue in its latest quarter) probably can't offset an abrupt slowdown in its AI chipmaking business.

Broadcom's stock looks like a bargain, especially after it declined more than 30% over the past six months, but only if you expect the AI market to keep expanding. If you expect AI spending to slow as macro headwinds intensify and the Democrats tighten their grip on data centers, it might be smarter to wait a few more quarters to see if its stock gets even cheaper.

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3185. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3184. Sandisk Stock Has Lost About 64% Since June. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy It.

How many years of boom-time profits should a buyer be willing to pay for?

Sandisk (SNDK +3.55%) stock sank about 22% on Thursday, Nov. 5, adding to a painful stretch for the flash memory maker. At roughly $806 as of this writing, shares are down about 64% from their June 25 close of $2,335, a record.

Thursday's slide continued a sell-off in AI data center stocks that started after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, as investors weighed whether the outcome might slow data center construction.

And it's been quick. Sandisk closed around $1,330 on Oct. 29, the day it posted fiscal first-quarter results and guided for even higher profits in this quarter. So the growth stock has fallen about 39% over the past week, even though the company's outlook calls for earnings to keep rising.

I think the sell-off has finally brought the stock to a price worth paying. And Sandisk's guidance is what I'd use to set it.

Showing how much the company has changed, Sandisk's earnings per share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis grew 26% sequentially, to $49.51 in its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (which ended Oct. 2, 2026). That followed sequential gains of 278% in fiscal Q3 of 2026 and 68% in fiscal Q4. Fiscal Q1 revenue came to $11.0 billion, up 23% sequentially and 378% year over year, and data center customers accounted for about $4.8 billion of it. For fiscal Q2, management guided to adjusted earnings of $55 to $57 per share, implying about 13% growth over fiscal Q1 at the midpoint.

Put simply, profits are still climbing. But the growth rate is slowing quickly, and it might keep falling from here.

After all, memory profits can swing fast. A year before, in fiscal Q1 of 2026, Sandisk earned just $1.22 per share on an adjusted basis, with a gross margin of around 30%.

And in the three months ended March 28, 2025, it had an adjusted loss of $0.30 a share.

True, the company looks different now. Data center revenue was under $300 million in the year-ago quarter, and the gross margin has since climbed to 85%. But flash memory is still a product whose price can fall when supply outruns demand, and Sandisk's earnings would probably drop with it.

Sandisk's guidance covers only one quarter, so the simplest way to use it is to annualize it. Four quarters at the $56 midpoint would total about $224 per share in adjusted profit. At around $806, the stock trades at under 4 times those annualized earnings.

In other words, a buyer at today's price is paying for less than four years of profits at the current pace. Even on actual results, shares sell for about 7 times earnings over the last four quarters.

By comparison, at the Oct. 29 close, shares traded for about 6 times annualized guided earnings.

With a valuation this low, investors seem to expect the boom's profits to fade within a few years. I think that's a fair worry for a memory company. It's also why I wouldn't pay much more than the stock goes for now.

My price is around $900 per share -- the point at which four years of earnings at the fiscal Q2 guidance pace would equal what I'd pay. Asking a company this cyclical for much more than four years of boom-level profits feels like too much to me.

The coming stock split changes how that number looks, but not what it means. Every shareholder of record on Nov. 9 gets seven extra shares for each one held. The new shares arrive after the Nov. 19 close, and split-adjusted trading is expected to start Nov. 20. Divided by eight, my $900 price comes to about $112, and the $56 guidance midpoint becomes $7 a share.

At roughly $806, Sandisk is under that price. Sure, a stock that has dropped this far this fast can keep falling. And if flash prices start to slip, the earnings behind my price might follow.

With that in mind, I'd consider taking a small position now, maybe adding to it over time rather than all at once. If the stock gets back above $900 (or $112 after the split) before I buy, I'd hold off.

#3183. Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump

Iran threatened to attack subsea cables if US escalates military strikes again.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.

The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.

Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region’s undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

One cable under construction, the 2Africa cable, is owned by a tech consortium that includes the US company Meta. That was one of the major cable corridors visited by the drifting Iran-linked ships.

Windward used both ship-tracking data and satellite images to track the vessels as they slowed down and looped around near multiple cables, with some ships then “going dark” by switching off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders that normally broadcast their location and other information.

Such movement and behavioral patterns suggest the Iran-linked ships may be “mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark,” Windward told the Financial Times.

Windward highlighted the examples of two sanctioned tankers linked to Iran that spent days drifting “directly over regional cable corridors… both with no commercial reason to stop” in a blog post on October 26. Both ships carried no commercial cargo.

Since the US and Israel first launched a major war with Iran in February 2026, Iran’s response beyond targeting US military bases, ships and aircraft has included attacking commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and hitting oil refineries and other energy infrastructure along with airports in various Gulf countries.

Iran has also made a point of threatening or attacking US Big Tech infrastructure in the Middle East, including launching multiple drone strikes on Amazon data centers. In May 2026, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Iran would “impose fees on Internet cables” belonging to US tech companies and other owners.

But more recently, multiple Iranian officials and commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have warned that they could directly attack the undersea cables running through the Strait of Hormuz. This came after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to renew major US military strikes on Iran and warned he could “annihilate” the country during a speech at the United Nations in New York on September 22.

“Seven major cables run through the Strait of Hormuz, supporting global Internet operations and commercial data transmission,” one IRGC spokesperson said on October 20. “We remind the enemy of this.”

The latest phase of the war has involved more limited US military strikes against Iranian targets, even as Trump has alternated between threats and touting the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough. Meanwhile, Iran has increased drone strikes and other attacks on commercial ships to exert its own pressure on the United States, with October marking the highest number of ship attacks since the war began.

Much damage has already been done. The limited fleet of cable-laying ships used for installation and repair has not been able to venture safely into the region since the war began, which forced the Meta-backed 2Africa cable to pause its planned expansion. The war has also compelled US tech companies and Gulf countries to accelerate efforts to develop alternative cable routes bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

The Middle East is not the only part of the world where threats to the Internet’s undersea backbone have intensified. Subsea infrastructure is increasingly at risk from sabotage and gray-zone warfare from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

We are focused on ending the year strong, delivering a new sales record and converting the sales growth into earnings and cash. Turning to Slides 13 and 14. We now expect 2026 sales of $895 million to $902 million or 13% pro forma growth at the midpoint over the prior year period. The low end of the range eclipses our previous record of $885 million, so we are on pace for the highest annual sales in Helios' history. The top end of the range has increased as a result of anticipated sales from the completed acquisition.

For the full year, we expect Hydraulics sales of $564 million to $568 million, 15% pro forma growth at the midpoint and electronics sales of $331 million to $334 million, 12% growth at the midpoint. We expect consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.2% to 20.4% and adjusted diluted earnings per share of $3.08 to $3.15. We are tightening both the margin and earnings ranges from our prior outlook to reflect the current cost environment, along with the impact of the Radio Sound acquisition. The new adjusted diluted earnings per share midpoint reflects a 22% annual growth rate, approaching twice that of our expected midpoint top line growth of 13%.

For the fourth quarter, we expect consolidated sales of $205 million to $212 million. This includes hydraulic sales of $135 million to $139 million and electronics sales of $70 million to $73 million, reflecting current order visibility, component availability and the benefit from the acquisition. We expect fourth quarter adjusted EBITDA margin of 18.5% to 19.5% and adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.60 to $0.67. As a reminder, the fourth quarter of 2025 included an interest expense benefit of $5.4 million related to an interest rate swap that was originally due for maturity that quarter and was terminated as a result of our debt refinancing in 2024, which favorably impacted earnings per share by approximately $0.12.

This impacts the year-over-year comparison in the fourth quarter. There are several considerations behind this outlook. First, we expect the fourth quarter growth rate to moderate from the third quarter pace as we are lapping tougher compares, combined with the fact there was a full extra week in the shipping calendar in the fourth quarter last year. Last year, in the fourth quarter, we reported 17% sales growth and 29% pro forma growth without CFP. This is part of those tougher compares mentioned. Second, we remain in an inflationary cost environment. And although we have taken targeted pricing actions, we believe the benefit will start to show more in 2027.

Third, we will incur integration costs in the fourth quarter related to the acquisition, which were not originally anticipated in our prior outlook, while expected synergies will start to be reflected in early 2027. Our outlook, therefore, balances the strength of our year-to-date performance and commercial pipeline with a measured view of the orders for the balance of the year while layering in timing of initiatives to offset cost inflation as well as the recent acquisition. With that, I will turn the call back to Sean for his closing comments.

Sean Bagan: Thank you, Jeremy. Our 2026 key focus areas shown on Slide 15 remain intact and have guided our direction as we prioritize serving our valued customers while launching and executing against the core strategy. As we close out our prepared remarks, I'd like to return to the sports analogy I referenced earlier. The New York Yankees, Montreal Canadians and Real Madrid each achieved the rare feat of winning 5 consecutive championships, yet their legacies were never defined by whether they won a 6. They were defined by the strength of the organizations they built and their ability to compete successfully year after year.

While our recent growth reflects a strong start, we remain focused on building capabilities, culture and operating discipline that can create value through market cycles. We recognize that the pace of growth may vary from quarter-to-quarter, so our focus remains on disciplined execution, strategic investment and operational excellence. With record year-to-date sales, strong order trends and a healthy pipeline of new product releases, we are confident in our ability to close out 2026 and enter 2027 well positioned for continued profitable growth. With the initial stages of 2027 planning completed, we are cognizant that comparisons are becoming tougher with component availability, inflationary costs and the geopolitical landscape remaining dynamic.

What gives us confidence and excitement that we can continue the momentum ignited this year is the work taking place inside Helios, the customer relationships we are strengthening, the business we are winning, the products we are developing and the operating capabilities we are building. We are not providing specific 2027 guidance today, but the priorities remain the same. As we committed with the core strategy, we are targeting a 5% plus organic growth CAGR through 2030. Our Helios momentum model has driven our performance this year to exceed that targeted pace, demonstrating the strength of our portfolio.

However, we are focused on delivering sustainable compounding growth over the long term and would not assume that this year's double-digit pro forma growth rate is indicative of our expected annual growth profile going forward. We look forward to providing additional perspective on 2027 when we report our fourth quarter results. I want to thank our colleagues across Helios for their commitment to our customers and to one another. Their work is what turns our strategy into results. To our customers, distributors, suppliers and shareholders, thank you for your continued partnership. We remain focused on finishing the year with momentum and building a stronger Helios for the long term. With that, operator, let's open the lines for Q&A, please.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question will be from Chris Moore with CJS Securities.

Jeremy Evans: Yes. Tomo, I would -- this is Jeremy. Jeremy Evans: Yes. Let me touch on the cost pressures that we're seeing first. It's primarily around 3 areas. One is input costs. On the electronics side, it's really on the electronic components. Biggest drivers are the memory chips, but also some of the circuit boards. We're seeing inflation as well in freight. So freight costs remain elevated. Fuel surcharges are as high as they've been since COVID. And so we're seeing that increase. We're seeing an increase in utility costs as well, primarily in Europe.

And when we look at the year-over-year impact on the quarter, that's over 100 basis points from a sequential standpoint, more than 50. And so it's a meaningful impact on the gross margin line. Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).
