#3180. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3179. Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions

SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth.

As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm, which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile, potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network.

SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off.

Follow along for the latest updates on Starlink’s major mobile carrier ambitions.

Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.

Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”

Bloomberg has a breakdown of how Starlink Mobile will operate — and what SpaceX still needs to do to get its hybrid 5G network up and running.

SpaceX is teaming up with Qualcomm to build out its nationwide mobile network. Under the multi-year deal, SpaceX will bring Qualcomm’s Dragonwing technology to “tens of thousands” of 5G cell sites across the US, with the first deployments set for 2027.

The news of the partnership comes as part of SpaceX’s push to make Starlink Mobile a “major” carrier in the US, competing directly with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The Elon Musk-owned company has already snapped up a swath of spectrum, while recent reports suggested that SpaceX was exploring an acquisition of Boost Mobile.

SpaceX has discussed a deal with Boost Mobile to launch its own service through the budget-friendly carrier, according to a report from The Washington Post. The deal, which comes as SpaceX aims to make Starlink a “major” mobile carrier, reportedly involves the Elon Musk-owned company acquiring Boost Mobile or accessing its network.

Musk discussed the potential agreement with Charlie Ergen, chairman of Boost Mobile parent company EchoStar, last month, as reported by The Washington Post. Boost Mobile’s network is currently powered by T-Mobile and AT&T, meaning SpaceX may need permission from the two carriers to launch its service.

SpaceX plans to access at least 80,000 cell sites as part of efforts to compete directly with Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T, according to a report from Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that SpaceX is in talks with Crown Castle Inc., one of the nation’s largest cell tower owners.

The move would give SpaceX access to half of the 158,500 cell towers currently operational in the US, according to Reuters. When asked about a potential partnership with SpaceX, Amazon, or other satellite services during an earnings call on Wednesday, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said, “I don’t think I want to get into customer-specific detail, but you can assume that we’re talking to all parties.” SpaceX plans to pair a network of cell towers with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites.

SpaceX has acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses — a move the company says “will pave the way” for its Starlink Mobile service to become a “major” US carrier. When the Federal Communications Commission signs off on the deal, SpaceX says it will deploy its new architecture that combines its satellite-to-mobile constellation with a terrestrial mobile network, directly competing with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon.

The licenses include up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which SpaceX says will allow Starlink Mobile’s signal to penetrate through walls and buildings. SpaceX previously acquired 2GHz spectrum from EchoStar as part of efforts to bolster its direct-to-device service.

“The spectrum that we purchased from EchoStar does have terrestrial components, so we definitely intend to build out the terrestrial component,” said Shotwell. “You will have not only the capacity from the satellites themselves, but you will have a buildout of the terrestrial, basically the hardware and systems necessary to make a true mobile service exactly what you want it to be.”

#3178. First Financial: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

A majority of First Financial's loan portfolio reprices within 15-30 days, letting the bank capture rate gains before deposit costs rise.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, First Financial (FFBC +0.21%) announced record quarterly revenue driven by expanding fee streams and high interest margins. For long-term shareholders, the bank's ability to generate steady non-interest income provides an important balance against shifting interest rates.

Three takeaways from management's comments show how the business is building long-term value.

First Financial generates revenue from loan interest and fee-based services like wealth management or foreign exchange. Non-interest income reached $77.6 million during the quarter, which gives the bank reliable revenue that doesn't depend on lending volume.

A majority of the bank's loan portfolio reprices quickly when rates move because loans tie to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), a benchmark interest rate for commercial loans. That rapid repricing expands the net interest margin, which measures lending profitability, ahead of rising deposit expenses.

First Financial received regulatory approval to acquire Finward, a regional banking company, with the deal expected to close on Jan. 1, 2027. The acquisition expands the bank's operational footprint and adds future earning capacity despite initial tangible book value dilution.

Commercial loan demand remains active in major Midwest markets. The bank maintains a loan-to-deposit ratio of 78%, which measures loan volume against deposits, giving it flexibility to fund loans without raising deposit rates. Management tracks credit quality while maintaining a steady allowance for credit losses (ACL), the reserve set aside to absorb bad loans.

With regulatory approval secured for its pending merger and fee businesses performing steadily, the bank is positioned to build on its regional momentum.

Basic economy tickets come with plenty of restrictions, but holding the right credit card is my top trick for avoiding some of them.

As airfares remain high, that basic economy fare might look more tempting than ever. Saving $100 on a round-trip domestic flight could mean more money for hotels, dining or other experiences at your destination.

I’ve flown my fair share of basic economy flights, which come with restrictions like being unable to select a seat, earning no award miles and boarding last. You also can’t make changes or cancel your itinerary without paying a hefty fee, and — specific to United Airlines — you can’t bring a full-size carry-on on board.

But as a United frequent flyer, I have a secret to share with you: Holding the United℠ Explorer Card (annual fee: $0 intro for the first year, then $150) lets you avoid several of those basic economy restrictions.

Right now, new United℠ Explorer Card applicants can receive this welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first 3 months your account is open.

Most major airlines no longer let you earn points or miles on basic economy fares. United is an exception, though — assuming you hold the right credit card.

Eligible cardholders, including those who have the United℠ Explorer Card, earn at least 3 miles per $1 spent on United basic economy tickets, excluding taxes and select fees. That’s half of what a standard economy ticket earns for cardholders (6 miles per $1), but it’s better than zero. If you have elite status, you’ll earn more.

Those miles are in addition to the 3 miles per $1 you earn on all United purchases when using your United℠ Explorer Card.

With the card, your miles can become more valuable. That’s because cardholders get at least 10% off award tickets that are operated by United or United Express. If you have United status, that discount gets bumped up to at least 15% off.

With the credit card, you have access to priority boarding in Group 2. That means you’ll be able to board earlier compared to the rest of the basic economy passengers in Group 6, making it more likely you’ll find space for your carry-on bag.

Now, you might be thinking: Wait a minute… Basic economy doesn’t allow you to bring a carry-on bag. Let me explain how that works.

United enforces its full-size carry-on restriction based on your boarding group. Group 6 passengers can't bring a full-size carry-on.

Because the credit card gets you Group 2 boarding, you essentially skip that restriction.

Premier members — who board in Group 2 or earlier — are also exempt from the full-size carry-on restriction when flying basic economy.

If you don’t want to deal with the hassle of a carry-on bag, you can opt to check it instead.

As long as you pay for your ticket using your United℠ Explorer Card, you’ll be able to check your first bag — and your companion’s first bag — for free when traveling on United. (If you’re booking an award ticket, make sure to use your card to pay for the taxes and fees.)

Keep in mind that if the first flight on your itinerary is operated by another airline, that airline’s baggage rules would apply and you would have to pay for your bag.

Of course, holding the right United credit card only gets you so far.

With basic economy, you’ll still need to pay a fee to change or cancel your ticket, and you won’t be able to select a seat for free.

Ultimately, whether basic economy is a good deal depends on a few factors.

If your plans might change, pay up for standard economy. Otherwise, the penalty to change or cancel will end up costing you more than you saved.

Another thing to consider is whether you’re willing to sit in a middle seat. You might be fine with it for a few hours, but what about a long-haul flight to Asia? Everyone’s threshold is different, so you’ll need to decide whether the middle-seat gamble is worth it.

If your plans are firm and you don’t mind a potential middle seat, booking a basic economy ticket can be a solid way to save money. Just book with a United card like, the United℠ Explorer Card, to avoid the biggest downsides.

#3176. We Write About Saving Money; Here’s How We Trick Our Brains Into Doing It

Even personal finance writers and editors need psychological hacks to save money. Here are the tips we use, and why they work.

While staring at the Container Store cart on my phone at 11 p.m., I did something for the first time that I’d read about a hundred times. Instead of spending $200 on more organizational boxes that I categorically did not need, I transferred that amount to my savings account.

Normally, my willpower is no match for the very real psychological phenomenon called present bias: Our brains light up more when we’re rewarding our current selves than our future selves.

Research has also shown that you imagine your future self almost like a stranger — it’s tougher to care about that stranger than about who you are right now. But that night, I saw near-future-me using that $200 on next summer’s vacation. I wanted the vacation more than the boxes. So I abandoned my cart.

I had managed to use a psychological savings trick: Find a goal that helps you envision your future self. With this epiphany in mind, I asked some of my fellow Nerds to share the savings habits they’ve put to work in their own lives. Perhaps reading these can give late-night you some saving inspiration.

Kimberly Palmer, senior writer and spokesperson: I let nonessential items sit in my online shopping cart for at least 24 hours before buying them. It definitely makes me realize I don't need a lot of them! I also informed my children of this rule, and it has helped cut down on their requests — or at least they know they have to be patient.

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: Fellow let-it-sit-in-the-cart person here. I wait for notifications that something's at least 30% off before I make any moves. Ideally, 40% to 50% off.

Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor: When I browse online, I add an item to my shopping cart and wait 24 to 48 hours. After that, I either decide it’s a waste of money/an impulse purchase and delete it from my cart (or forget about the cart altogether), or I decide I want it and make the purchase — it’s the former 99% of the time.

Why it works: “Waiting 1 to 2 days allows me to take the emotion out of purchasing. I no longer succumb to marketing or sales, and instead make spending decisions based on what my family and I actually need or can use.” — Julie again, eloquently making the point for me.

Caitlin Constantine, managing editor: My one real shopping weakness is books, and I’ve found I can get a very close approximation of that feeling without spending an outrageous amount of money by going to the library, wandering around the stacks to see what books might look interesting, and checking out a bunch of them. Even if I don’t end up reading them, I’m still helping the library with circulation numbers, so I see it as a win-win.

Spencer Tierney, senior writer: Plus one to Caitlin Constantine’s “my one real shopping weakness is books.” If I want an older or smaller book, I'll try to find it at one of four libraries I belong to on Libby, the library e-book reader app. (The Libby waitlist for new books can take months, so I have to account for that.)

Why it works: There’s no secret here: It’s nice to get free stuff. You might be surprised what the library has to offer, like movies, magazine subscriptions, games, classes and theater tickets.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: We always tell people to automate savings, and I do in my high-yield savings account, but Dasha Kennedy, the woman behind “The Broke Black Girl”, told Elizabeth Ayoola on the Smart Money podcast that you should invest, even a little bit every week or so, for future you. So I just set up a small recurring deposit to my robo-advisor.

Why it works: You only have to make this decision once for your future self, not over and over again. And if you do it early enough, you could avoid being part of the 41% of Americans who wish they had started investing earlier, according to a 2026 NerdWallet survey.

Athena Cocoves, managing editor: To cut down on food delivery, I started cooking when I feel like it instead of when I’m supposed to. I exercise free will and make soup at 10 p.m. It sounds more obvious than it feels, and it's made a big difference in my budget. And it'd make an even bigger difference if I wasn't also rewarding myself with fancy spices and vinegars, but a girl's gotta splurge somehow.

Ryan Brady, lead writer: My wife takes advantage of a T-Mobile freebie that gives us a discount for DoorDash deliveries. She uses it to buy groceries from Aldi instead of takeout. Aldi is far from us. Publix is right across the street, but more expensive. So this saves us money on the actual items and also helps us not impulse buy (as we often do when we're in-store shopping).

Why it works: You don’t need to call on willpower if you can avoid the situation that tempts you to spend money.

» Read more: Strategies to save on groceries that actually work

Kenley Young, managing editor: I use credit cards for most purchases to get those sweet, sweet rewards, but there's a lot in this article that I've also taken to heart.

I've started using library resources more, and it's saving me money on things like monthly subscriptions.

I've negotiated down several monthly bills, too: refinanced my car loan, got cheaper homeowners insurance, opted for a little less auto coverage in exchange for a lower premium, and haggled online with everyone from Xfinity and SiriusXM to my local newspaper until they all gave me a discount.

Plus, I've opted for some home improvement projects with the expectation that my utility bills would be lower. A plumber finally fixed our toilet, which has led to lower water bills, and I even installed solar panels.

Lastly, my analog skill (playing live music) has become a steady side hustle. I play eight to 10 gigs a month, where (on top of my baseline rate) I also get tips, free food and beer.

Why it works: Because you’re Kenley and you put in a lot of effort.

But you don’t need to be Kenley to find a savings habit that works for your personality, your financial situation and even your musical talents. You just need to experiment. Pick the strategy that speaks to you most, and test it out. Which one are you going to try first?

#3174. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

#3172. AI Voice Agents Are Easy To Demo; Production Is Where The Engineering Begins

Alexandro Picolini is a technology executive and software architect focused on telecom, cloud and AI.

Voice AI demos have become surprisingly easy to build. With a real-time model, a microphone and a good prompt, a team can create something impressive quickly. But a demo is usually a controlled environment: clean audio, a stable network, cooperative users and readily available data.

A real telephone operation is very different.

I am a CTO and software architect with more than 25 years of experience in telecommunications and software development. My company develops contact-center platforms that connect telephony, digital channels and customer management. Our work integrating voice AI into these environments has shown me how much production depends on systems beyond the model.

One of the first problems we faced was telephone audio quality. As a call passes between carriers, its audio may be compressed and converted along the way. Receiving it in a higher-quality format at the final connection does not restore detail already lost. A person may still understand the conversation while a speech-recognition system struggles.

Speakerphone calls add background conversations, television and traffic. Voice activity detection—the technology that detects when someone is speaking—does not always distinguish the caller from surrounding voices.

It’s important to test through the actual telephone routes customers use, not only a headset connected to a computer. Teams should include mobile phones, speakerphones and noisy environments. They should listen to the audio reaching the agent, not just the voice it generates.

Human conversations include brief acknowledgments: “Uh-huh.” “Okay.” “Right.” These do not always mean someone wants to take over the conversation. If interruption detection is too aggressive, a simple “okay” stops the agent mid-explanation. If it is too conservative, customers must speak over the agent before it stops.

In some of our implementations, around two seconds has been a workable compromise. It is not a universal setting: Turn detection requires more than detecting sound.

It’s critical to test acknowledgments separately from deliberate interruptions. The goal is not to eliminate every overlap but to let customers interrupt when they need to without making ordinary listening behavior break the conversation.

An API taking three or four seconds during a WhatsApp exchange may barely register. On a phone call, those same seconds feel long.

You can ask customers to wait or provide subtle audio feedback. We have experimented with sounds that simulate typing while information is retrieved. That may work once; repeated pauses quickly become frustrating.

Whenever possible, information the agent is likely to need should be available through a fast data layer. In some implementations, we use Redis to cache customer information and reduce slow backend requests.

Teams should identify which lookups must happen during the call and which can happen beforehand. They should set a waiting limit for each dependency and decide what happens if it fails. A reassuring phrase is not a substitute for a responsive integration.

When someone shows me a voice AI demo and says it is production-ready, I ask: “How do you dynamically deliver the contact’s data to the bot?” The system may already know the campaign, customer account, recent interactions or reason for calling. Making the customer repeat everything wastes that context. Retrieving each detail only when requested adds delays.

Start by defining the minimum information needed for each use case. Pass it into the conversation through a consistent structure rather than loading an entire customer record. Separate background information from data that must be refreshed before an action, such as confirming an appointment.

Define what the agent should do when a record is missing, outdated or inconsistent. Restrict information to what the task requires, and verify identity before disclosing sensitive account details. A recognized phone number should not, by itself, authorize disclosure. Test those failure cases as deliberately as the ideal scenario.

Human transfer is not merely a rescue mechanism for a failed AI. Customers may request a person, a situation may exceed the agent’s scope or an action may require human authorization.

Define these transfer triggers with the operations team before launch. Specify the destination queue, its operating hours and an alternative when nobody is available. Test busy queues, unavailable agents and failed transfers—not just a successful connection. The transfer should carry a concise summary: why the customer called, what has been verified, actions already attempted and what remains unresolved. Make that information available where the human agent actually works.

Do not tell the caller that a transfer succeeded merely because the system requested it. Confirm the outcome, explain any delay and offer the agreed alternative when necessary. The customer should not lose the conversation’s progress at the moment human help becomes necessary.

Many problems do not appear with one or 10 simultaneous calls. At thousands of concurrent calls, we have seen delays in audio delivery over SIP that were almost invisible at small scale. It’s important to test the complete path under realistic concurrency, including external APIs and human transfers. Measure the time callers wait to hear a response, not only the time a model takes to generate one. Include slow dependencies and provider interruptions in those tests.

A polished demo may prove that the model is capable. It does not prove that every connected system will remain responsive under load. A good demo proves the AI can talk. Production proves whether the whole system actually works.​

#3168. Identity Governance And The Challenge Of AI Agents Moving At Machine Speed

Praerit Garg, CEO, One Identity, trusted leader in identity security, helping enterprises protect and simplify access to digital identities.

​An employee might spend an afternoon retrieving customer records or checking account details. Meanwhile, an AI agent might tick off those tasks within seconds, then repeat them thousands of times without pausing. We’ve reached a golden age of automation, where AI can do more than just automate—it can make decisions and act upon them at speeds that even a whole team of humans could fail to match.

But there’s a catch. While every individual action performed by an AI agent may fall within defined permissions and parameters, all it takes is one excessive entitlement or poorly designed approval process for an AI to cause significant damage. And because AI makes automation much simpler to achieve, allowing employees to turn existing permissions into powerful automated workflows with a single prompt, it’s becoming much harder to govern. With McKinsey reporting that up to 40% of organizations are already scaling an agentic AI system in at least one business function, this is quickly becoming one of the year’s defining security issues.​

Much of the industry’s response has focused on building entirely new identity and governance architectures specifically for AI agents, but they actually already have the right tools at their disposal in the form of identity governance and administration (IGA) and privileged access management (PAM). The same questions that are asked of humans should be asked of machines: Whose authority is the agent exercising? What information can it access? Which actions can it take, and when should additional approval be required? Instead of rebuilding governance architectures from the ground up, businesses simply need to refocus the tools and learnings already at their disposal, particularly zero-trust architectures.​

Microsoft made a significant investment in exploring a more code-centric approach with code access security (CAS) some 25 years ago, but the company later deprecated it and no longer treats CAS as a security boundary because too many paths can allow privileges to be elevated. Microsoft now directs developers toward enforceable operating-system boundaries, including user accounts, which reinforces the idea that creating a specialized control layer doesn’t necessarily provide stronger protection than applying established security boundaries consistently.​

I was recently introduced to an elaborate access governance system designed specifically to stop AI agents from taking actions their users never intended. The organization’s concerns were legitimate, of course, but the solution their team proposed, like Microsoft’s, added so much complexity that they didn’t even consider they may already have the answer.​

An agent acting on someone’s behalf should, at most, only be able to use the permissions granted to that user. If an employee can view a customer record but can’t export an entire database, an agent working for that employee should also have the same limitations applied to it. If the agent can approve a payment or gain access to another business function that the user could not, the first question should be why those permissions were available in the first place.​

The early internet created a similar “trust crisis.” As businesses began distributing software online, users had no easy way to know who had created a program or exactly what it would do once installed. Worms such as Code Red and Nimda showed how quickly malicious code could spread when software was allowed to move and execute across connected systems. That’s when the industry decided that a form of trust infrastructure should be built around digital signatures, certificates and policies, which governed which software was allowed to run.​

Step back into 2026, and the same story is unfolding. Organizations need to establish where an agent and its underlying model came from, authenticate the identity it uses, restrict the systems and data it can reach and require approval before any actions are performed. A trusted model may reduce the risk of deliberately malicious behavior, but identity controls (based on least privileged and zero trust principles) still provide the enforceable boundary when prompts are ambiguous, permissions configurations are flawed or an agent reaches an “unintended” conclusion.​

AI magnifies the consequences of every single entitlement decision. A permission that posed a manageable risk when exercised occasionally by an employee can pose a greater risk when an agent uses it continuously across thousands of tasks. It’s up to humans to assess whether those permissions are still appropriate, what limits should apply and when additional approval is needed. PAM already provides the means to control and audit privileged access according to those decisions, helping organizations put their assessment of business risk into practice.​

Each autonomous service simply needs to have its own identity, a clearly defined supervisor and permissions tied to its specific “role.” In a multi-agent workflow, one agent might retrieve customer data while another updates a business system. Giving both access through the same broad credential would make it difficult to determine which agent performed an action or revoke one agent’s access without disrupting the entire workflow. Existing IGA and PAM capabilities can provide that accountability, provided they’re equipped to govern all identities continuously and revoke access at machine speed.​

AI is new and exciting, but we need to move away from the idea that an agent’s ability to reason about an action gives it the authority to perform it. That decision must remain external to the model and enforceable through the identity infrastructure.​

There’s no escaping the fact that AI agents will become more capable, more autonomous and more deeply embedded in everyday business operations. Every one of those agents must act through an identity, exercise permissions and encounter moments when additional authority is required. As agents become more capable, every organization should be able to explain which permissions were granted, on whose authority and, ultimately, who is accountable for their actions.​

#3165. If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation

Merlin Bise is the CTO of Inbenta. He has built conversational AI since before generative AI.

​A lot of the AI deployed into the customer experience over the past three years isn’t performing. That’s just the reality. And the default response I hear, over and over, is to start all over again, evaluating and paying for a new platform.

In most cases, that’s an expensive way to rebuild the same problem.

I’ve been building AI for customer experience since before generative AI showed up. I watched intent matching give way to generative layers, and now we’re into agentic systems that can reason and act on their own. The platforms keep changing. But it isn’t the model that causes the deployment to fail—it’s the knowledge underneath it. I’ve seen that pattern in nearly every underperforming deployment I’ve looked at, going back years.

And look, none of this is a knock on the decision you made three years ago. You made it with the tools that existed then. Those were very different tools.

Here’s what’s new. Fixing the knowledge layer used to be a multiyear, hand-built project. That’s why re-platforming seemed faster, even when it wasn’t. AI now does the heavy lifting up front. It reads, structures and tags your content before anything goes live, so what customers hear is approved, not improvised. Work that used to take a room full of contractors a full year can now get done in weeks, not quarters. If you wrote off your knowledge problem 12 or 18 months ago as too slow or too expensive, it deserves a second look and, honestly, a lot more optimism than it would have earned back then.

Before you run another evaluation, check three things. You can diagnose all of them without a new vendor.

Content written for someone browsing a help site does a different job than content a model has to parse. A model can have the right document and still give the wrong answer. Why? Because two records that aren’t the same can look the same to a system reading them. If a customer asks about one product configuration and gets information about another, that isn’t because the company chose the wrong model or the customer botched the prompt. It’s a structure and authorship problem, and no new platform is going to fix it for you.

Count them. Most organizations have more duplication than they think. As mentioned earlier, a lot of platforms started with intent matching, then added a generative layer later and kept the original intent base underneath. So, now you’ve got two copies of your content, two governance surfaces and two possible answers to the same question. Contact center stacks do the same thing by channel—one store for digital and another for voice. The answer changes depending on which door the customer walked through. If a policy lives in more than one place, you have a consistency problem, not an AI problem.

This is the one that kills deployments. If the subject matter expert who spots a wrong answer has to file a ticket and wait on an engineer, corrections will never keep pace with the business. The person with the knowledge can’t act. The person who can act has no way to judge whether the answer was right. Give that six months, and the system has drifted away from how the company is supposed to operate, without a single error in the logs. You don’t get an alert—you get confused customers.

In the end, you should have one knowledge store instead of several, content structured so a machine can find the right answer and the people who own the policies in control of the answers. And there’s no need to replace your platform.

The economics back this approach up. A full platform replacement is a six-figure commitment before you even count internal time, and moving off an entrenched stack can run several times that. Fixing the knowledge layer costs a fraction of it. And you keep the asset, no matter what you run on top. If you want to switch platforms later, fine. You’ll be moving a structured, governed knowledge base, instead of hauling the same mess to a new vendor and paying them to discover it.

There’s a second-order benefit, too. A consolidated, governed knowledge layer gives you an audit trail. When a regulator asks about a specific conversation, you need to show the question, the answer, the source and who approved it. It doesn’t matter what platform was used. If you can’t see why your AI said something, you can’t defend it.

Here’s my takeaway. Before you run another evaluation, figure out whether you have a platform problem or a foundation problem. Most of the time, it’s the foundation. And it’s more fixable today than it was when you signed that original contract.

#3163. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3160. ​The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure

Bill Wong - AI Research Fellow, Info-Tech Research Group.

​​In my previous article, we examined the emergence of a new data center asset, the AI factory, which is optimized to run AI workloads. Compared to traditional data centers, AI data center campuses require up to 10 times the total facility power capacity, driven by GPU server racks that consume 12 to 28 times more power per rack and thermal density that requires advanced liquid cooling to handle five times the heat generation.

This new industrial revolution is driving an unprecedented demand for power, transforming the utilities industry from a relatively stable and quiet industry to a growth sector.​ Nations and organizations alike will need to optimize their AI energy strategy in order to flourish during and after this revolution.

After reviewing several national AI energy infrastructure strategies around the world, four distinct strategies stand out. These strategies will shape how nations are planning to build the required energy infrastructure for AI workloads.

• Sovereign Regulation-Driven: These jurisdictions introduce legislation to ensure that AI developers must fund their own power requirements, maintain the reliability of the grid and provide the supporting water infrastructure required for these data centers to prevent rising utility costs. In Canada, the country’s recently published AI strategy champions their grid’s 83% investment in clean power. Australia will require data center providers to generate as much energy as they consume. The EU has introduced a sovereign AI compute platform, EuroHPC JU, which aims to “develop innovative energy-efficient HPC software technologies tailored to exascale and post-exascale supercomputers.”

• Market-Driven: These countries rely on the private sector to drive the building of data centers and leverage easily accessible energy resources. The U.S. has begun by reinvesting into nuclear power plants and the use of small modular reactors. The UK has accelerated AI projects through its AI Growth Zones, fast track permits.

• Localization-Driven: Rather than adding additional workloads to the existing energy grids, some countries are locating new data centers near clean energy sources. Japan’s new collaboration strategy leverages nine designated green energy zones. South Korea’s new strategy directs the movement of 18.4 GW of data center workloads out of Seoul to regional nuclear and small modular reactor clusters.

• State-Driven: China’s government is planning to connect renewable energy resources from its western region to its computing hubs in its eastern region.​

In order to assess a nation or organization’s AI energy strategy, one must examine its energy value chain. This involves identifying the source of its energy, determining how power is generated, determining how power is managed and deployed, understanding the nation’s thermal management and understanding the sustainability strategy the nation or organization has implemented.​

Meaningful metrics in this area focus on the total volume, dependability and carbon footprint of the electricity required by the organization in question’s compute infrastructure. Countries and organizations using clean and renewable energy resources will be able to differentiate their energy infrastructure in a positive manner. On the other hand, countries leveraging fossil fuels, like natural gas, may have the short-term benefit of accessing low-cost energy resources, but they will also encounter long-term emissions problems, which expose them to carbon regulation and creates cost volatility.​

Metrics in this area focus on an energy infrastructure’s capacity and its ability to connect, control and optimize high-density energy flow between the bulk electric grid (external) and its computing facilities (internal).

From a macro-grid point of view, which focuses outside of the data center, leaders can use ultra-high-voltage transmission lines, battery storage and AI-driven load-balancing software to absorb the violent swings in demand from GPU clusters, which can dramatically improve power management.

From a micro-grid standpoint, which focuses inside the data center, leaders have a few things to consider. Today’s AI racks demand 130 to 600 kW, and pushing that much power through legacy wiring can generate wasted heat and requires multiple inefficient conversion steps. Modern operators can implement ±400V or 800V DC systems and solid-state transformers to reduce internal heat loss and conversion steps.​

Legacy air cooling can no longer dissipate the heat generated by today’s AI factories. How a company handles this heat is becoming a competitive advantage for any organization running its own sovereign AI infrastructure. I’ve observed some leading operators switching to direct-to-chip liquid cooling in closed-loop systems, which can slash operational water consumption.

Embracing robust environmental stewardship can help nations and organizations keep their data center expansion efforts sustainable, minimizing ecological disruption while preserving critical local environmental resources. Beyond conservation, some advanced operators are turning thermal management into a revenue stream. By establishing facilities in colder climates (like Canada, the Nordics or Hokkaido, Japan) and capturing the 60- to 80-degree Celsius waste heat directly from server racks, those operators can sell that heat to municipal district heating networks.​

Which AI energy infrastructure strategy is the best for a given organization will depend on several factors, and not all options are available for a given country or geographical location, especially those strategies that can leverage a country’s colder climate to reduce cooling costs.

Countries and organizations need to prioritize and align their energy infrastructure architecture with their nation’s sovereign AI strategy. For instance, sustainability initiatives will likely have the best success in countries like Canada and Nordic nations.

Finally, organizations need to learn how to address the current backlash from people regarding AI data centers near their communities. Builders and operators should be prepared to address questions and concerns surrounding the AI energy value chain they’re leveraging, along with its regional costs and benefits. Leaders should focus on sustainability, environmental impact and delivering an accountability framework for the operations of their proposed AI data center.​

#3151. ​Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows

Corey Ercanbrack is CTO at Vasion, leading the AI-native transformation of a cloud-native platform under FedRAMP High.

A state agency mails benefits notices to citizens, with personal data on the page and legal rights tied to what’s printed. When I asked the administrator responsible for its 30,000 endpoints what governs that output process, he said it runs elsewhere, on infrastructure owned by a different team.​

He wasn’t dodging me. That’s how these environments get built, and it produces a blind spot most leaders inherit rather than create. Information is governed where the data lives. Output is governed where the devices live. Those are two teams with different budgets, reporting lines and definitions of accountability, so the artifact carrying the heaviest legal obligation sits furthest from the controls protecting the information inside it.​

The same split appears across other organizations I work with. Major American cities operating under state public records law must produce any official communication upon request, whatever the medium. Their digital channels are instrumented. Paper isn’t. The specialist responsible for its endpoint estate acknowledged that if he sent a printed memo, someone would still have to find it.​

That gap has been survivable because a person stands in it. The employee who printed the memo knows he printed it, and if a request arrives two years later, someone can ask him. In audit terms, he’s a compensating control: what you document and test when the designed control can’t be implemented. Nobody documented this one. It’s been load-bearing for 30 years without appearing in a control matrix, which is why removing it looks costless.​

Agents remove it. Deloitte’s 2026 “State of AI in the Enterprise” report surveyed 3,235 business and IT leaders across 24 countries. Nearly three in four companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, while one in five reports a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Among the capabilities Deloitte names as crucial are audit trails capturing the full chain of agent actions.​

When an instruction comes from a system rather than a person, there may be no human intent to reconstruct later and no awareness that a records obligation was triggered. Unless the workflow was designed to capture that context, automation can generate unaccounted output far faster than the informal human process it replaced. Leaders may be automating away a control they never knew they depended on.

Most AI governance programs are scoped to the application: which model acted, what data it reached, what it was authorized to do and what it produced. That work is necessary, but it is not sufficient, because operational documents don’t stay inside one application.​

I have watched a prior authorization request move from a medical record to paper, to a fax machine, to an insurer and return days later as an email. Each system recorded its portion and completed the step it was designed to handle, but none held the thread connecting them: the only view from which the organization could reconstruct the full event. The application finished its task. The business did not, and governance was scoped to the first while the obligation attaches to the second.​

An IT leader at a global distributor gave me a paperless example. More countries where his company operates now require documents to be deposited with a government authority. The regulation specifies where the document must be sent without specifying how it gets there. Treating the output boundary as a printing problem misses the broader obligation to govern the document throughout its journey.​

If an auditor picked up an AI-generated document tomorrow, what could you prove about it? Four questions help determine the answer.

1. Identity: Who or what produced it? Once a document is printed, exported or faxed, the chain of identity breaks. The artifact no longer shows which agent created it, who initiated the action or where the information came from.​

2. Authorization: Who approved its release? Knowing who generated a document is not the same as knowing whether release was authorized. A finished document proves neither.​

3. Audit: What happened between input and output? An agent extracts information, changes content and generates instructions. Record only the finished document, and you can’t show what it did. The record has to replay what went in, what changed, who acted and where it went.​

4. Retention: Can you find and classify it? Without the first three, you accumulate documents you’re obligated to protect and unable to trace, turning a governance gap into a storage liability.​

Miss one, and you don’t have end-to-end AI governance. Instead, you have a partial record of an action that continued without you. I recommend running these four against a live workflow before expanding agent authority. The gaps you find are the ones an agent will only widen.

The instinct is to connect every system, but these integrations are often fragile and require ongoing maintenance whenever one side changes.

Start with the work instead.​ Pick one operational document this week and follow it from creation to final disposition. Mark every point where somebody prints, exports, faxes, signs, scans or retypes information, and keep going after the data leaves the application. The handoffs are where governance stops without announcing it. Test the four questions at each one. Wherever context breaks, you’ve found the real boundary of your program before an auditor does.​

The workflows that hold up often share one trait: The record was designed before the agent was deployed, rather than reconstructed after someone asked for it. That means someone decided where human review belonged and what needed to be recorded at every step, including the agent’s actions. You can’t deploy first and gather the evidence later. The record has to be created when the action occurs, or it may not exist at all. And the destination is rarely as modern as the agent. I’ve watched sophisticated automation end with a fax because that’s what the recipient accepts.​​

Governance has to follow the information through every handoff. The practical perimeter is everywhere the information goes.​​

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

#3148. Midterms Are Over. Here's What History Says the S&P 500 Does Next.

With the election behind us, investors can have a lot more confidence in what the future holds.

The 2026 midterm elections are officially behind us. The 120th Congress is set to convene on Jan. 3, 2027, with quite a few new representatives and senators.

The legislature can play a significant role in the stock market's performance through laws that impact consumers, businesses, and investors. But there's always some uncertainty about what a new Congress will be able to accomplish, especially in a divided government.

So, many investors may be wondering how the stock market usually performs after midterm elections.

Investors don't like uncertainty. The value of a stock is based on expectations for future earnings, but with greater uncertainty, there's a broader range of potential outcomes. As a result, investors demand a larger margin of safety for stocks when uncertainty is higher.

The lead-up to a major political election like the midterms brings a lot of uncertainty. But once investors know the results of an election, they can create forecasts with much more confidence.

As a result, stock returns are typically lower in election years and higher in the off years. Since 1990, midterm election years have produced far weaker S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) returns than any other year in the four-year election cycle, averaging just 2.8%.

That said, 2026 has seen the market hold up better than average. The S&P 500 was up more than 10% for the year heading into the election. Still, that's not outside historical norms, as the average is weighed down by dismal market performance in 2002 and 2022.

That means the strong post-election performance we've seen throughout history could be poised to repeat itself. The S&P 500 has produced positive returns in 19 out of 19 of the 12-month post-midterm-election periods since 1950. The average return for the index during those periods is 15.1%. That's well above the historical average returns for the S&P 500.

While Congress (and expectations for what the legislature will do) play a big role in the everyday lives of Americans and the prospects for American businesses, the biggest force impacting corporate profits is the economy itself. Steady GDP growth, low unemployment, stable prices and interest rates, and consumer spending will have a much bigger impact on stock prices than Congress.

Analysts at U.S. Bank stripped out a handful of outlier years in history when major economic shocks had an outsize negative impact on stock returns during midterm election years. They found that excluding those years from the average market returns in midterm election years since 1900 yielded returns that were very similar in the 12 months leading up to the election and the 12 months following it. That said, the analysts don't account for positive economic surprises that may have led to outliers on the other side of the equation.

Investors are better off focusing on the fundamentals of specific companies, sectors, and the economy as a whole. Politics can certainly play a role in those, but it's not the be-all and end-all in determining corporate profits and stock returns. Maintaining a steady passive investment approach and investing at regular intervals should produce solid results regardless of the election cycle. Those focused on individual stocks can always find opportunities in any market, regardless of who's in charge of the legislature.

Adam Levy has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends U.S. Bancorp. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3147. Draymond Green reveals what Steve Kerr told 0-3 Warriors to fuel winning streak

Draymond Green reveals what Steve Kerr told 0-3 Warriors to fuel winning streak originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Steve Kerr did not remember what he told the Warriors after they fell to 0-3. But Draymond Green and Steph Curry do.

Golden State beat the Miami Heat 120-100 on Thursday night for its sixth straight win, with Curry scoring 29 points, Yaxel Lendeborg adding 17 points, eight rebounds and six assists, and Green dishing a season-high 11 assists.

Afterward, Green joined "Warriors Postgame Live" on NBC Sports Bay Area and was asked what changed since that start, and he pointed to Kerr's message in the locker room.

"One thing I've always said is Steve Kerr always knows what to say, and even when no one else may feel the way that we should feel, he's going to say the right things," Green told Bonta Hill, Juan Toscano-Anderson, Chris Mullin and Festus Ezeli. "So when we were 0-3, he came into the locker room and gave this speech as if we were 3-0, and it was kind of in that moment where people may start to wane a little bit, and he got us going. And then we got the Denver win and everything else has rolled since."

Asked if he remembered the speech, Kerr could not recite it, but he remembered the thinking behind it.

"I don't remember what I said, but I felt good about our team even when we were 0-3," Kerr said. "We had a really good training camp, we have a deep team, we have a lot of talent."

Kerr said the timing of the losses mattered more than the number.

"The main thing is if you lose three in a row in the middle of the season, nobody notices, but when you lose three in a row to start the year, everybody sees it," Kerr said. "I just tried to get the guys to relax and play because I knew we were going to be pretty good."

Curry said the speech came after the third loss in Phoenix, and that the message was about patience and what Kerr saw on film.

"He just mentioned sticking with the process and the things that he noticed on film and just the feel in games," Curry said. "We were really close to being able to put together winning performances."

The Memphis loss was a good example. The Warriors led by 12 with 3:47 left in the home opener before losing 111-108, and Curry said the pieces of a winning team were already there apart from the final four minutes. What stood out to him most about Kerr's message was something simpler.

"I think the biggest part was that he was proud of how hard we were playing, and everyone is taking on that challenge as well when they come in the game," Curry said.

Green said the other change has been Lendeborg, whose rise has lifted the group's confidence.

"The way Yaxel's stepping up, it definitely has changed the mindset a little bit," Green said. "Obviously the mindset here is to always try to win games, but I think you just feel a little more confident about it than we did before."

Kerr said the group has been easy to coach. He praised Green's leadership, along with that of Curry and Al Horford, and the energy from the young players who come off the bench or, in Lendeborg's case, start.

"It's a really connected group of guys," Kerr said. "So it's a fun team to coach."

Kerr might not remember the words, but the Warriors have won six straight since he said them.

#3146. Stop Measuring Technology Adoption And Start Measuring What It Changes

Gayathri Kolandaisami | Doctoral Researcher | Human-centered digital and AI transformation in water utilities and critical infrastructure.

A technology investment can succeed on paper but still fail to solve the problem it was meant to solve.

I saw this happen long before the AI era. When I started my technology career in 2005, my job was to build and maintain the software used by my clients. Over time, I learned that building the technology was only part of the equation. We also needed to understand why it was needed and how the work was being done:

1. What problem were we trying to solve, or what improvement did we want in productivity, efficiency or service delivery?

3. What should the ideal process look like?

That way of thinking stayed with me as my career moved from software development into larger digital transformation projects. It left me with a principle I still believe today: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

I was in a position to observe an organization’s reaction when an AI coding assistant was introduced to its developers. The management had invested in this technology long before I got involved in the organization. However, they hadn’t understood or researched where and how that technology could help the developers, what the benefits of using it would be or whether the tool was apt for their environment. The outcome was a KPI introduced at an organizational level to measure the tool’s adoption. So, a developer was considered to have met this part of their KPI by simply showing that they’d adopted this tool.

This left me asking myself: Had we moved away from measuring the outcomes of the technology to simply measuring its adoption? That’s when I realized that we’d started working for the technology and not the other way around.

Make no mistake—every cell in my body screams technology. I want to develop new technologies that could solve a lot of global challenges. I’m a strong believer in new technologies, and I’m fascinated by how quickly AI is evolving. But I also think that we’re forgetting why we invented these technologies in the first place. Sometimes, we race toward adopting the newest technology without knowing what we were trying to make better.

Technology is a means to solve a problem, improve a process or create a better outcome. The technology itself isn’t the outcome.

I came across a 2025 study published in Management Science. The researchers estimated that using an AI coding assistant increased completed tasks by 26.08%. In contrast, another 2025 study that examined experienced open-source developers working on mature repositories found that developers took 19% longer when using the AI tools that were tested.

The lesson from these studies is that technology doesn’t produce the same result in different environments.​

Organizations can easily measure the wrong outcome.

Take software development, for example. Building new software or making a change to existing software can involve requirements gathering, design, programming, testing, bug fixing and implementation. Let’s say we implemented an AI coding assistant. We may think that this tool could cut programming time substantially. However, that isn’t the whole picture, is it? What happens if the AI-assisted code requires more testing? What if developers spend additional time reviewing and correcting it? What if defects increase, and some of the time saved in programming is consumed later in the process?

If we measure only programming time in this scenario, we may conclude that the technology has been highly successful. However, if we measure the entire journey from requirements to delivery, we may reach a very different conclusion.

The entire process matters when measuring the outcome of the technology. If the problem that the technology is addressing is slow delivery, measure the complete cycle from requirements to release. If the problem is quality, understand defects and rework. If the objective is greater capacity, determine whether the team can actually complete more meaningful work.

The metric should originate from the problem, the context and the process, not simply from the technology.

I prefer piloting the technology before widely adopting it. A pilot isn’t simply an opportunity to prove that a technology works. It’s an opportunity to discover whether it works for your people, your processes and your particular environment.

If employees aren’t using a technology, that should initially be treated as information rather than a performance problem. Perhaps they need training. Perhaps the technology doesn’t fit their workflow. Perhaps it works well for some tasks but not others. Perhaps the existing technology environment, including legacy systems or code, limits its usefulness. Or perhaps it simply isn’t solving a sufficiently important problem.

Adoption is only one part of the story. Technology can also affect employee and customer experience. It may remove repetitive work and allow employees to focus on more meaningful activities, but it may also create additional work when people have to check, correct or validate its output. Some outcomes are tangible, such as time saved, costs reduced, greater capacity or more work completed. Others are harder to quantify, such as employee satisfaction, customer satisfaction, trust and confidence in the service being delivered. They’re still outcomes.

As organizations embrace increasingly powerful technologies, the temptation will be to measure what’s easiest to see: licenses purchased, systems deployed, users onboarded or usage rates. Those numbers have their place, but they don’t answer the most important question: What became better because we introduced the technology?

Always remember: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

#3143. The AI Control Gap: Companies Adopting AI Must Learn What Wall Street Learned The Hard Way

Samuel Kaluvuri, CEO of ApyHub, works on API infrastructure and runtime policy enforcement and holds a PhD in security assurance.

Somewhere inside a large bank, an AI agent has a name, a login ID and a manager who has to write its performance review.

This is less eccentric than it sounds, and it’s one of the more rational things I believe banking has done this year. These are institutions with serious risk functions and long memories for things that lose money quickly. Looking for a way to control software that acts on its own, they reached for the instruments they trusted: an identity, a reporting line and someone answerable for it.​

They are developing ways to manage a new kind of software, and the questions they are working through are ones other companies adopting agentic AI will increasingly need to address.​​

Enterprise software has always come with controls: permissions, approval chains, segregation of duties and audit logs. That worked for 30 years because a person asked for something, another looked at it and the system did exactly what was approved.

All three assumptions have stopped being true. The requester is now software operating at machine speed, and approval no longer describes the action. When someone signs off on “handle customer onboarding,” nothing in that sentence says which systems get touched, what data leaves which jurisdiction or what the agent does when it meets a case nobody thought about. The approval covers intent, but the risk lives in the path.

Put an approval workflow in front of a system taking thousands of autonomous actions, and you have not built oversight. You have built a very fast queue of things you already agreed to.

Finance learned this the hard (and expensive) way. Sign-off on trades worked until trades stopped happening at human speed. In 2012, Knight Capital pushed faulty code into production and lost more than $460 million in 45 minutes. By the time a conventional approval process notices a problem like that, the money is gone.

The response was not a better approval workflow. Control moved into the execution path: limits enforced before an order left the building, kill switches and real-time surveillance. Regulators then went further, and this is the part I believe is worth borrowing. Under the Securities and Exchange Commission’s market access rule, those controls must sit under the firm’s direct and exclusive control.

A broker may buy the risk technology from a third party, but it must keep the ability to monitor and adjust the controls in real time and cannot simply rely on the provider’s assurance that they work. The point of intervention moved to where the machine acts and stayed with whoever carries the liability.

So where does control over an agent actually live?

Not in the model. It sits below where these products are demonstrated and sold, in the software that determines which systems an agent can reach, what it may do with them, when it stops and what gets written down. Change the model, and the agent gets cleverer. Change that control layer, and it can no longer touch your payments system.

Three capabilities determine how effective these controls are: the ability to limit an agent’s actions before they happen, stop them while they are underway and independently reconstruct what the agent did afterward.​​

Running infrastructure that sits in the path of these calls gives you a different view. Human traffic arrives one action at a time. Agent traffic arrives in bursts: dozens of calls in a few seconds while the thing works through a task. Everyone can check whether the task completed, but few see what it read on the way or where it sent what it found.​

This is where the buying decision becomes important. A company does not necessarily have to hand this layer to its vendor. An enterprise can retain control over its access policies, gateways, transaction limits and logging, as many already do for systems used by employees. But those controls need to be deliberately extended to cover agents. Otherwise, buyers may inherit runtime rules configured by engineers focused on task completion or rely on defaults that are rarely revisited. These settings may also fall outside the governance documents boards and compliance teams regularly review.​

An employee’s limits are typically enforced through systems the bank controls and can adjust as needs change. An agent’s limits depend on the systems governing its actions, which may be managed by the buyer, the vendor or both. If the buyer has not established who controls that layer, important decisions may effectively be made elsewhere. The purchase is therefore not just software that performs tasks; it also involves a set of operating rules, some of which may already be in place before the buyer evaluates them.​

Platforms should be assessed not only on what an agent can do in a demonstration but also on where controls are enforced and who can change them. If a platform does not provide the necessary oversight, building a replacement layer may be one option, but it is not always practical or sufficient. In some cases, the better decision may be to keep a workflow under human supervision until the organization can establish controls appropriate for autonomous operation. That may be a less appealing sales proposition, but it can be the more responsible choice.​​​​

The regulatory direction is visible. In June 2026, the Financial Stability Board warned that the autonomy of AI agents can amplify risks that materialize at great speed.

Supervisors are no more likely to accept “our vendor handles that” than they were for outsourced trading infrastructure. Meanwhile, the platforms are sold on handing the work off entirely.

Every autonomous system runs inside rules that determine what it can do, and those rules exist whether or not the board has seen them. The question for a vendor is not merely who wrote them but whether you can inspect them, change them and, when the machine is already moving, enforce them yourself.​
