#3142. Luka Garza is making life easier for the Celtics

Hours before the Boston Celtics and Milwaukee Bucks faced off Wednesday night, Luka Garza was already getting to work. He joined the team's Stay Ready crew, warming up alongside Mitchell Robinson and Jordan Walsh while his father, Frank, watched from courtside near the baseline.

Garza wasn't in Boston's Jayson Tatum-less starting lineup, but that didn't matter. His routine remained the same.

That's standard for Garza. Each night, he knows the moment could arrive when Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla calls his number. On Wednesday, it came early, with 5:37 remaining in the first quarter. He checked in for Hugo González and knocked down his first shot — a wide-open 3-pointer from the wing — to extend Boston's lead over Milwaukee to 25-8.

Down the other end, less than a minute later, Garza came away with a steal. Payton Pritchard capitalized on the extra possession by draining a jumper. Garza knocked down each of his three 3-point attempts to lead the Celtics with 11 points at halftime. Mazzulla didn't turn to him nearly as much in the second half, but he had already made his impact felt.

In just 18 minutes against Milwaukee, Garza reinforced his reliability.

Oct 14, 2026; Boston, Massachusetts, USA; Boston Celtics center Luka Garza (52) shoots the ball during warmups prior to a game against the Charlotte Hornets at TD Garden. Mandatory Credit: Bob DeChiara-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

He went from playing 8.9 minutes per game through the first five games of the season to averaging 18.7 over the last three against Orlando, Houston and Milwaukee. In return, Garza has rewarded Mazzulla's increased deployment of the 27-year-old veteran, posting averages of 12.3 points, 4.7 rebounds, and two assists since the start of November.

Throughout it all, Garza has maintained his knack for creating second chances on the offensive glass. He's grabbed 15 offensive rebounds, just behind Robinson (17) and Neemias Queta (18) for the team lead. He's also re-emerged as a dangerous 3-point threat, much like last season. His 52.4% clip from beyond the arc leads the Celtics and ranks first among Eastern Conference centers averaging at least 2.6 attempts.

From the corners, Garza has shot 6-of-8, going 11-of-21 overall from three through the first eight games this season.

The drive-and-kick option for teammates like Paul George and Pritchard to find Garza on the perimeter was utilized Wednesday night, and it's proven to be an effective one. Garza is Mazzulla's best 3-point shooter among Boston's centers, making him a legitimate outside shooting threat that opposing defenses can't afford to leave unattended.

Entering a season where Queta vs. Robinson starting center debates dominated the discourse surrounding Boston's front court, Garza has quietly made his case to play each night. He's done his part to support the group amid Robinson's early-season adjustment struggles by remaining prepared to contribute. And despite understanding what playing behind Queta and Robinson could mean for his minutes on any given night, Garza has emerged as a leader by example in Boston's reserve unit.

The Celtics can call on him to perform alongside the starters while also counting on him to work with those coming off the bench. Garza occupies something of an older brother role in helping teammates navigate the same challenges he previously faced during his three-year stint with the Minnesota Timberwolves.

In Boston, he's able to simultaneously shine and stay hungry.

It doesn't take much for Garza to make a difference either. Sometimes it'll go unnoticed when he battles for a second-chance opportunity because the Celtics fail to convert. Other times, he might not get the seven 3-point attempts he did in Houston. But the effort is always there.

This season, he's averaging 7.5 points with 3.1 rebounds on 48.7 percent shooting. That doesn't even begin to tell half the story of what he's been doing on the floor.

The Celtics can't offer Garza 60-plus starts, but the coaching staff remains vigilant at all times. His impact off the bench has been rewarded, sending the message that the team is well aware of what he's brought to the table. That's certainly encouraging for Garza, who's begun to carve out a role in a Boston front court that was heavily considered crowded throughout much of the offseason.

#3139. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3138. Why The Same Threat Means Different Things To Different Companies

Anuj Goel is CEO and co-founder of Cyware, a company focused on intelligence-led cybersecurity and operational resilience.

Every threat intelligence feed shares a blind spot: It knows the threat but nothing about our specific environment.

The feed carries threat data; only our environment provides context. The industry has spent a decade refining data when it should have focused on environment-specific context.

As a practitioner, the hardest conversations were never about explaining suspicious activity. They were about explaining why it reached us when the best intelligence available had already flagged it. We had the indicators. We just weren’t connecting them to the assets they might reach. What surprised me then, and still does, is that the problem was never a shortage of intelligence or its accuracy. It was the missing step between knowing about a threat and knowing, in real time, that it applied to us. That experience shaped how I think about this space, and it is why I believe context, not volume, is where the real work is.

Intelligence has no universal version; “good intelligence” depends on sector and geography, not sheer volume.

Financial institutions require fraud-focused reporting, while industrial operators need OT intelligence built around controllers and plant-floor realities. Neither is “better,” but they aren’t interchangeable. Relevance is inherently specific to who we are and where we operate.

No feed can see inside our walls, and that’s where we decide which known threats matter to our environment.

Relevance is derived from the assets we actually run. The identities and access paths that connect them. What is business-critical versus incidental? Where our controls are strong and where they are thin. This is the ground truth every external indicator has to be measured against. An indicator evaluated against our environment becomes elevated to a prioritized, actionable risk. The same indicator, without an environment behind it, is just a rumor about someone else’s network.

Relevance is the product of the two: the intelligence our sector trusts, correlated with the infrastructure, data and assets we have. Neither input alone produces it. The best feeds in the world, unmeasured against our environment, cannot tell us what to do first on Monday morning. A perfect map of our environment, with no sector intelligence flowing into it, has nothing to act on either.

Consider when identical intelligence arrives at two different organizations.

For one, the indicator maps to a critical, internet-facing application reachable by elevated identities. This context resolves to a high-urgency risk, requiring immediate isolation and escalation.

For the second, the same indicator maps to a decommissioned service or a segment with existing controls. This context resolves to a low-urgency risk requiring only logging.

Same feed. Same indicator. Same morning. Two entirely different answers, and two entirely different actions determined by adding the context.

This is what customer-specific context means in practice. It is not a cleaner presentation of the same data. It is a different computed result for every organization, because the inputs on the other side of the equation differ for every organization. It determines not only whether to act, but what action is warranted, in what order and with how much confidence. Any system that skips this step applies one global severity score to environments that share almost nothing in common.

One line is worth drawing sharply, because the industry constantly blurs it. Tagging an indicator as malicious is enrichment, attaching a known attribute to a piece of data. Knowing that the same indicator belongs to a campaign actively targeting our sector, that a machine on our finance team touched it three days ago and that the identity behind that machine is exposed, that is context. Enrichment adds metadata. Context fuels risk reduction.

This is also why dozens of feeds never added up to an answer. More raw indicators, unmeasured against our environment, is a larger pile to triage, not a clearer picture. Most security leaders have a graveyard of unused subscriptions to prove it.

Increasingly, the systems making security decisions are not human analysts reading a feed. They are platforms and agents consuming intelligence to prioritize, correlate and act, and a decision engine is only as good as what we put into it.

Feed a system raw, one-size-fits-all intelligence and it inherits the problem we started with: It cannot tell a live risk from an irrelevant one, because the feed never carried that distinction. The input has to be measured against that specific environment, already resolved into what is relevant, exposed and worth acting on.

This reframes what “having threat intelligence” should mean. A feed is not the same as threat context, and a raw feed piped into a decision-making tool does not become context on arrival. Intelligence has to be made relevant before it becomes an input, per sector, per environment, per organization or every tool consuming it is reasoning from a rumor.

The organizations—and increasingly, the systems—best positioned for what is coming are not the ones holding the most feeds. Instead, the organizations receiving actionable context are those that understand what threat intelligence means for them and are equipped to drive necessary security actions.​​

#3135. Drilling Tools (DTI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Offshore push and a pending Saltire deal shape the quarter's outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Drilling Tools International Corporation (DTI +1.42%) reported sequential improvements in revenue and adjusted EBITDA, citing a recovery in North American rig counts and the initial contribution from offshore technology investments. Management stated that the company is currently focused on its international growth strategy, highlighted by the pending acquisition of Saltire Energy, which is intended to increase the Eastern Hemisphere's contribution to approximately 40% of pro forma revenue. The company reported that it has raised its capital expenditure outlook to fund specialized tools for new offshore contracts in Europe, which began generating full run-rate revenue in September. Management indicated that it is prioritizing deleveraging the balance sheet following the Saltire transaction, with a target of reaching 1x net leverage within two years of closing.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the Drilling Tools International Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Ken Dennard, Investor Relations. Thank you, Ken. You may begin.

Ken Dennard: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate your joining us for DTI's 2026 Third Quarter Conference Call and webcast. With me today are Wayne Prejean, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and David Johnson, Chief Financial Officer. Following my remarks, management will provide a review of third quarter results, an update on the pending acquisition of Saltire Energy, and the 2026 outlook before opening the call for questions. There will be a replay of today's call, and it will be available by webcast on the company's investor website at investors.dti.inc. There will also be a telephonic recorded replay available until November 13.

Please note that any information reported on this call speaks only as of today, November 6, 2026, and therefore, you are advised that time-sensitive information may no longer be accurate as of the time of any replay listening or transcript reading. Also, comments on this call will contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the United States federal securities laws, including statements regarding the proposed acquisition of Saltire Energy Limited and Foxley Energy Limited, together known as Saltire. The anticipated timing, completion, and benefits of the transaction-related financing and the expected financial impact and future operating performance of the combined company. These forward-looking statements reflect the current views of DTI's management.

However, various risks, uncertainties, and contingencies could cause actual results, performance, or achievements to differ materially from those expressed in the statements made by management, including the possibility that the transaction may not be completed on the anticipated terms or timing or at all, the failure to satisfy closing conditions or obtain required approvals, financing risks, and integration risks. The listener or reader is encouraged to read DTI's annual report on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, current reports on Form 8-K, and the registration statement on Form S-4, including the section entitled Risk Factors therein, to understand certain of those risks, uncertainties, and contingencies.

In connection with the proposed transaction, DTI has filed a registration statement on Form S-4 with the SEC that includes a preliminary proxy statement and prospectus. Investors and security holders are urged to read these documents carefully, including any amendments and the definitive proxy statement and prospectus documents when available because they contain important information about DTI, Saltire, and the proposed transaction. Free copies will be available on the SEC's website at sec.gov and on DTI's Investor Relations site. DTI, Saltire, Foxley, and their respective directors and executive officers may be deemed participants in the solicitation of proxies from DTI stockholders in connection with the proposed transaction.

Information about these participants and their interest is contained in the proxy statement and prospectus. DTI undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statement except as required by law. The comments today will also include certain non-GAAP financial measures, including but not limited to adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA margin, adjusted free cash flow, adjusted net loss, adjusted loss per share, net debt, and with respect to Saltire, run-rate adjusted EBITDA. We provide these non-GAAP results for informational purposes and they should not be considered in isolation from most directly comparable GAAP measures.

A discussion on why we believe these non-GAAP measures are useful to investors, certain limitations of the use of these measures, and reconciliations of DTI's historical non-GAAP measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures can be found in the earnings release, which is available on the Investor Relations section of the website at investors.dti.inc and in the filings with the SEC. Saltire's run-rate figures are management estimates based on Saltire's unaudited monthly financial information, have not been reviewed by DTI's auditors, and are not necessarily indicative of Saltire's results for any future period. And now with that behind me, I'd like to turn the call over to Wayne Prejean, DTI's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. Wayne.

R. Prejean: Thanks, Ken, and good morning, everyone. I will provide some opening remarks before handing the call over to David to review the financials. I'll then come back and provide a few additional thoughts before we open it up for questions. We are pleased with our third quarter performance. As we anticipated, the second half improvement is underway, and our results are building momentum heading into the fourth quarter. Rising rig counts in several of our key operating areas drove much of that progress, and utilization continues to improve as our tools gain traction in high-performance well applications.

We generated $40.6 million of revenue, up approximately 7% sequentially and 5% year-over-year, and $9.5 million of adjusted EBITDA, up 14% from the second quarter, with adjusted EBITDA margin expanding to approximately 23%. We also generated $3.8 million of adjusted free cash flow, even as we continued our planned growth investments in Norway and other offshore markets. Building on that momentum, shortly after quarter end, we announced the transformative acquisition of Saltire Energy, a pivotal step in DTI's growth story and one that is expected to significantly expand our international scale. I'll discuss more about this important event later in the call. Turning back to the quarter, we were encouraged to see that our results built steadily each month.

Revenue grew sequentially across North America and in key Eastern Hemisphere markets, and margins improved across the business. September was our strongest month of the quarter and our first month of approximately $4 million of adjusted EBITDA in 2026, providing a healthy exit rate as we enter the fourth quarter. Our average monthly adjusted EBITDA has stepped up each quarter this year, and we expect that progression to continue in the fourth quarter. Combined with a stable to growing rig count environment, that positions us well as we work toward our full-year goals. In North America, the recovery we began to see late in the second quarter carried through the third.

The average U.S. rig count increased more than 6% sequentially to 589 rigs in the third quarter. And that momentum continued into October with the rig count surpassing 600 rigs for the first time in more than 2 years. On U.S. land, our own activity rebound trailed the initial rig addition slightly. This 2- to 3-month lag is not uncommon in our business, but our activity caught up as the quarter progressed, and the number of rigs running DTI tools has grown alongside the broader rig count, supporting higher tool utilization in the largest part of our business.

In Canada, activity rebounded sharply following the seasonal spring breakup, with the average rig count up more than 40% from the second quarter. That recovery built through September, and the Canadian rig count exited the quarter above 200 rigs and ahead of prior-year levels. Offshore, our ClearPath technology continues to gain traction in the Gulf of Mexico. Commercial terms held firm throughout the quarter, and as our customers finalized their 2027 budgets and contract awards, we are focused on securing long-term agreements with attractive economics that reflect the value we deliver. We continue to win business on the strength of our reliability, service, and the specialized tools that today's high-performance wells demand.

And our North American business, which remains the foundation of DTI, is growing again. In the Eastern Hemisphere, we continue to make targeted investments in our ClearPath stabilizer technology during the third quarter to support significant new contracts in Europe, under which we are deploying a fleet of ClearPath and other specialized tools across Norway, the broader North Sea, and other offshore markets. These investments are backed by long-term rental agreements, and we expect them to generate attractive returns. In the Middle East, activity was relatively flat in the third quarter as the regional conflict persists. And we expect modest improvement there in the fourth quarter.

As I noted in our Saltire call last month, operators, service companies, and national oil companies have largely found ways to manage logistically around the ongoing disruptions. And on the ground, it is business as usual. Looking ahead, several of the industry's largest service companies have pointed to the Middle East as a key area of growth in 2027, and our own customer conversations support that view. Our Deep Casing Tools and Drill-N-Ream product lines continue to contribute to our growing Eastern Hemisphere story.

As I mentioned at the outset, last month we announced a definitive agreement to acquire Saltire Energy, an Aberdeen-based international downhole tool rental company with an established presence across the North Sea, the Middle East, Asia Pacific, and other key Eastern Hemisphere growth markets. This is a significant transaction for DTI and marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter for our company. For those of you who were unable to join our call last month, Saltire's business closely mirrors our own. Like DTI, Saltire rents the mission-critical downhole tools operators depend on, including bottom-hole assembly components, pipe and tubulars, and pressure control equipment, and it does so in markets where we have long wanted to be at scale.

These are two highly complementary businesses with similar operating models, distinct geographies, and limited customer overlap. Saltire dramatically accelerates an international growth strategy we have been executing for years. We have deliberately grown our Eastern Hemisphere business from about 8% of revenue in 2024 to 14% in 2025 and approximately 19% in the third quarter of this year. Saltire takes that to approximately 40% of pro forma revenue in a single step.

It grows our rental fleet from approximately 63,000 tools to a combined fleet of more than 100,000, more than doubles our addressable rig market, and gives us an established distribution network to bring technologies like ClearPath, Drill-N-Ream, and Deep Casing Tools to Saltire's international operator, OFS, and national oil company customers. Just as importantly, the combination leaves DTI well balanced across the global drilling market. If disruption in the Middle East persists, we would expect higher commodity prices to continue supporting activity in North America, where we have a strong and growing position. If the region stabilizes, we expect international activity, led by the Middle East, to accelerate, and Saltire gives us the scale to capture it.

Our tools and personnel are also highly mobile, allowing us to redeploy them wherever activity is strongest rather than carrying idle capacity in a slower market. Either way, we are positioned to benefit with meaningful revenue and earnings in both hemispheres and the flexibility to follow activity. Financially, we expect the transaction to be immediately accretive. We expect it to be accretive to adjusted EBITDA margin and adjusted free cash flow per share in the first year following closing. And that expectation does not depend on cost or revenue synergies. Any synergies we realize would be incremental. Saltire's strong cash generation also gives the combined company a clear path to delever quickly, which David will walk through shortly.

Finally, the Loggie family's decision to take approximately 30% of the combined company in DTI common stock reflects our shared conviction that these businesses are stronger together and that the most meaningful value creation is still ahead of us. Since the announcement, I've met with numerous customers and Saltire employees throughout Europe and the Middle East. The Saltire employees I've met are excited about joining DTI and are looking forward to the opportunities that a diversified platform can offer. The customers we have spoken with have been equally encouraged by the prospect of a broader product offering and greater financial strength behind the service they rely on.

We are working through an amended Form S-4, the process is progressing as planned, and we look forward to the special meeting of stockholders in the coming months. We continue to expect the transaction to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to DTI stockholder approval, any required regulatory approvals, and other customary closing conditions. In the meantime, we have already begun integration planning with teams from both companies working together on systems and processes so we are positioned to execute from day 1. Lastly, I'd like to highlight an important moment for our identity as a public company. Late last month, we rolled out our new brand.

While we have historically gone to market as Drilling Tools International, going forward, we will be known simply as DTI. Our new tagline, "At the Core of Drilling," captures what we have always done, delivering the mission-critical tools at the heart of every well we support. Our people and our tools are at the core of our customer success, and that is exactly where we intend to stay. The rebrand is the natural next step in our One DTI initiative. As we have discussed on prior calls, our goal as we've grown through acquisitions has been to bring every business we've acquired under 1 roof with a common identity. The new brand is more than a new logo.

It reflects who we have become, 1 company with 1 culture, and a shared commitment to safety, service, and our customers. We also see it as a catalyst to engage and unite our employees around a common purpose. And the timing is deliberate. As we work toward closing the Saltire acquisition, One DTI gives us a clear framework for welcoming the Saltire team into the DTI organization. Now, I'll pass it over to David to take you through our results in great detail, provide an update on the Saltire acquisition, and discuss our 2026 outlook. David?

David Johnson: Thank you, Wayne. Please refer to yesterday's earnings release for a detailed breakdown of our third quarter financial results and the related financial tables. I will use this time to offer further insight into specific financial metrics, provide an update on the proposed Saltire acquisition, and discuss our 2026 guidance. We generated total consolidated revenue of approximately $40.6 million during the third quarter, with tool rental revenue of $32 million and product sales revenue totaling $8.7 million. Net loss attributable to stockholders for the third quarter was approximately $2.6 million, or a loss of $0.07 per share, which includes approximately $2.2 million of transaction expenses, primarily related to the pending Saltire acquisition and related financing.

Adjusted net loss was approximately $433,000, or an adjusted loss per share of $0.01. Third quarter adjusted EBITDA was $9.5 million, and adjusted free cash flow was approximately $3.8 million. I'll offer a bit of color on the movement in revenue and margins. Tool rental revenue increased approximately 8% sequentially and was essentially flat year-over-year, reflecting improving North American land activity and the first meaningful returns on our growth investments in the prior quarter. Tool rental gross margin improved to approximately 77%, benefiting from improved utilization and firmer commercial terms. Product sales revenue increased approximately 25% year-over-year, driven primarily by higher tool recovery revenue. As activity levels increase, we typically see more tools lost downhole or damaged beyond repair.

And as a result, September was one of our strongest tool recovery months in some time. As our value-added product lines continue to gain traction with operators, we expect to benefit from operating leverage with improved margins alongside higher revenue. Capital expenditures in the third quarter were approximately $5.7 million compared to $4.2 million in the second quarter, with the bulk of the increase reflecting our planned ClearPath investments in offshore markets. We also built some additional tools with specific geometry during the quarter to support rising activity on U.S. land.

With those investments, we expect lower capital expenditures during the fourth quarter, and any incremental growth investments will be focused on high-demand tools to support momentum into 2027, guided by customer contracts and planned activity. Maintenance CapEx for the third quarter remained approximately 12% of total revenue. As we always like to remind everyone on this topic, our maintenance CapEx is primarily funded by tool recovery revenue, which keeps our rental tool fleet relevant and sustainable regardless of market trends.

Turning to the balance sheet, as of September 30, 2026, we had $3 million of cash and cash equivalents and net debt of $47.4 million, a reduction of approximately $4.3 million from June 30, even with our targeted growth investments made during the quarter. In light of increased investments in the third quarter, that reduction primarily reflects our exit of an existing product line through a sale-leaseback to its original inventor with the approximately $4 million of proceeds used to immediately pay down debt. Now turning to our Saltire acquisition. We are making good progress on securing financing for the proposed transaction.

As we said at the transaction announcement, we expect to fund the cash portion of the transaction through new debt financing together with borrowings under our existing credit facility. We will provide additional details as soon as practical. As a reminder of what we disclosed at the time of the transaction announcement on October 8, total consideration for Saltire consists of approximately $80 million in cash subject to customary adjustments and a fixed 17.4 million shares of DTI common stock, the value of which will fluctuate with our share price until closing. Using the 20-day volume-weighted average price as of October 1, 2026, this represented approximately 5.5x Saltire's run-rate adjusted EBITDA.

Based on management estimates derived from recent monthly performance updates at the announcement date, we expected Saltire to add approximately $50.4 million of run-rate revenue and $22.5 million of adjusted EBITDA, representing an adjusted EBITDA margin of approximately 45%. Importantly, this would increase DTI's adjusted free cash flow by more than 80% on a pro forma basis based on our guidance at the time of the transaction announcement. These figures do not include any synergies. Also, as announced related to leverage, we expected pro forma net debt to trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA of approximately 2.2x at closing.

With the enhanced free cash flow of the combined company, we also expected to reduce net leverage to approximately 1x within 24 months of closing, an improvement of more than 50%. Until we reach that target, debt reduction will be our primary use of free cash flow alongside high-return growth investments consistent with how we have always managed this business. In closing, as it relates to the Saltire acquisition, we expect to file a revised Form S-4 that will reflect improving financial metrics for both Saltire and DTI. So be on the lookout for that filing shortly.

Now turning to our geographic segment mix, our Eastern Hemisphere segment represented approximately 19% of DTI's total revenue in the third quarter compared to approximately 18% in the second quarter. The sequential increase was driven primarily by our new offshore contracts in Europe, which began generating substantial revenue in the third quarter. As outlined when we announced the transaction, Saltire is expected to take that figure to approximately 40% of pro forma revenue. We are confident that the Eastern Hemisphere will play an increasingly meaningful role in our future results.

For now, our Western Hemisphere segment continues to represent the bulk of our standalone business, and we are encouraged by the steady rig count additions we saw in the third quarter. Importantly, both hemispheres grew sequentially in the third quarter, and we expect both to grow again in the fourth quarter, with our Eastern Hemisphere expected to surpass 20% of total company revenue on a year-end run-rate basis. Turning to our outlook, with September providing a supportive run rate heading into the fourth quarter, we continue to expect full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA to be within our previously disclosed guidance ranges of $155 million to $170 million and $35 million to $45 million, respectively.

We expect to finish the year toward the lower end of both ranges, consistent with what we have communicated throughout the year. Separately, we are raising our full-year capital expenditure outlook to $22 million to $23 million to reflect the aforementioned targeted growth investments we made during the second and third quarters. As a result of this change to our capital expenditure outlook and expected lower end of our EBITDA range, we are also revising our full-year 2026 adjusted free cash flow range to $13 million to $22 million. And we expect to be near the low end of this revised range.

As we have discussed on prior calls and disclosed in our earnings materials, we have made targeted growth investments in our ClearPath technology to support new offshore contract awards, which will add approximately $4 million of capital expenditures above our original plan. Excluding the incremental discretionary ClearPath investment, we would have been within our original adjusted free cash flow guidance range. More importantly, these investments are already generating revenue, and we expect them to deliver attractive returns into 2027, which is why we maintain discretion when it comes to strategic investments. That concludes my financial review and outlook section. I will now turn the call back over to Wayne for closing comments.

R. Prejean: Thank you, David. We are entering the final quarter of 2026 with real momentum and at an important moment in DTI's history. The second half improvement we anticipated has begun to materialize. Our offshore investments in Europe are now contributing. And with Saltire, we have taken a transformational step to balance the global platform we have been building since going public, one that leaves us appropriately hedged across the global drilling market. We remain committed to consistent execution, technological innovation and differentiation, and operational excellence, and we will continue to prioritize profitable growth and long-term shareholder value. Before we open the call for questions, I would like to highlight a few key takeaways. The second half improvement is underway.

Revenue and adjusted EBITDA grew sequentially. September was our strongest month of the quarter, and we entered the fourth quarter with a supportive run rate toward our full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA goals. Our targeted offshore investments are nearly complete and already contributing. September was the first month of full run-rate revenue under our new European ClearPath contracts. And we expect these investments to continue generating attractive returns. Together with investments to support rising U.S. land activity, they bring full-year adjusted free cash flow below our original range, a deliberate high-return use of capital to carry our momentum into 2027. Saltire positions DTI for its next chapter.

It takes our Eastern Hemisphere business to approximately 40% of pro forma revenue, leaves us appropriately balanced across the global drilling market, and is expected to be accretive to adjusted EBITDA margin and adjusted free cash flow per share in the first year following closing, before any synergies. Our planned debt financing, together with borrowings under our existing credit facility, are expected to fund the cash consideration, and we expect the combined company's cash generation to provide a clear path to approximately 1x leverage within 24 months of closing. Finally, we are bringing our business together under 1 name.

Our new DTI brand unites every company we have acquired under a single identity and culture, and it gives us a clear framework for welcoming the Saltire team when the transaction closes. On prior calls, I said DTI remains a disciplined consolidator in a fragmented industry and that we would pursue only the opportunities that strengthen our platform and create lasting value for our shareholders. Saltire is exactly that kind of opportunity. We remain very excited about the scale, financial strength, technology offering, and earnings power of the combined company. And we look forward to demonstrating the value of this combination to our customers and our shareholders.

We will remain prudent and disciplined as we work to close the transaction and integrate our teams with an unwavering focus on free cash flow generation and debt reduction. I want to thank every member of the DTI organization for their continued commitment to working in a safe, inspired, and productive manner, with special thanks to our personnel in the Middle East who continue to operate in a challenging environment. To the Saltire team, we look forward to closing this transaction and welcoming you to DTI. Our employees' commitment and dedication have been essential in navigating a constantly evolving energy landscape, and they are central to the success and future growth we are building together.

Together, we are at the core of drilling. With that, we will now take your questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Steve Ferazani with Sidoti & Company.

Unknown Analyst: Good morning. This is Alex on for Steve. Just to start us off, you described September as a supportive run rate into Q4. So, curious if you're expecting the typical year-end slowdown in activity from there, or will elevated WTI prices lessen the slowdown?

R. Prejean: Thanks for that question. It's typically, historically through the shale plays, you've seen some spending compression and people kind of hit the end of their budgets, but that's not the case this year. We're seeing somewhat of an acceleration in activity taking shape in the second half. And there seems to be just steady-as-she-goes kind of activity. So I don't know if we're going to see more acceleration, but I do not believe we're going to see deceleration in the last quarter. We're optimistic about the last quarter into the first and second part of next year.

Unknown Analyst: Great context. Thank you. And then on capital allocation, I think some investors may have thought, given DTI's recent share price, a buyback would have been perhaps more optimal than an acquisition. What would you say to that? What are your thoughts on that?

R. Prejean: So we were in the process of M&A and had to pause our share buyback activities because we were fully into developing this transaction. So we focused on M&A to try to get more scale going into next year. And what we see is an up-cycle, so the limited float and amount of volume that we have, the ability to make an impact with share repurchases was, we believe, very limited. And that is something we can do down the road after we get a little bit larger and get a little bit more float. So that was kind of our decision tree on how we pivoted from our original strategy of buying back shares, albeit limited, to more M&A.

Unknown Analyst: Got it. And yes, so I guess given the solid cash flow you guys are generating, sounds like a buyback is something you might revisit following deleveraging?

R. Prejean: So we're going to focus on deleveraging by having a net debt reduction as we move through the transaction going into next year. But that'll be our priority, is deleveraging. And as far as share repurchases, sometime down the road, we can probably revisit that, depending on how the stock's performing and what our liquidity and float situation is. But we believe the best use of cash today, or capital today, is to fund our existing business and find M&A opportunities while they exist. We still feel like the market is poised for us to take that action, particularly in the Eastern Hemisphere.

Unknown Analyst: Very helpful. Just a couple more. One quick one. How are you thinking about the pricing environment? Are we approaching a point where higher pricing could be on the table or help offset any inflationary pressures?

R. Prejean: So we're seeing some relief of the price compression that existed in prior quarters, considerably, because supply and demand is tightening. And I think the ball is shifting towards increased ability, the ability to hold or increase your commercial terms or improve them. And we're seeing that. I think our customer base is still being disciplined with their capital spending, not going crazy, but they are taking advantage of these improved margins and improved economics due to higher commodity prices, and they're doing more activity. But they're being cautious. So I think it's an improved environment, and hopefully, it'll continue to improve. So we continue to hold firm on our commercial terms and materially create improvement over time.

Unknown Analyst: Thank you. Last one from us. I know it's early. You know, the market's volatile. We just completed the midterms. But could you talk a little bit about how you're preparing DTI for 2027?

R. Prejean: Sure. We believe that the industry, although there's some concerns in the Middle East with the war and the conflict going there, we feel like this strategy we're deploying has us appropriately hedged for wherever the activity might rebound because there will be a supply gap forthcoming as a result of the war premium and transportation and shipping and logistics war premiums. So I think the world is going to pivot around and find where the best barrels can be produced and transported with the least amount of risk and lowest amount of cost. And I think there's going to be a geopolitical shift on energy security in different parts of the world.

And with this new acquisition, we will be appropriately positioned in various markets with the Saltire acquisition to enable us to be positioned to be hedged in all these markets as they ebb and flow. So we think that's a good positioning move for us going forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from Peter Sidoti with Sidoti & Co.

Peter Sidoti: A quick question. You've been very careful about talking about synergies with Saltire on the revenue side and the expense side. I'm more interested, I think, on the revenue side. Is there the ability to cross-market? Is there the ability to expand, use their sales team more efficiently? What's your thought on the revenue side there?

R. Prejean: So, thank you, we believe there are synergies that we can create operationally and commercially as a team, but stronger, we'll be a lot stronger as a company pulled together. As far as cost synergies, we were reluctant to bake too many of those in because the time and effort to go and unpack different facilities and things takes some time, and they don't have a large management team. So it's not like a big reduction of 2 replicated management teams, but the revenue and commercial synergies are what we think is a lot of upside. And with a little market participation and stability, we are highly confident we can execute well on those synergies.

Peter Sidoti: And I'm sorry, will any of the Saltire management be joining the Board of Directors?

R. Prejean: So we're not sure. I think they have the right to have a Board seat, but we're looking at how that might function. So it's undetermined yet, but there is an opportunity for them to be a part of the Board, for sure. And the management team will be staying on, and the owner will continue to be an advisor and a supporter and a participant in the business to make sure we transition it effectively. But the main management team will continue because there's little replication for us in some of the areas we operate.

Peter Sidoti: And forgive my ignorance, but I assume that you've known the management of this company for a long time, long before you began acquisition talks.

Operator: We have reached the end of our question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the floor back over to Mr. Prejean for closing comments.

#3129. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3127. Closing The Enterprise AI Security Gap: From Blind Spots To Stronger Defenses

Vasanth Mudavatu, Senior Principal Software Engineer at a Fortune 50 company, dedicated to the security of generative AI and ML systems.

Enterprise AI security is no longer just about preventing inaccurate answers. It’s about preventing an automated system from using legitimate access to expose confidential information or execute unauthorized actions.

EchoLeak, which was disclosed in June 2025, was a Microsoft 365 Copilot vulnerability that allowed a crafted email to trigger data exfiltration without requiring the victim to click a malicious link. Microsoft assigned it a CVSS severity score of 9.3, while NIST separately rated it 7.5.

Microsoft patched the vulnerability, and no evidence of exploitation in the wild was reported. This was a demonstrated vulnerability rather than a confirmed breach, but it exposed a consequential failure: External content could influence a system operating with access to internal information.

If an AI agent put customer data, revenue or reputation at risk today, could your organization explain what happened and stop it before the damage spread? The answer depends less on reassuring model behavior than on enforceable boundaries.

The framework below connects four activities: assessing six security blind spots, prioritizing findings, implementing controls in phases and verifying that those controls work.

Attackers can automate reconnaissance, credential harvesting and data extraction. Enterprises need to examine both how AI can be attacked and how it can accelerate attacks.

Being aware of the following six blind spots turn that concern into an actionable security assessment:

A downloaded model shouldn’t become a trusted production asset simply because it comes from a familiar repository. Modified weights, backdoor triggers and unsafe model-file deserialization are areas requiring scrutiny.

Recommended controls include verifying artifact signatures and hashes, documenting provenance, scanning inbound files and testing model behavior before deployment. Integrity verification establishes whether an artifact matches an approved baseline; behavioral testing examines whether it performs as expected. Neither replaces the other.

Disabling an agent isn’t necessarily the same as removing its access. Credentials, active tokens and downstream permissions may remain usable.

Agents need distinct identities, least-privilege access and short-lived credentials, and revocation workflows should be tested. Assessment should also consider combined permissions across tools, as individually acceptable capabilities may collectively create an unacceptable access path.

A useful operational test is straightforward: Disable an agent and verify that its downstream actions actually stop.

Inspecting the final response covers only one potential exit point. Sensitive information may also appear in tool-call arguments, logs, traces or data written to vector stores.

Monitor these boundaries, restrict outbound destinations and correlate activity across requests. That correlation matters because information can leave in small fragments rather than one easily detected transfer.

The assessment should follow the complete data journey, not just the conversation visible to the user.

The security boundary includes more than the model. Build workflows, libraries, containers and deployment dependencies also require review.

Scan inbound model artifacts, pin third-party GitHub Actions to specific commit hashes and maintain an AI-specific inventory of model and software dependencies. These measures help teams identify what they deployed and investigate compromised components.

The objective is traceability, knowing which artifacts and dependencies support each production capability.

A compromised agent may use legitimate tools and credentials to interact with connected systems. Shared memory and agent-to-agent communication introduce additional paths through which malicious instructions can propagate.

Organizations should authenticate communication, verify message integrity, inspect memory and implement per-agent quarantine. Additionally, review Model Context Protocol tool metadata for adversarial instructions or unapproved changes.

Trust should be established at each boundary rather than inherited automatically from another agent.

An agent inventory must capture more than a name. Security teams need ownership, approved capabilities, authorization context and a defined retirement process.

Automate discovery, log audits at the action level and decommission workflows that revoke credentials, address retained memory and preserve required audit records. These controls connect governance decisions to what agents do.

A gap analysis becomes useful when it drives priorities. Evaluate risks using likelihood, impact, difficulty of detection and an exposure multiplier for multi-agent environments.

Treat the resulting score as a prioritization aid, not an objective prediction. Organizations should document their assumptions and calibrate escalation thresholds to their own systems and business consequences.

• The missing control and supporting evidence.

• The test that will demonstrate closure.

Don’t consider a control complete merely because a policy or configuration exists. Closure should require evidence that it works.

The roadmap begins with agent discovery, model integrity checks, outbound monitoring, pipeline hardening and kill-switch implementation. Subsequent phases introduce managed identities, behavioral testing, inter-agent authentication, memory inspection and automated response workflows.

This sequencing provides a practical starting point—establish visibility and containment first and then deepen prevention and detection.

The strongest contribution of this framework is its operational focus. It asks teams to connect model provenance, agent permissions, runtime activity and incident response rather than assess each in isolation.

Leadership reporting should emphasize measurable coverage and tested effectiveness. Useful measures include the proportion of agents under governance, model integrity verification coverage, supply chain scanning coverage and decommissioning compliance.

These measures should be considered alongside the evidence used to close individual findings, connecting implementation progress to demonstrated control effectiveness.

For enterprise leaders, the goal isn’t to eliminate every uncertainty before deploying AI. It’s to make that uncertainty manageable with accountable ownership, observable actions and tested intervention paths. Governance sets expectations; operational evidence shows whether the organization can enforce them.​

The completion of the review gives us added confidence in both our in-force business and the new business we are writing. Finally, third-party capital remains a core element of our capital management strategy.

These structures provide an opportunity for third-party investors to participate in the returns of our business while generating incremental fee income over time and enhancing our flexibility to fund growth and return capital to shareholders. In the quarter, I'm very pleased that we showed the continued execution of this strategy with the full deployment of Ruby Re capital. Turning now to the regional results. In the Americas, the results for the quarter were driven by strong investment income, sound underwriting experience and the continued favorable impact of in-force actions executed in prior periods. In EMEA, earnings outperformed our expectations, benefiting from favorable claims experience and higher investment income. We are also encouraged by the momentum we are seeing in the market and in our pipeline. Asia Pacific delivered another strong quarter, driven by the earnings contribution from recent new business and strong investment income.

Leading with biometric expertise, local experience and long-standing client relationships, we closed several flow deals in the region, notably in Hong Kong and Japan. These deals were in our sweet spot, leveraging both sides of the balance sheet and showcase the expertise of our exceptional local teams. Our ability to deploy capital across all our regions and the range of products gives us a significant advantage. Just as important, we remain selective, maintaining discipline in pricing, underwriting and capital deployment. Let me emphasize that our capital deployment into in-force transactions and flow business this year has been focused on exclusive arrangements with attractive risk-adjusted returns, and we are very pleased with the high-quality nature of this business.

Taking a step back, what connects these results to our strategy are our strengths in 4 key areas. First, win-win transactions. We pursue transactions that deliver strong returns for RGA and real benefits for our clients. Our 5 decades of experience, global presence and local market knowledge let us focus where we are best positioned. We focus on both sides of the balance sheet, pairing deep biometric expertise with diversified investment capabilities. Second, scaling our global platform. Demand for risk and capital solutions continue to grow, and our strong balance sheet and global brand make us a trusted counterparty. Third, optimizing our balance sheet.

We do this through in-force management, improved risk-adjusted investment returns and both internal and third-party sources of capital. And finally, disciplined capital stewardship. We balance investing in attractive opportunities with returning capital to shareholders. Here are some examples from this quarter of how we are putting this approach to work around the world. In the U.S., our underwriting capabilities continue to set us apart. Case volumes remained significantly above prior year levels. Our strategic underwriting program accounted for almost half of this quarter's cases and is the largest source of growth in our underwriting products. These programs will further entrench our strategic partnership with the client, including new product development, creating exclusive business that is very durable.

In Asia, our underwriting and product development capabilities supported client wins across the region. In Japan, we supported the launch of a simplified underwriting mortality product or the corporate-owned life market. In Hong Kong, one of our embedded digital underwriting capabilities was highlighted by a client for its role in accelerating medical underwriting decisions, widening consumer access to cover and improving the new business experience. We will continue balancing capital invested in the business with capital we return to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. Over the intermediate term, we continue to target a 20% to 30% payout ratio, but will remain opportunistic. Turning to book value. We extended our long record of growing book value per share. In the quarter, excluding AOCI and B36 effects, our book value per share rose to $178.59, reflecting a compound growth rate of 10.2% since the start of 2021.

To sum up, this was another very good quarter, driven by consistent execution of our strategy. Our business fundamentals remain strong and investment results continue to support our strong returns and earnings growth. New business momentum is healthy with high-quality opportunities that meet our return expectations. We remain disciplined in deploying capital, focusing on transactions and flow business that meet or exceed our return standards and fit within our risk limits. And our strong financial position allows us to invest capital into our business to deliver future earnings power while also returning capital to shareholders. Our priorities are unchanged: deliver attractive, sustainable returns, manage risk well and deploy capital where we see the best long-term value.

As a final note, I'd like to let you know that starting in the fourth quarter, we plan to simplify our reporting into 4 segments: Americas, EMEA, APAC and Corporate, and no longer call out Traditional and Financial Solutions business separately. We view this as another step in our ongoing effort to improve how we communicate with stakeholders, and this change will be consistent with how we manage the business internally. It supports my previous comments on the need to look at Traditional and Financial Solutions better when assessing premium growth. In support of this change, we plan to provide recasted historical financial results in advance of our fourth quarter earnings call. Thank you for your continued interest in RGA.

This concludes our prepared remarks. We would now like to open it up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question will come from Alex Scott with Barclays.

Taylor Scott: I wanted to see if you could give a little more color on some of the work you've done on the in-force actions on capped cohorts? And maybe just a broad update, but also to what degree some of the actions that flowed through this quarter improved go-forward earnings?

Laura Cockrill: Sure. Thanks, Alex. So managing in-force business continues to be part of our ongoing strategy to find incremental ways to improve the value of our book. The impact this quarter was $57 million in total and included actions across the U.S., EMEA and APAC. Consistent with the past, we expect to remain active going forward, though the timing and size of these actions are difficult to predict. In the last several quarters, in-force actions have primarily occurred in uncapped cohorts and resulted in an increase of approximately $10 million to $15 million to the ongoing run rate. And again, these are a key part of our strategy that will continue.

Taylor Scott: Very helpful. Second one on APAC growth. Can you just talk about maybe in some of your bigger geographies, how you're viewing the competitive landscape, where the opportunities are, just how we should think about momentum of the growth in that business over the next year or 2?

Tony Cheng: Happy to take that. APAC continues to be very strong. Our 2 largest markets there are Japan and Hong Kong. As you know, Japan has had strong tailwinds from the recent regulatory changes, which result in considerable opportunity for RGA. And we're incredibly well positioned with our strong local presence, trusted client relationships and world-class expertise on both sides of the balance sheet. In Hong Kong, we continue to really do the product development incredibly well. We're complementing that with more and more electronic underwriting systems that can join up with the product development expertise, the capital management expertise to essentially white label products in partnership with our clients.

It's a strategy that we've had for now over 2 decades and continues to have a long runway going forward.

As it relates to the second part of your question on about $400 million of capital to support that organic growth, I believe that was the question, that was your question, yes. Thanks, Joel.

We can do the capital deployment into in-force transactions as well as organic flow business, notably at returns that meet or exceed our expectations. And we also have positive contributions from our investment portfolio, effective in-force management, balance sheet optimization actions and the return of capital to shareholders, which includes higher share repurchases when they make sense. So we can and do use a combination of those levers to really achieve our targets.

Joel Hurwitz: Okay. And then just shifting gears, with Ruby Re now fully deployed, I want to see if you have any updates on your thinking for future sidecar launches?

Laura Cockrill: Yes, I don't have a comment on our next vehicle at this time other than to reiterate that third-party capital is a priority for us, and we will discuss more when appropriate.

#3124. Georges Niang offers amusing analogy for Jimmy Butler, Heat after Warriors' win

Georges Niang offers amusing analogy for Jimmy Butler, Heat after Warriors' win originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Beating your former team always feels good, even when you're not on the court.

The Warriors stretched their winning streak to six with a 120-100 win over the Miami Heat on Thursday night at Chase Center but a rehabbing wing Jimmy Butler had the most fun on the bench.

After the win, Warriors forward Georges Niang explained why he recognized Butler's energy against his old squad.

"I can't even count the number of teams that I have a spot that wants to stick it to them, so I can understand why Jimmy feels the way that he does," Niang said. "He hasn't really voiced it. Jimmy is probably listening to country music in the weight room right now, screaming. But yeah, I get it. It's like a relationship that ends and do you want to see your ex do better than when she was with you? Not really. I don't think anybody else does."

The Warriors star posted a humorous AI-generated video on Instagram after the game, depicting Steph Curry and former Warrior Klay Thompson in the 1999 movie Blue Streak.

Butler signed with the Heat prior to the 2019-20 season and spent five seasons with the organization before being traded to Golden State during the 2024-25 season in exchange for a package involving Andrew Wiggins.

In his Miami tenure, Butler earned three All-NBA selections and led the Heat to two NBA Finals appearances in 2020 and 2023.

Butler's presence on the Warriors has been similarly impactful. Golden State was below .500 when they initially traded for Butler but won over 67 percent of the games he played in over the past two seasons.

The six-time All-Star is working his way back from a torn ACL suffered in January and is expected to return around the All-Star break.

Despite not being on the court, Butler has made an effort to stay connected with his teammates and provide his support, even hosting a players-only event in San Diego before the season.

"You talk about someone that doesn't have to be as giving as he is, but I texted him the other day, and I was like, 'Hey, how's rehab going? Just checking on you,' " Niang said. "And he was like, 'It's great, you know. Keep playing well. Is there anything I can do for you?' And I looked at my phone, and I was like, 'Am I reading this right?' Like Jimmy Butler's asking, 'Is there anything he can do for me?'

"You talk about selfless people, and he's been completely selfless and giving, even when he's not a part of it, going through the toughest time of his playing career tearing his ACL. He's been phenomenal and great to be around."

Golden State appears to have found its groove after a slow start, but its entire outlook will change once Butler returns to the court.
