#3123. 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow

Startups often move quickly because they have to, making the most of limited resources and adapting as circumstances change. As tech companies scale, added layers of process, approval and hierarchy can gradually slow decision making and erode the flexibility that helped them grow.

The good news is that companies don’t have to abandon the habits that fueled their early success as they expand. Here, Forbes Technology Council members share startup habits established tech companies should preserve—or relearn—to maintain their agility as they grow.

Established tech companies should preserve the startup habit of staying close to the raw customer experience. As organizations scale, dashboards and layers of interpretation can obscure what people actually struggle with. Leaders should keep speaking directly with customers and empower small teams to act quickly on what they learn. Scale should improve execution, not distance companies from users. - Leah Wang, Karpo

The tech market in the AI era is changing super fast—the cycles for product demands, work methods and tools, and customers’ needs and requirements have all become very short. The one thing companies must preserve is agility within the boundaries of their focus. It is easy to get lost and try to achieve everything, only to end up with nothing. Being able to stay agile while knowing the problem your company solves is critical. - Yoav Amitai, Elsight

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Startups are great at prototyping new products and services and moving on quickly from ideas during the research and development phase. As companies scale, this “create fast, test fast, decide fast” capacity is often diminished. One way to keep it alive is to engage early with a customer or partner to confirm requirements or do testing. It puts healthy pressure on the development process while gathering valuable external feedback on pricing, functionality and positioning. - Eva Rudin, Thales Cybersecurity

Preserve the willingness to challenge assumptions. Startups move quickly because they don’t treat “this is how it’s done” as an acceptable answer. As companies scale, process can quietly replace curiosity. The best teams keep questioning their own products, decisions and assumptions, especially when something appears to be working. Scale should give you more resources to challenge the status quo, not more reasons to protect it. - Alissa Knight, Assail, Inc.

Keep saying no to the wrong business. When you are small, you cannot serve everyone, so you get good at turning down the wrong customers and use cases, and that focus is half of why you survive. At scale, every deal looks worth taking, and the muscle for walking away weakens. You must protect it on purpose. The companies that keep rejecting what does not fit stay sharp long after they could afford to lose focus. - Vytautas Savickas, Oxylabs

Solve problems close to where they occur. As organizations scale, issues often get escalated to the most senior person rather than the person best connected to the customer or the detail of the issue. That introduces delays to fixes being made and promotes permission-seeking rather than judgment and accountability. Push authority down and let the people closest to the problem make the call. - Rob Sloan, Zscaler

Knowing when to stop is crucial. Startups have to focus because their resources are limited. The ability in a startup to know exactly what is going on means not only decisions to invest but also decisions to divest are made faster. - Véronique Özkaya, DATAmundi

AI-first thinking is the biggest thing established players need to adopt from the startup realm. New ventures have the luxury of AI being the starting point, not something they need to bolt onto old, outdated processes. That blank slate is a real edge—no legacy systems standing between them and AI-driven gains. So, I’d begin every problem by asking where AI can make the biggest impact and build from there. That mindset will define the future enterprise. - Tarek Nseir, Valliance

Preserve the habit of testing before debating. Startups rarely have enough data to eliminate uncertainty, so they build something small, put it in front of users, and learn. At scale, debate can become a substitute for discovery. Established companies should relearn how to turn unanswered questions into fast, low-risk experiments, using evidence from the market to resolve what meetings cannot. - Melissa King, Paylocity

Let the people closest to a problem try things without asking permission first. In many cases, our team members have made our most impactful suggestions. We discussed it, tried it out and looked at the results together. Nobody wrote a proposal. Give teams a sandbox, clear data and security rules, and a few weeks to test. You’ll learn more than you would from a six-month planning cycle. - Merav Yuravlivker, Data Society

Keep communication lines efficient. The best startups have an uncanny ability to throw unnecessary hierarchy to the wind and flatten communication lines. That’s how startups home in on solutions rather than simply admiring the problem. - James Stanger, CompTIA

Cross-department talk is essential. In a startup, everyone can talk to everyone without wondering about politics and the org chart. You never know where the next good idea will come from—it often comes from an “unexpected part” of the org chart. If Joe from team X is afraid of talking to Mary from team Y just because they don’t have the same boss, the company’s capacity to innovate is severely impacted. - Stephane Donze, AODocs

Startups move fast because they accept higher risk, while large organizations slow down to protect reputation, revenue and investors. As companies grow, they must consciously balance risk appetite to keep innovating. Teams should also keep the startup habit of “relentless iteration”—sharing early “sh***y first drafts,” as referenced by Brené Brown—for fast feedback instead of waiting for polish. - Mandy Andress, Elastic

Ship things that aren’t ready and learn from real users instead of extensive internal reviews. Process exists to prevent mistakes, but it also prevents speed and discovery. Talk directly to users without a layer of research, summaries or account managers in between. - Amy Gu, Dynamsoft

Create rituals early and maintain them throughout your growth. Startup life is hard. One of the things that inspires and preserves team alignment is the rituals created in early startup life that create an identity, a battle cry and a touchstone to the mission. As new employees join the company, these same rituals become part of their orientation, which helps encourage unity. - Amy Brown, Authenticx

Preserve fast, reversible decision making. Let teams run small, bounded tests without routing every choice through layers of approval, then use the results to adjust quickly. Reserve heavyweight reviews for decisions that are costly or difficult to undo—not every experiment. - Nagesh Nama, xLM Continuous Intelligence

Share the full picture with everyone. In a startup, the whole team knows the revenue, the biggest customer problem, and what worries the founders most. As companies grow, that context gets held back at the top, and teams start working on tasks without knowing why they matter. People make better decisions when they know what the company is facing. - Asad Khan, TestMu AI

Preserve the startup habit of a hard work-in-progress limit. Early teams cannot pursue 20 “top priorities,” so starting one thing means stopping another. At scale, portfolios expand faster than capacity, and coordination becomes the bottleneck. Force every new priority to displace an old one. Speed comes as much from limiting concurrency as from moving faster. - Akhilesh Sharma, A3Logics Inc.

Do it by hand before automating it. Startups run a new process manually for a few weeks and learn where it actually breaks. Larger companies jump straight to automation and lock in their guesses. In mature organizations we audit, roughly a third of flows either duplicate another or barely run. A month of manual work first is cheaper than a year of maintaining the wrong automation. - Sergii Grushai, Peeklogic

#3119. One win won’t fix everything, but Phoenix needed this one

The Phoenix Suns' four-game losing streak came to a much-needed end on Thursday night. Maybe it was the defensive intensity. Maybe it was the fact that I started wearing my watch. Maybe it was because their opponent was dealing with its own rash of issues, particularly at the point guard position. Or maybe, and hear me out on this one, it was because Devin Booker was wearing a headband.

Whatever the reason, the relief was both welcomed and desperately needed, especially considering the brand of basketball the Suns had put forth through the first six games of the season.

The standings now say 2-5, but there were some noticeable adjustments in this game. While those changes might not have been directly responsible for the victory, particularly when you consider the opponent, the fact that head coach Jordan Ott was willing to make them carries some weight. Could more adjustments be made? Quite possibly. Baby steps, right? Overall, the team looked considerably more engaged, even if its weak-side defensive rotations still appeared a little out of sync and out of rhythm.

And the stats? On paper, they're certainly impressive. Phoenix shot 17-of-30 from beyond the arc, an outstanding 56.7%, while holding the Magic to 13-of-38 from deep, or 34.2%. Of course, there's also the fact that Phoenix built a 30-point lead at 105-75 before surrendering a 25-10 run that made things considerably more interesting than they needed to be. But you know what? We've had plenty of negative and frustrating things to discuss this season, so we're going to leave that one alone. At least for now.

The hope is that this wasn't simply a game of shooting variance for the Suns and that they can build upon what we witnessed moving forward. I remain cautious about looking at one game's numbers and declaring that Phoenix has turned some sort of corner. Consistency is what ultimately defines success.

Thursday's victory is encouraging, even if it doesn't erase the concerns we've developed over the first seven games. We saw adjustments, better energy, and stretches of basketball that resembled what this team is supposed to be. Now comes the difficult part. Doing it again. And again. Because one good night doesn't establish an identity, but it can provide a foundation for building one.

Of course, if the headband turns out to be the answer, I'm all for it.

For those who are new around here, you might ask yourself, "What? MC? Why?" Somehow, some way, Mariah Carey has become a symbol of how we express our collective frustration. That after a poor team-wide performance, we'd rather watch the vocal stylings of Mariah Carey and acknowledge her greatness rather than the Suns.

#3117. Why Airbnb Stock Popped Today

The home rental platform is "back in growth mode," according to CEO Brian Chesky.

Shares of Airbnb (ABNB +11.67%) leaped more than 11% on Friday after the online lodging marketplace said its pace of expansion was quickening.

Airbnb's revenue climbed 19% year over year to $4.9 billion in the third quarter.

Nights and seats booked on its platform rose 16% to 155 million, driving a 21% rise in gross booking value to $27.7 billion.

"It's rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that's exactly what we're doing," CEO Brian Chesky said. "In Q3, we delivered our fastest revenue growth in more than three years, with acceleration across our business, including our most established markets."

Chesky said Airbnb has redesigned its app to make it easier to find and book a home. "Our growth isn't being driven by any single product or feature," Chesky said. "It's the result of hundreds of improvements we've made across Airbnb over the last several years."

Notably, more people are making their first transaction on Airbnb's platform. First-time booker growth rose 13%. Younger, Gen Z customers were the company's fastest-growing cohort.

All told, Airbnb’s free cash flow soared 29% to $1.4 billion in the third quarter and 35% to $4.9 billion over the trailing 12 months.

This impressive cash generation enabled Airbnb to announce a $12 billion stock buyback program, as it moves to return more capital to shareholders

Healthy global travel demand trends also prompted Airbnb to lift its full-year revenue target. Management now projects a revenue growth rate in the "high teens" with further profit margin expansion.

#3111. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3107. Stephen A. Smith believes Steph Curry's title window still is open for Warriors

Stephen A. Smith believes Steph Curry's title window still is open for Warriors originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Stephen A. Smith is not ready to close Steph Curry's championship window.

On Friday's episode of ESPN's "First Take," Smith made his case for the Warriors a day after they won their sixth straight game, improving to 6-3 after an 0-3 start. Curry is averaging 29.9 points in seven games, and on Thursday he passed Oscar Robertson for 17th on the NBA's career scoring list.

"In life there are transcendent figures. Steph Curry would apply when it comes to that," Smith said. He used one of his favorite phrases, calling Curry "the greatest shooter God has ever created," and said that at nearly 39, Curry is "doing stuff we haven't seen pretty much anybody his age do outside of LeBron and a couple of others."

Smith's argument for the window rests on the 2022 NBA Finals, when the Warriors beat the Boston Celtics.

"I did not think the Warriors were a better team than the Boston Celtics. I did not look at Steph Curry and say, you know what, he can definitively take out both Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum. But that's what he did," Smith added, crediting Curry's shooting, his movement without the ball and his conditioning.

The conditioning is the part Smith kept returning to. He said Curry and LeBron James separate themselves by how they prepare.

"It's a difference between getting ready and staying ready. Those brothers stay ready, they don't use the season to get ready, they come into the season ready because they are taking care of themselves in the offseason," Smith said.

Smith was careful not to overstate it. He did not call the Warriors favorites.

"I'm not trying to tell you that they should be favorites, but I can't dismiss Golden State, not as long as Steph Curry is looking the way that he's looking," Smith said.

The Warriors still have plenty to prove. ESPN's experts projected them to finish 35-47 and land in the play-in, with Jimmy Butler, Moses Moody and Kristaps Porziņģis currently not playing. But Golden State has not lost since the 0-3 start, and Smith is pointing to the player at the center of it.

#3106. Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at Age 65

At 65, most retirees face a permanent reduction in benefits because they haven't reached their full retirement age.

Age 65 is often a pivot point for retirement planning because it's when Medicare eligibility begins. However, for current near-retirees, it's not the finish line for Social Security. The average benefit for people who are 65 is $1,607.27 per month, according to December 2025 data from the Social Security Administration (SSA), the most recent figures available. This number is lower than the $2,088.79 overall average for all retired workers reported by the SSA as of September 2026.

While you're eligible for health coverage at 65, your full retirement age (FRA) is 67 if you were born in 1960 or later. Claiming Social Security at 65 results in a permanent 13.33% reduction in your monthly benefit.

The average benefit varies by gender, with men receiving $1,772.00 vs. women $1,457.40, a gap of about $314.60 per month. This difference generally reflects historical earnings gaps and variations in work history. For most retirees, these monthly payments serve as a foundation for their retirement income but are rarely enough to cover all expenses.

The dollar amounts in this table reflect SSA data as of December 2025. These figures provide a baseline for what people who are currently 65 receive, rather than a projection for those who claim at 65 in the future. Your personal benefit depends entirely on your own earnings history and when you choose to file.

If your full retirement age is 67, claiming at 65 is technically an early filing. The SSA bases your benefit on an average of your wages across your 35 highest-earning years, which are adjusted for inflation and run through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. Filing two years before your FRA prevents you from reaching that full baseline amount.

A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027. That adjustment will add about $58 a month on top of the overall age-65 average listed above. These adjustments are designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation, though they often lag behind the actual rising costs seniors face.

Social Security was designed to replace only 40% of pre-retirement income, a share that's well short of what most retirees need to cover their living costs. This makes it a supplemental source of income rather than a full replacement for a salary. Most retirees must bridge the gap with savings or other income sources.

Balancing your Medicare enrollment at 65 with a Social Security strategy helps ensure you don't lock in a lower monthly check than your long-term budget requires.

Claiming Social Security at 65 could make sense if you have a short life expectancy, you lack personal savings or a job to help you cover your living costs until your FRA, or if you just don't want to wait any longer for your benefits to begin.

But it's worth thinking through all your options before deciding which claiming age is right for you. Every month you delay increases your checks slightly until you qualify for your largest checks at age 70. Waiting until then could lead to a much larger lifetime benefit if you live into your mid-80s or beyond.

If you do decide to wait until you qualify for larger checks, keep in mind you'll have to pay for your Medicare Part B premiums out of your own pocket for the time being. Once you apply for Social Security, the government will start taking these premiums out of your benefits, so you don't have to pay a separate bill.

For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide.

Klay Thompson gave a 'little' thought to returning to Warriors in offseason originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Returning home to play against your former team usually is a bittersweet moment, and Thursday night was no different for Klay Thompson.

The Warriors took down the Miami Heat 120- 100, but it was Thompson coming back to Chase Center that made the matchup even more meaningful.

After the game, Thompson was asked if he thought about signing with the Warriors this offseason.

"A little bit," Thompson said. "And I'm so grateful for the support I have in the region. Just going to breakfast this morning and seeing familiar faces, it was awesome. And I'm very, very grateful for the fandom. It really inspires me to keep going."

Steph Curry didn't hesitate to have some fun with Thompson during the game either, posing for a picture during the action.

Thompson, of course, is a Bay Area legend who spent 11 seasons with Golden State and was a part of four title-winning rosters.

Curry's "Splash Brother," Thompson is widely considered among the greatest shooters of all time, hitting 41.3 percent of his 3-pointers during his Warriors tenure and making five All-Star teams.

Thompson's returned from ACL and Achilles injuries to help Golden State win the 2022 NBA Finals but ultimately was traded to the Dallas Mavericks in a six-team deal after the 2023-24 season.

The Mavs agreed to a contract buyout for Thompson, who eventually signed a two-year deal with the Miami Heat, where he's averaging 13.8 points per game on 41.3 percent shooting from distance in nine games.

Andrew Wiggins, who was traded from Golden State to the Heat in the Jimmy Butler exchange, also had a homecoming in San Francisco.

In typical Thompson fashion, he couldn't leave without shouting out a local Oakland restaurant he visited during his stay.

"I don't want to blow up the local spot, but it's called Egg Shop in Montclair," Thompson said. "Classic. The best waffle on the West Coast."

Thompson might face off against the Warriors a few more times, but the significance of those matchups will always remain high.

Our crude oil business, with a more durable and predictable cash flow stream post-NGL sale, really positions us well for a variety of macro market conditions. As we show on Slide 9, we continue to execute our efficient growth strategy. The three announcements this quarter again demonstrate the multiple levers that we have to drive growth, including organic investments, inorganic bolt-on M&A and balance sheet optimization. We remain committed to capital discipline, maintaining a stable and flexible balance sheet and continuing to return cash to unitholders. With that, I'll turn the call back to Blake to lead us into Q&A.

Blake Fernandez: Thanks, Willie. [Operator Instructions] With that, Marvin, we're ready for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Manav Gupta of UBS.

Manav Gupta: I wanted to ask you a little bit more on the 270,000-acre Midland dedication. As you ramp towards the 225 target of volumes, how should we think about the earnings uplift that this opportunity provides?

Jeremy Goebel: Manav, this is Jeremy Goebel. We're going to give you some more guidance on that in February. But think of that as existing production. So it's not a ramp to production. It's just a matter of timing for connection. So that contribution will likely be late 2027, early 2028, when the connection is done, but we'll give you more guidance on capital and timing next year. But we're excited about the opportunity to partner with a top-tier producer and look forward to providing those services over a long period of time and expanding our Midland footprint.

Manav Gupta: Perfect, sir. The second question I wanted to ask you, I mean, we understand there's crude volatility, but what are you hearing from the producers generally in the Permian? Do they expect to continue to grow production? We know the big guys, Exxons of the world, definitely want to grow. And what we are trying to solve from our side is, when does the Permian egress start to get tightened again? Is it late 2028? Is it 2029? When do you see to the point where these existing Permian pipes, even with the Cactus III expansion, are like almost 90% full?

Jeremy Goebel: Got it. Manav, that is a great question. What I would say is the volatility you experience every day in waking up and seeing a headline and crude move $8 to $10, they're experiencing the same. So from a planning perspective, I think you can expect 200,000 to 300,000 barrels a day of growth for the foreseeable future based on the activity you see today. You've added 30 rigs this year. You've gotten more efficient this year. You're just starting to add completion crews. So the 200,000 barrels a day of growth that we've seen through this year, we would expect that to continue. The pipes to the coast are close to 90% full now.

I think what you would see is the total basin will grow 200,000 to 300,000 barrels a day. The basin will clear for several more years. But I think your timing is appropriate for additional brownfield expansions in that '28 to '29 time period to see additional capacity come to market. So there's no need for a greenfield large pipeline at this time based on the ratable growth that we see and the smaller number of players driving growth, it seems like it's going to be orderly and that growth will happen over that time period. But your -- sometime in 2028 to early 2029, I think you'll see additional brownfield expansions.

But by and large, I think rates are constructive, dialogue is constructive with counterparties. We continue to re-contract the pipes that we have now and look forward to continue growing the business.

Willie Chiang: Manav, this is Willie. I just wanted to add one thing. Your question is spot on. It's very difficult to predict the exact timing of it because just of the global volatility. But as I sit back and we think about what's going on in the world, global demand has remained fairly resilient. There's a lot of noise in the supply chains. If you look at where the resources are and where the demand centers are for the world, it all points to North America really being an incremental producer. So the capacity that we've got out of the Permian is meaningful, and we've got the ability to expand Cactus III.

And as we've said before, we're going to match that expansion capacity to what the demand is to get to the water, but I think it really sets up for a strong macro environment going forward. Trying to analyze and pick exactly when it's going to happen, is very, very difficult, but we'll be patient, and we stand ready to be able to meet the needs.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Julien Dumoulin-Smith of Jefferies.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Can you hear me okay?

Willie Chiang: We can hear you loud and clear.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Excellent. Look, a couple of things, maybe just zeroing in and nitpicking, just on the quarter itself, 4Q was implied here, how do you think a little bit about just implying down? Is there any specific drag here on the -- like forthcoming quarter? And then thinking a little bit more strategically to the last question here, what do you think the timing of evaluating that Cactus III expansion is vis-a-vis, you talk about that '28 timeline for a brownfield expansion? When do you start moving on that, and we're getting a little bit more detail on -- I presume that's the brownfield expansion you're getting at here.

Al Swanson: Julien, this is Al. I'll do the first part. Implied, obviously, in our guidance is about $700 million for the fourth quarter, down about $10 million from the third quarter. The real change is the market opportunities that we've experienced in 2Q and 3Q that's really driving the $10 million lower number plus the inclusion of Silver Creek for the fourth quarter. If you recall, our view is Silver Creek's an asset that's going to grow meaningfully over the next few years. 4Q included in our forecast is without the benefit of some of that growth, some transition services costs, integration costs, et cetera, and without the synergies.

So those two basically offset the step down in some of the market opportunities that we captured kind of as the war started for second quarter and third quarter.

Jeremy Goebel: Julien, for your second part, the shorter answer is we're continually evaluating them. Just as you saw this summer, we added 75,000 barrels a day. We're looking at incremental ability to add as the market demands. And so I think you'll see us ramp over that time period. There are segments of pipe we have to build to access additional markets. So it's not -- I don't know that you'll see one grand announcement, just a series of announcements to get the pipeline ready. And then as contracts and rates are appropriate, we'll add the additional capacity. So it's not -- I don't think it's going to be one step change another 300,000 barrels a day.

I think you're going to see a series of expansions that go based on market demand.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Got it. Excellent. And you picked up what I was trying to put down on that 4Q and on the Silver Creek piece and the contribution. But maybe talking about the PRB more broadly here. I mean obviously, you're acquiring here. How do you think about diversification in that geography here, post midterms, et cetera? Anything that you'd flag in terms of just this is more strategic repositioning and adding on the margin maybe, but any points to complement your latest position there?

Jeremy Goebel: Thanks, Julien. We're very excited about the Silver Spur asset. I think the Powder River Basin is one that's been candidly evaluated for over some time period, and they're just starting to figure it out. So I think it's going to ramp into 2028. We have to continue to build out the system now through 2027, but there's a series of MVCs. There's 915,000 of acreage dedications. There's 4 to 5 producers that are already telling us that the wells are better and they cost less, and they're looking to potentially add a rig into the system. So we can see the Powder River Basin as the next growth wedge in the Rockies.

And that positions well for us not only on the Silver Spur asset from a gathering standpoint, but it also from a pull-through benefit to our pipelines and terminals in the Guernsey area headed south through to Cushing. So it's an integrated play for us. It's a growth on a stand-alone basis but also an integrated play. So we're excited about the opportunity to work with some of our large producers that are also there.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jeremy Tonet of JPMorgan Securities.

Francina Kolluri: This is Francina on for Jeremy. Just wanted to zoom in a bit more on that kind of Silver Creek contribution point in 4Q. How would you kind of maybe frame or size run rate contributions and then the kinds of projects that might be incremental to kind of reach that run rate in terms of thinking about capital needs to really capture that low-hanging fruit?

Jeremy Goebel: So think of the fourth quarter as transition. There's a transition services agreement, which has some additional costs that will go away. So typically, it takes us a few months to shed costs, so we'll go into next year. It will be inside that cost of capital very quickly at our long-term run rate. So we have to -- from a -- there's an investment that needs to be made between now and the end of 2027. So it will really catch its legs in the 2028 and forward. Like I said, a series of MVCs and acreage dedications, but we'll be shedding costs, adding market opportunities, doing some pull-through benefits on the asset through 2027.

So that will be the transition year, and it will really -- 2028 forward will be a great thing for the asset. But it's inside of 10x when we start, and it compresses well inside of our cost of capital outside of that. So it's not -- from an EBITDA standpoint, you can think of this as roughly 9 to 10x in the first 12 months. And after that, it gets well inside of that.

Francina Kolluri: That's very helpful. And then I just wanted to maybe talk more broadly about the M&A landscape. A lot of your peers have taken on packages this year. And so is there anything that's remaining, anything that looks interesting at this point?

Willie Chiang: Yes. I'll go ahead and take that one. This is Willie. Clearly, we've done a lot of bolt-on M&A or bolt-on acquisitions. So I'll speak about bolt-ons and then broader activities. We've actually been the ones that have been executing on a lot of these bolt-ons. We look at everything. I would tell you that I think the bolt-on opportunities are probably a little less than what the pace we've gone in the past. I think we've done 15 of these over the last 3, 4 years. So it's been very critical to our piece. A broader M&A is obviously an opportunity. But right now, we focus on our crude business. We've got -- anything we do focuses on returns.

So if we think about assets that we might bring in or things we may do, it's really focused around capital discipline and returns. And it's with that lens that we think about broader M&A, but look at everything, well positioned. Opportunities come our way, we'll be able to hopefully capture them.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of AJ O'Donnell of TPH Research.

Andrew John O'Donnell: I was just hoping if I could just sneak in one more question about the new Midland dedication. Just wondering, as far as the makeup of the volumes, are there any MVC components that are built into that? And then if you could talk about any of the volumes that are currently producing because I thought you said it was existing production. Are any of those volumes currently moving on your intra-basin or long-haul systems?

Jeremy Goebel: AJ, this is Jeremy. What I would say is these are acreage dedications consistent with the rest of the system on the contract structure. The vast majority of this would be going into existing systems just into the Midland complex to say whether a specific barrel's flowing through us. They're not providing any meaningful contribution to us today. And so this is just something that is a new contract from the gathering system for us.

Andrew John O'Donnell: Okay. Maybe just going back to the Permian macro. If we start to see this kind of compounding multiple hundred thousands of barrels of growth over the next few years, where do you see the most upside? Or what part of your system do you get most excited about? Is it like the incremental C3 expansions that you can do or market-based opportunities on your marketing affiliate? Or is the highest torque, maybe higher utilization on your northbound assets out of the Permian?

Jeremy Goebel: AJ, it's a great question. I'd say it's a bit of all of the above because filling the pipes is one thing. What we really get excited about is longer term, the additional improvements that the industry makes on recoveries, sustaining this for long periods of time, which is what we hear over and over again from our producer customers. The excitement around the surfactants, the excitement around the different completion techniques, the investments Exxon, Chevron, and the other integrators are made to extending the tail, that's what really gets us excited is that the long-term recoveries.

There's a lot of gas and a lot of NGLs, and there's a lot of excitement, but that's going to make those commodities worth a lot less. These still are going to be oil reservoirs driven by oil. So there's a real investment being made to continue to drive additional recovery. So on the oil side, flattening out the curve, having less capital to go chase this, big free cash flow generation and a stable balance and -- on the margin rates going out on the long-haul business is a plus, but the gathering business should be better. The long-haul business should be better, market-based opportunities around it.

So it's just an integrated platform that we have to serve our customers, and we look forward to expanding with them.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of John McKay of Goldman Sachs.

John Mackay: I'll go back to the Midland dedication, congrats on that. I just want to make sure we're thinking about it correctly. I know we'll get color later on kind of associated EBITDA and any associated spend. But given this is production that's already flowing elsewhere, I mean, is there an acquisition opportunity here for you guys over time on kind of whatever this production is touching right now?

Jeremy Goebel: John, I'd say at this point, that's inappropriate for us to talk about. But from our standpoint, we look forward to executing under the contract that we have today.

John Mackay: All right. Fair enough. And -- sorry go ahead. Please go ahead.

Willie Chiang: I'm sorry. John, this is Willie. I mean as I think about it at a high level, right, our whole business is integrated. So we've got gathering, intra-basin, long haul. So the thought of getting another 900,000 dedicated acres into the system, this is just what we do.

John Mackay: No, absolutely. That makes sense. Maybe I...

Willie Chiang: I'm sorry. I was quoting -- I misquoted the -- it's 270,000 acres here versus the 900 (sic) [ 900,000 ] was up in Silver in the Powder River. My apologies on that.

John Mackay: Absolutely. And maybe just on that point, you've probably increased the size of the dedicated acreage on the JV by looks like 30% since you kind of put it together about 5 years ago. I think we're just past that 5-year anniversary. Can you take this opportunity to give us your view on kind of the longer-term strategic plan here? Is there an opportunity to kind of buy in the other piece at some point? Is this going to be a kind of vehicle you can kind of continue to grow in? Maybe just give us an update now that we're kind of 5 years past the launch of it.

Jeremy Goebel: Sure. We've had a great partnership with Stonepeak and the Oryx team, and we'll continue to have a great partnership with them. That's their decision on when they decide to get out. But we've proven with them that we can grow, like you said, 30% growth over 5 years is really a 50% growth from where you started like when you think about it. So it's been a great run. It will continue to be a great run. We're happy for them to grow with us. But just like everything else, we've bought a lot of our partnerships in when that's the right time if that works, great. If they want to stay outstanding, great.

If a new partner comes in, we're prepared to work in any scenario. And we continue to grow as we've proven with them as a partner, we can grow with them or if the opportunity comes, we could do that. So I think there's no obligation to do it. There's an opportunity to do it, but there's no different than the opportunity to buy in other partners that we've had across our system.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Praneeth Satish of Wells Fargo.

Praneeth Satish: So I know it's still early, but maybe you can help us think through some of the puts and takes for 2027 EBITDA. I know you've got a few tailwinds here, $50 million cost synergies or cost efficiencies in the full year, Silver Creek, Cactus III, probably going to see volume growth on the oil side with the flush volumes coming in. So you put that all together, it does seem like you could see some reasonable growth in '27. So maybe what are some of the key headwinds that are kind of offsetting factors that we should think about when modeling '27 growth?

Al Swanson: Hi, this is Al. Yes, I mean, we've articulated kind of the four things, and I think you answered a meaningful part of our -- of the question. Clearly, PLA, we came in this year pretty highly hedged in the low 60s, we'll probably be in the low- to mid-60s by the time we exit with realized prices this year. Clearly, it's setting up for meaningful improvement there, $10 a barrel is a little over $40 million. So that's a definite tailwind. Clearly, the production growth, the $200,000 a day, that 1,000 (sic) [ 100,000 ] barrels a day that Jeremy mentioned, a lot of that came late.

We expect that to benefit '27 in addition to the excess rigs and the '27 growth itself. So we see the Permian volumes as a benefit. Clearly, the investment capital, whether it's our true investment expansion capital like the recent Cactus expansion, in addition, the Silver Creek acquisition as well. Those benefits will come to '27. And then the additional efficiency gains that we've talked about, the incremental $50 million, probably the one caveat or "headwind" we would point to, if you're taking that the last three quarters of this year, the crude is right around $700 million a quarter.

If you were just taking that, annualizing it and then putting all this growth on it, clearly, we've had some market benefits in those numbers. So we would encourage you to maybe dial in a little bit of taking out some of those market opportunities. Maybe we'll see the opportunity to get those in '27, but it wouldn't be -- we wouldn't come into the year expecting to see a repeat of some of that opportunities.

Praneeth Satish: Got you. No, that's helpful. And then there are several proposed Western Canadian egress projects that could bring more barrels into the Mid-Continent. I think at least one project that would go directly into Cushing. And I don't think they're expanding capacity from Cushing down. So I guess as you look across your asset footprint, and I don't know whether it's Capline or other systems, do you see any opportunities to participate or capture that incremental flow?

Jeremy Goebel: Praneeth, that's a great question. And certainly, any of the crude projects we're looking to see if we can benefit, complement, participate, so we'll keep you posted along the way, but we're constantly looking at opportunities to see if we can either partner with good projects, participate, create new projects. So we'll have more updates in the next 6 months if any of that comes to fruition. But certainly, things that complement us, we're actively looking at on the organic side as well as the acquisition side.

Operator: I'm showing no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn it back to Willie Chiang, Chairman and CEO, for closing remarks.

Willie Chiang: Great. Well, listen, thanks for your ongoing support questions, and we look forward to seeing you on the road soon. Have a safe day. Thanks.

#3100. Stock Market Today, Nov. 6: Micron Technology Jumps as Chip Stocks Rebound From Thursday's Rout

Memory chip demand and bargain hunting lifted the stock today, Nov. 6, 2026, as traders looked past the prior day's sharp sell-off.

Micron Technology (MU +5.12%), a memory chips and storage solutions provider, closed at $690.00, up 5.12%. Shares surged as chip stocks bounced back from Thursday's rout, and investors are watching AI memory demand and the next earnings report.

Trading volume reached 44.5 million shares, coming in about 59% above its three-month average of 28.0 million shares.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) rose 0.31% to 7,377, and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.09%) climbed 1.09% to 24,579. Among semiconductor memory and storage solutions peers, Western Digital (WDC -1.44%) closed at $263.78, down 1.44%, while Seagate Technology Holdings (STX -1.19%) finished at $460.99, down 1.19%.

On Friday, Nov. 6, Micron Technology joined a broad semiconductor rebound after Thursday's rout, as investors realized shares were oversold yesterday. Micron, in particular, looks cheap. Its stock's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 3.8 is at a low point over the past year, and far below Seagate's 12.4, for example.

Wall Street has been hesitant to jump into Micron shares because the memory chip industry tends to follow a cyclical pattern. After memory became scarce this year due to the artificial intelligence boom, and prices soared, Micron announced efforts to expand supply. This tends to eventually lead to an industry downturn as the memory shortage abates and prices drop.

However, the AI sector is expanding around the world, resulting in data center buildouts that require memory for years to come. Micron's latest guidance points to tighter memory and storage supply-demand conditions extending into fiscal 2027 and 2028, which remains a key backdrop for the stock.

The AI infrastructure explosion seemed threatened by this week's U.S. midterm election, when the Democratic Party gained control of Congress. Investors were concerned that incoming Democratic leadership might drive tighter AI regulations and pause data center construction projects, leading to yesterday's sell-off.

Those fears were tempered by Micron's bargain valuation, and the company's strong success to date. On September 30, Micron reported record fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results, and that update brought the market's focus back on strong memory pricing and demand.

Robert Izquierdo has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Western Digital. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3093. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#3085. Sixers look to keep rolling for sixth-straight win vs. Cavaliers

The Sixers just keep on rolling. After a 112-106 win on Wednesday against the Pistons, they're sitting comfortably at the top of the Eastern Conference with an 8-1 record.

Next up on Friday, the Sixers are continuing on the road with their second matchup against the Cavaliers, in what's also their next NBA Cup game.

There's another new name added to the injury report, too. And in typical fashion for this season, it's a center: Adem Bona is now listed as doubtful with a cervical spine sprain. Jarrett Allen is questionable for the Cavs with a right knee contusion.

So far, the Cavs haven't gotten off to the best start this season. They're sitting at 4-4 and with this initial small sample we have, rank a dead average 15th in net rating at +1.9, largely thanks to their ninth-ranked offense. It's defense that's hurting them most, where they rank only 21st.

The Sixers' dramatic 29-point comeback to beat the Cavs last month was a good indicator of how dangerous these Sixers can be when their stars click. Tyrese Maxey was electric last time. He finished with a team-high 32 points, and along with Jaylen Brown, the two stars both scored 17 points each in the second half to help power the comeback.

If Maxey can have his way again vs. Donovan Mitchell and James Harden in the Cavs' backcourt (as he has against every opponent this season, really), it wouldn't be surprising to see Maxey lead the Sixers' offense yet again with another high-scoring night.

Even after his first quieter night of the season on Wednesday, shooting only 5-of-16 against the Pistons, Maxey is still making his average of 28.0 points on a 60.7 true shooting percentage look easy.

Mitchell remains the biggest threat for the Sixers to handle. He dropped 32 points on 11-of-19 shooting last time to lead the Cavs, and is averaging 21.9 points with a 59.9 true shooting percentage for the season so far. As tenacious as both Maxey and VJ Edgecombe have been on defense, and as good as Joel Embiid has been protecting the paint, Mitchell is always a handful with his ability as a driver and high-volume three-point creator. How the Sixers cover Mitchell on Friday and limit his space in pick-and-rolls will be key.

Rebounding will be another crucial part of this game. The towering duo of Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen isn't exactly the ideal matchup for the Sixers and their depleted big man rotation. However, Philly did at least make a huge jump from ranking in the bottom half of the league in defensive rebound percentage earlier this week to ninth after beating the Pistons. Of course, that shows you just how much a single game and tiny samples change things this early in the season. But it was still a stronger effort from the Sixers on Wednesday, led by Embiid stepping up with 15 rebounds and LeBron James grabbing 10 of his own.

It'll be interesting to see if the Sixers can build on that. Keeping Mobley and Allen (if he's active) in check, being alert with boxouts, and fighting as much as possible on the glass will be important in maintaining an edge in this one. This is especially true with Bona doubtful. Despite his struggles this year, his likely absence still leaves the Sixers with even less size. We could well see Jabari Walker get increased minutes now, who will be in for a challenge at 6-foot-7 against the Cavs' size, but has played well since preseason.

The Cavs' bigs haven't historically been able to slow Embiid down much either, and last time was no different.

The big fella scored 24 points, including 15 in the second half with some big buckets late to help secure the win. It'll be fun to see how Embiid looks again on Friday.

Jaylen Brown was efficient against the Cavs before too, and he's in fine form after putting together his best performance as a Sixer yet on Wednesday. He shot 11-of-19 overall for his first 30-point game on the team. Brown showed off with a balanced mix of buckets, scoring with strong drives, smooth mid-range pull-ups, and a 3-of-5 mark from three. Pair that with his strong defense and work to help contain Cade Cunningham, and Brown was excellent.

A late clutch block on a Cade three-point attempt was crucial in sealing the victory as well.

If Brown plays like this again on Friday, and Edgecombe and Maxey continue to excel as they have defensively, the Sixers' perimeter stars look ready to give the Cavs a hard time.

As our Paul Hudrick put it after this week's win against Detroit, this team feels real. Sure, it's early days and there are things to work on, like the backup center situation and the offense only ranking 20th for now. But from the defense and the way they're closing out games, to the sheer talent and amount of fun they're having, this group does feel special.

And as LeBron has said himself, the guys on this team simply enjoy being around each other. The value of that can't be overlooked either.

Let's see if they can keep the good vibes going in Cleveland.

When: Friday, November 6, 7:30 p.m. ETWhere: Rocket Arena, Cleveland, OHWatch: NBCSP/PCK-PHI, Prime VideoRadio: 97.5 The FanaticFollow:@LibertyBallers

#3083. Federal Reserve Board requests public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 2:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.
